Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on.

Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4.

The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying.

Now for the good.

The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look.

This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

We've used this primarily during the lockdown. During the summer, we were able to bust this out for at-home theater. It's not a bad projector by the cost alone, but it's not good enough. This is my first personal projector, and my experience comes from working much more expensive projectors at work.
The projector comes with a storing case, flimsy tripod, remote, and cables. The power cable is very short. If you're using this outside, be prepared to use an extension cable, even if you have an outdoor outlet near. The remote is fine, but most controls can be accessed on the projector. The tripod is very unstable. Even though it's metal, it feels very brittle and I never trust the tripod alone. With a bump, the project can move quite a bit. I therefore use a couple of books for stability.

The projector's zoom features are nonexistent; to create a smaller or bigger picture, you need to manually move the device. Not too bad, but there's a lot of fiddling around. The focus is okay; it doesn't have wide range, but we usually can find a sweet spot pretty quickly. So far we've had success connecting a Chromecast and phones, and therefore are able to watch anything that streams. The picture quality is pretty good, and seems to be right around 1080p. We've never had trouble watching anything or felt that something from the picture was out of focus. Colors seem to be adequate. There are also speakers on this thing, but, as expected, they're not very loud. Thankfully there's a 3.5mm audio jack, which we've used for external speakers.

Good sound quality but not the best for noise cancellation. It is inconvenient they are not foldable and, considering so, they should at least come with a case. Fit feels snug and they have not fallen off on accident. Bluetooth range is very good, I have been able to walk 3 floors down in my house and did not lose connection.

The headphones themselves are comfortable and easily adjustable, the range is nice, and the sound quality is great, but the controls themselves are frustrating. The pairing says that you hold until the light flashes blue then red, and I did this. But what happened to me is I held it and it flashed blue once then it would flash red repeatedly. The manual said nothing about repeated red flashing so I assumed it was in pairing mode and I was confused as to why it wouldn't appear on my phone. After a while, I realized that if I held the pairing button longer after it started flashing red then it would flash blue and red alternately and then I could pair. I still have no clue what the red flashing means. Also, the way the skip/volume is set up is weird and temperamental. You hold the button to change the volume and press once to skip or go to the previous song (depending on which volume buttons you press), but sometimes after letting go from holding the volume button the song will change anyway. I think it would be more efficient to switch to press to change volume and hold to change song to prevent accidental switches. I have yet to try a phone call but if the volume/song switch buttons weren't so annoying this would be a great product.

I'm a burgeoning audiophile and I'm always eager to try new cans to add to my listening experience. A while back, say 2007 or so, I jumped into the deeper waters and decided to upgrade my stock Apple ear buds (why I didn't sooner is beyond me). I haven't looked back since, and continue to look forward this very day.

But do these headphones do my ears and music justice?

Right now my arsenal consists of some Sound Blasters I use for my computer and my trusty ol' Sennheisers which I've had since 2007 (the selfsame headphones with which I used to help me jump from Apple), along with Monoprice ear buds I keep at work. I'm not the most professional audiophile, but I sure as heck can tell some differences in quality, especially if the sound source is in FLAC.
Unfortunately, I'm not the most ecstatic about SMS Audio's STREET by 50, especially at the higher premium for Star Wars branding.

I've always been wary of celebrity-endorsed products; never trying Beats, I've been bombarded by them on the streets of Chicago by the candy-colored headbands on people's heads. I've always wondered about their integrity, until a fellow flesh-and-blood audiophile renounced them after she had used her ATH -M50s for some time. I took her word for it and never considered using Beats.
But me, being the Star Wars fanatic, had to try the SMS Audio. When they arrived I admit I was impressed by the fancy packaging. For $200, the headphones arrived looking like it.
They came in a slipcased box that was a little difficult to remove as the vacuum-sealed enclosure proved a tough fit, but they open up sweetly after that.

There are some nice manuals that come with, along with some neat little Star Wars stickers and papers. There's even a cleaning cloth and nice soft zippered case. The headphones came folded inside the case.
When I opened 'em up and took out the included removable cable and tried them on, I was a bit dumbfounded and how uncomfortable they felt around my head with such soft ear pads. I'm not sure if I need to break them in longer, but I've been using them steadily for a month and so far I haven't noticed a difference. My ears ache after just 20 minutes.

The sound was very disappointing at first, though I admit it did warm up (or down?) after a few weeks. But are they a large improvement over my $30 Sennheisers? A little, but not considerable. I can hear more background noise--that is, in the music--but there's not much balance as I have to turn up the volume to notice any huge improvement. There's a bit more bass than I'd like, but not enough to drown my ears in it.

I like the fact that the cable is detachable, but the ones they included feel a bit cheap and they tangle easily. I HATE the fact that they have the buttons, something which I've always hated since the iPhone came standard with them. But that they are removable altogether makes up for the buttons, as I'm able to change them out with custom, and higher quality, gold-plated cables.

The colors are fantastic; honestly, they were the reason I was drawn to them, but they look metallic in the press shots whereas, when you get them, the material is actually plastic, forcing the colors to be a lot lighter, more matte, and cheaper in feel. I'm all for matte, but I had hoped the headphone band was metallic; alas, it's plastic.

So that's my take on the cans. Take them or leave them. They're nice headphones, and I've gotten plenty of complements on them both from friends and at work, but at the steep price tag I can't recommend them, especially when you can get far superior headphones for much less (like the revered Audio-Technicas).
I have these speakers attached to my computer so that I can listen to music while I work.  They are compact and light weight, but the sound they put out is just average.

This is my second tablet but by far, my least favorite. The sound quality is terrible, you are forced to use ear buds and even the case is a total pain as it collapses constantly.  I truly hate it. I also do not have my antenna on my jeep since my last FM transmitter worked better with my antenna off)

I've been a Clarion fan for over 20years and have used their latest products in each of my vehicles and even my boat throughout the years. First off, I am not an audiophile. This is a review from a simple person who wanted music at work.

I am a Rural Carrier for the United Stated Postal Service. I deliver mail in an LLV truck and these vehicles are basically mobile tin cans. Every panel rattles, making for quite an unpleasant environment, audio wise. I tried playing music directly off my phone, but alas my speakerphone is only so loud and is constantly drowned out by the LLV.

So, I researched Bluetooth speakers and, based on the reviews and popularity, recently purchased two:
-[[ASIN:B016XTADG2 Anker SoundCore Bluetooth Speaker with 24-Hour Playtime, 66-Foot Bluetooth Range & Built-in Mic, Dual-Driver Portable Wireless Speaker with Low Harmonic Distortion and Superior Sound - Black]]
-[[ASIN:B01LZV6TYQ OontZ Angle 3 PLUS Splashproof Bluetooth Speaker - Designed & Engineered by Cambridge SoundWorks for Richer Bass, HD Sound, and 30-Hour Playtime, 10W+ Power, Water Resistant, Portable Wireless Speaker]]

The Anker SoundCore is being returned while I am keeping the OontZ Angle 3 Plus and here is why.

I tested both speakers in my home at first. My very first impression, out of the box:
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - was nice to touch and just felt solid and very well built.
Anker SoundCore - just felt like a simple lightweight brick. It really didn't give the impression of longevity or durability.

The set-up guides were quite different from each other.
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - Extremely easy to read, follow and understand (remember, I am not a music nut lol. This was my first time ever using a Bluetooth speaker and was in completely uncharted territory.) It was all in English, and only English and the diagrams were detailed and made the entire set-up process seamless and carefree.
Anker SoundCore - This guide was very hard to follow. It is printed in darn near every language, in tiny print and the diagrams were quite small as well. I ultimately did get the speaker paired with my phone and figured out what buttons did what, but it took nearly 15 minutes to do so.

Bluetooth Pairing
With both speakers and my phone lined up on a table (well within the proximity specified in each set-up guide), both speakers paired, however:
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - MUCH faster in pairing (mere seconds!).
Anker SoundCore - took nearly two minutes to complete the pairing process.

Pause/Play Button
Since I dismount to deliver packages to a customer's door routinely on my route, I really need to have a simply way to pause my music. I really like how both speakers offer this function on directly on the units, saving me from having to handle my phone.
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - I barely press the Play/Pause button and the speaker immediately reacts. There is NO hesitation.
Anker SoundCore - I press the Play/Pause button and there is a delay of about 5 seconds.. just long enough to make me think I didn't press hard enough and reach to do it again only for the speaker to finally react.

Volume/Overall Playback Quality
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - Wow. Just wow. It is truly unbelievable to hear such full sound, and bass(!), coming from such a small unit. I found myself perfectly pleased with the output without ever reaching max volume on the speaker itself. So I am looking forward to how well it will work in my LLV during my first road test. As for now, I am thoroughly impressed!
Anker SoundCore - I maxed out the volume on my phone and the speaker and was just not impressed. If I could guess, I'd say the max output this speaker achieved was only about 25% more than my speakerphone alone (while the OontZ Angle 3 Plus blew it out of the water with close to double, if not more, output than my speakerphone alone).
I also noted some kind of distortion or interference type background sound with the Anker SoundCore at mid volume and above.

Speakerphone/Mic
I was able to answer an incoming phone call on both units as described in each set-up guide. The quality of in-call sound on each speaker differed:
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - My husband's (the caller) voice was crisp and clear, as if he was sitting talking right next to me. There was no distortion or feedback out of the speaker. Husband reported nothing but a clear voice on his phone.
Anker SoundCore - Husband's voice was clear, but echoed horribly. No matter what volume level I used. There was no distortion (I was expecting this given the distortion with the music playback) bu the continuous echoing is a major issue for me. Husband reported a slight "faded" type of echo on his phone.

Road Test (in my LLV)
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - The sound is amazing in the truck! Thinking I would need it, I maxed the volume on both the speaker and my phone then pressed play on my music. Well, I certainly don't need max volume. I reduced the volume on both the speaker and my phone and found a very happy medium output. This speaker performs perfectly in the loud, rattling setting of a USPS LLV.. even while bouncing down rural dirt two tracks and washboard gravel roads. I am extremely pleased with this tiny speaker.
Anker Soundcore - Even with maxed volume settings, I could not get this speaker to perform anywhere near as well as the OontZ Angle 3 Plus. It had volume and was loud enough to hear over the vehicle's own noise, however the distortion/interference mentioned earlier was still present and in the truck during the road test it had what I would describe as an echoing effect on the music, specifically the singers' voices. It just wasn't clear. (I hope that makes sense.)

Battery Life/Listen While Charging
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - So far, the battery life is impressive. After receiving it, I charged it overnight (as recommended). I then had it connected to my phone for about an hour of home testing. Turned it off and I next used it at work on a Saturday.. had it powered on and connected to my phone and actively playing music for about 5.5 hours. I then used it again on Monday (much longer and busier days in the USPS, FYI).. had it on, connected and active continuously for nearly 9 hours. I have yet to see the low battery light come on. I plan to see just how many days of work I can get out of a single charge.
Anker Soundcore - I have no information for this section on this speaker since I am returning it.

Exterior/Cleaning
At first, I had the OontZ Angle 3 Plus setting on the dashboard of the LLV. This didn't last more than two stops. Despite having the four rubber "feet", the speaker still slid around causing more of a distraction than I would like. I ended up setting it on top of my personal bag, in a bin by my feet with the speaker facing up. This move really helped my piece of mind, knowing it will not go anywhere. This speaker has a soft rubber exterior. It is quite nice and feels luxurious, however... this exterior attracts all dust particles within 50 feet! USPS LLVs are *not* known for being the cleanest and even though I moved the speaker from the dust-ridden dashboard to a bin, it was still slathered with dust and dirt by the end of my route. I figured it was a fair trade, sacrificing the appearance for the gain of having decent music. But.. I got home and went to clean it. I will tell you, my expectations of this working were very low. I didn't think the dust would come off that supple rubber. But with a wet paper towel and a few slow wipes, it did. So, it can be cleaned up!

Case
I did purchase the case for this speaker ([[ASIN:B01NBDY6VP [Official] OontZ Angle 3 Plus Bluetooth Portable Speaker Carry Case, Neoprene with Aluminum Carabiner, reinforced zipper, by Cambridge SoundWorks [NOT FOR OontZ Angle 3]]]). I was mainly wanting a safe way to transport and store the speaker, but after reading the other reviews I was hoping I would be able to keep it clean in the case and still enjoy my music on my route. I received the case and used it yesterday. The case is extremely nice and I appreciate the interior mesh pocket. I have no need for it now, but I'm sure it will come in handy if I ever take this speaker on vacation and need to take the charging cables along. As for playback while in the case? Yeah, it was terribly muffled. It didn't work for me as it apparently has for others. Yet, the case itself is exactly what I was wanting for taking it to and from work. It is not as thickly padded as I would have expected, however it does protect the speaker.

Overall, for my specific purpose and intended use for a Bluetooth speaker, the Anker SoundCore simply won't cut it. However, it is still a nice speaker and will perhaps fit your needs perfectly. After all, most people don't drive LLVs and have the same high demands that go along with that. For me, the OontZ Angle 3 Plus is what I'll be bopping down the road to, mailbox to mailbox.

Happy hunting! Hope this review helps you out!
Has good sound but no sound control
I’m sure this would have been fine if it was brand new but it had sound issues and didn’t quite work right. I will probably buy a brand new one.

It seems to work fine for everything but games, and it seems that the sound processor may be the source of the audio and video glitches. Certain sounds seem to cause more problems than others, including dropped audio, glitchy video, and sometimes a blank screen. This happens with both XBox Ones and a PS3. I mainly play Forza 6 and Gran Turismo 6, and certain engine sounds seem to be associated with these problems more than others. Streaming video doesn't seem to cause any problems with any of the input devices or either TV. The normal solution is to cycle the power off and back on. Different cables or settings don't seem to make a difference. I'm not using the audio splitter at all. Personal opinion (from decades of experience with processors of all kinds), is that whatever processor is used simply cannot process some sounds correctly, even to pass the signal through. I may be wrong. I've been wrong before. This may be a quality control issue, or it may be an engineering issue. Either way, I'm looking for a better product, and most of the ones in this price range seem to be identical except for the name on the box. In fact, many more expensive devices seem to be exactly the same layout, and likely use the same circuitry. There's no way to tell from the name on the box, or the Amazon description.

This will give you better sound than the typical flat screen TV, but don't expect much in the way of volume or dynamic range.  The remote provide is infrared which is awkward unless the bar will be at eye level. I got a good deal on a sale price so I'm going to complain too much.
Nice sound for such a small speaker

We have only used it once, during a four (4) hour bus ride from Ma to NY, with my teenage son, and it worked pretty well. There were minor interruptions in the sound, but nothing that killed our vibes.

Does the job if you just want music or podcast while you’re sitting outside. Doesn’t get loud enough to use for a big crowd, no bass. But good price. You do get 2 speakers. Might be useful indoors for kids rooms, esp since you get 2.

This is a great deal on outdoor cameras. They are easy to set up and work well with the software you can download. They are sturdy and compact. I got them to replace some cameras that are around our barn so we can see the horses, and the only surprise was that they didn't pan. The other cameras were able to move up and down, right and left so that I could see where the horses are.
I was going to give them 4 stars, but then I realized it was my issue. The description never said they would pan and I just missed that.
So, if you want remote cameras and don't mind that they are stationary, this is a great deal. You get three cameras for $160. However, if you look at the current description, one camera is $49.99, so you can buy three individual cameras for slightly less than the 3 pack. Goofy, but that's sometimes the case.
UPDATE: I also noticed that the speaker on the camera, so I can talk to whoever is there, has such a low volume it cannot be heard over 1 foot away. Not very helpful for a remore camera. I sent in a request to their support team asking if there is a volume control on the camera or the mobile app. They responded with a request for the model number, which is fine, and then didn't reply to my response for over a month. Their next reply was to ask a bunch of questions about firmware and app permissions, which was not helpful. This indicates to me there is a problem with support and also possibly a problem with the deveopment group. Any retail product should have a features list somewhere, maybe not available to the public, but certainly available to the support team. That feature list should indicate if there is a way to control the volume. Rather than taking a month to ask additional, irrelevant questions, the support people should have either looked at the feature list or asked the developers if there is a way to increase the volume.
That did not happen, and so I'm reducing the rating to 3 stars. All products can have problems and the test of a good product is having a support group that can quickly and accurately respond to the problem (or question), and that is not the case with Merkury.
Since I planed to install this about 6 feet off the ground, the camera is of limited value. It doesn't pan, which was my issue, and no one can hear what is said through the app, which is their issue. Support is not helpful so I don't know if this is a problem with the camera or a feature they left our or a feature they intend to include later. I can no longer recommend this product, unless you are going to install it very close to whoever you are wanting to speak with.
Took along time to get them but they sound great

I bought this for use primarily while sleeping. Positive: microfiber is comfortable; color is very pretty; construction is high quality; sound quality of speakers is surprisingly good. The sound is not at all like the Echo.  I am still on the fence if I want to return it and just buy another echo because of the sound quality.  It works for having an "extension" for your Echo to add things to your list(s), playing your music etc.

Playback ( shadowing & freezing especially with YouTube and some websites. ) After talking with APPLE, it seems like it was probable that mine might have a bad video chip. So now I'm on the hunt again for a replacement.

The sound was not great. I think it doesn't have enough bass and it was also very hard to see what channel you were on.
For around the same price get the JENSEN CD Sport . It has excellent sound and better features.
I had low expectations, and they didn't let me down. These do not produce good sound. You get what you pretty for.

Someone previously mentioned that maybe there's a bad batch of these going out - I think I got one of them. This speaker is OK. It's very portable, which is a plus, and I love the fact that it uses USB for power. The USB cable is a bit on the short side, but it's workable. The power/volume control and mute button are nice pluses. It's a bit on the tinny side, but what do you expect for such a small and inexpensive speaker? The sound on these headphones is great but the headband adjuster slips out of the notches to easy it will not lock in place,cord is very long also

Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a reasonably priced MP3 player from Philips Electronics. Small and with a good deal of memory, this MP3 player offers enough of the basic features to satisfy casual MP3 users' needs.

Let's talk about the good points first. This MP3 player is a good value and it has a long battery life. A full charge can last the better part of a day so it is ready when you need it. The compact size and durable construction are also plusses with this MP3 player. It takes up very little space and the metal construction is made to last. I like the menu navigation as well and found it very intuitive.

Most important to an MP3 player is sound quality and in this area, my feelings are mixed. My MP3 player experience is limited, so I have little to which I can compare. But based on other MP3 players, the sound quality with this Phillips device is a little below average. I was also very disappointed with the Full Sound option. This is supposed to improve the sound quality, but I could barely tell any difference. It has a little too much bass for my tastes, but others might find it acceptable.

Probably my greatest complaint with this Philips MP3 player is the included ear buds. They are the type that hugs the ear, but they do not contain a foam cushion and thus are not very comfortable or very good at blocking outside noise. The good thing, of course, is that an accessory like this can be replaced, which I recommend doing if you purchase this product.

MP3 players are nice and Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a good MP3 player, especially for the price. There are certainly better MP3 players out there, but this is a good one for beginners or those with basic needs. I'm torn with my overall rating because of the division between the pros and cons. So, I will award this device with a middle rating of three stars and a modest recommendation.

The Defender GK300- 7M2 Hands Free 2- wire color video intercom system is a relatively inexpensive intercom system designed to provide peace of mind with minimum hassle. This device is simple enough to install and is instantly ready to use with the flick of a switch.

Besides the simple setup, this monitor has some other interesting features that make it useful. I really like the night vision option because it makes visible what would otherwise be difficult to make out. I like the sound- it is easy to tell exactly what is being said- and I like the loud, easily noticeable chime when someone rings the doorbell. The fifty- foot cable is also nice because it is long enough that I was able to place the viewing monitor in my bedroom with no problem.

As for the cons, I can find a few. The video quality isn't the greatest- it is a little fuzzy, even though I can still tell who is on the screen. Then, there is the duration of the video- it displays for only about thirty to thirty- five seconds. After that, the screen goes blank and you have to keep pressing the video button to get it back. This latter feature is one I wish was different. Often, you will want to watch and listen to the person at the door, but because you have to remember to keep pressing the video button, you could easily miss something important.

This is a basic intercom unit, hence the average quality overall. I know there are more sophisticated products on the market, but they all cost several times more than this, the Defender GK300- 7M2 intercom. I suppose for the price, it is an acceptable option but don't buy this expecting a fancy, high tech intercom unit. All you get with this are the basics, making it good enough for only for those with minimal security needs.

This product can work.My review is not to knock this product in a negative way but more to warn folks that if you do not live near the city (or where the TV towers are) then buy at your own risk.  I was really looking forward to cancelling my Comcast subscription so I purchased this antenna in lieu of a Comcast payment each month. I purchased the 35 mile radius as I live 25 miles from downtown Seattle. After installation and setup I received only 1 channel.  I have to admit the clarity of that one channel was fantastic however I do not speak Spanish so it was a let down. I believe this product works but not if you are on the outskirts of town. I would suggest only buying this if you live 20 miles or less away from city towers. Or if you live up on a hill that faces the city. Just my opinion for us more rural folks. I can tell (from the one channel I did get) that if I lived closer to the city this antenna would simply do the trick.  Hope this helps.

Whenever I need to capture some action footage and i'm worried I may damage my good camera, I use this little guy. You really have to kick it in the arse to get the white balance set. For more than a month I've been bounced between rehabilitation facilities and the hospital and quite often there's some patient who's unwell and acting out, yelling, screaming, throwing things. If you've ever spent a while in either type of facility you know the experience. When I saw these headphones available for review I jumped on the idea. I had a friend deliver them and where do I begin?
* They barely fit in the mesh like bag that offers NO protection to your headphones.
* I think I have a fairly normal sized head but they fit tight on my ears not painful for short term but extended wear could be an issue.
* Sound is muddy, bass is overwhelming, even after adjusting my equalizer over and over. I finally got them to sound ok, just ok.

Fit isn't great. Sound isn't great. Carry bag isn't great. I'll use these until I get home and can find a better pair. Not impressed.

Well, I've had this for a week or so now. It's honestly cute just because of its size. I've had books that were bigger than this is. The power cord is just a bit over three feet, that's a hindrance. I was lucky enough there was a plug just in range but an extra foot of power cord would be better. The unit comes with a set of thin but serviceable RCA cables. I have some pro level RCA cables I obtained when I worked for a TV station, springs protecting the cables at the connectors, super heavy cable and insulation. . . and when I tried them with this DVD player the weight of the cables literally pulled the player off the antique dresser I use as a TV stand but the picture using the included cables is fine, playback is sharp & crisp. The unit has a functional set of controls on the front of the player which are sometimes missing in this modern era. The remote is a little small for my hands and the layout is a bit cramped and wonky but it works as long as you're in the fairly narrow field that the remote and device can see one another.
I've binged a few of my older DVD sets so far. The unit has a resume feature that picks up wherever you left off. Actually there's quite a decent set-up menu for the unit. Enough to get you going but not so much you need a degree in sound and electrical engineering to figure things out.
My only complaints so far have been;
1 - the device when loading or searching for tracks can be a bit loud but while watching content its whisper quiet.
2 - occasionally it reverts to turning the closed captioning on. There's a control on the remote, 2-3 clicks and its fixed.
3 - the already mentioned too short power cord.
Pluses are many. The player is supposed to be region free, I have no foreign DVDs to test this with. The small form factor means you can (within the limits of the cabling) put it almost anywhere. It easily fits under the corner of my large screen TV with room to spare. The display is orange, I don't know why. It's not attractive but it is easy to read from across the room (maybe that's why it's orange). It does have a voice reading function for people with impaired sight. It will read every control or function as you select them.
Not a complaint and not a plus. Most devices have a single LED that stays on to let you know it's in standby mode and ready to go. This unit steps things up a notch. When it's off it literally displays "OFF" on the screen for all to see.
I've been quite happy with the functionality of this unit. I have a decent DVD collection I haven't been able to watch for a while so I'm pleased to be able to watch these old favorites, Serial Experiment Lain, Robot Chicken, Wonderfalls and many others.
Edit - I received the instructions from the manufacturer and another user on setting this unit up as Region Free. I followed them, several times, reverting back to Region 1 each time. When set to Test - Region 0 (supposedly the region free setting) Region 1 discs become unplayable! See the image I posted. The menus load but try to play any content and the message screen I shared "This Disc Not Formatted to Play In This Region." is all you get.
Manufacturer was unable to offer a solution.

The ear pieces are not replaceable there are no different size tips for these so they fit or they don't. If they do they sound pretty good. They're okay. Do you have a kid who's going through two pair of headphones a month? I debated between three and four stars these do sound quite good; fairly good highs and the bass isn't bad with a large 50mm driver. So in the end, they sound good but fit poorly on me. I do have a fairly large head so there's a majority of people whom these would fit just fine.

I bought this mouse because the shape mimicked the Microsoft mouse I've been using with my desktop PC for ages. I recently purchased my first laptop and I wasn't sure I was going to like using the trackpad. The mouse is pretty cheaply made of thin and brittle plastic. There isn't even a storage space for the USB receiver it was shipped loose, rattling about in the battery compartment.

The mouse works. It fits my thick, stubby fingered hand okay. It's affordable as something to throw in the laptop bag in case you need a mouse for something quick and infrequent. If you're going to be using a mouse all the time you might want to invest in something a little better than this.

I was really looking forward to trying this tablet out. To date I'd had no exposure to Windows 8.1 or a dedicated Windows tablet. I have had a decent 10.1 inch Android tablet.

First are foremost, the elephant in the room... or rather, the mouse. This is a seven inch wide screen tablet. I have friends whose who online lives are conducted via five inch cell phone screens and they're happy with it. The screen on this tablet is nice. Don't get me wrong. I was able to stream from Amazon video in HD (720) and the video was crisp and clean. Images display well but, again, the screen is just seven inches. I can't imagine trying to be productive with something so small.

For a device with only one gig of RAM this runs Windows fairly well. I wws able to load several Windows programs including the Calibrě eBook manager which took a little longer to convert eBooks between formats but did the job. I also loaded a legacy email and Usenet program that I've been using for a decade or longer. Along with directly installed programs I also downloaded a handful of apps from the very buggy Microsoft app store. The store worked less than 50% of the time while I was trying this tablet out. I at one point had to resort to switching to a local login account and then back to my Hotmail logi. It only took about an hour of reading web forums to find that solution to the Windows app store refusing to work.

Two problems I ran into were the sound which is from a single speaker hidden in a slot on one of the short sides of the tablet. If you want to listen to anything other than the default Window's beeps and tones you'll want to pair this with a blue tooth speaker or headphones. The speaker in this tablet is deplorable. The next problem I had was the tablet runs HOT. I was running a program designed for Windows 98, downloading and reading posts un Usenet and viewing a few posted vacation and astronomy images and I had to stop. The tablet was so hot it was uncomfortable to hold and I worried it might overheat and become damaged.

While I was impressed to see Windows running on a small tablet I was thoroughly unimpressed with Windows 8.1 the tile system is just terrible.

So, it has good video quality on a too small screen with horrible sound and a flaky app store to rely upon, though you can download and install normal Windows programs. I just wasn't that crazy about this tablet. And will definitely be sticking with Android and a much larger screen.

My first impression upon unboxing this camera was "Wow, that feels cheap." Everything's made from unattractive plastic. The single dial on the top rear of the camera (oddly blank) feels light, spins too easily and clicking it feels mushy. The other buttons on the camera, power, movie and flash all have the same, cheap, mushy feel. The shutter button has poor tactile feel.

The camera is surprisingly heavy; for me uncomfortably, painfully, so.The back is so taken up by the huge 4.8" LCD screen that the thumb rest is too short, more of an afterthought that cause me quite a bit of discomfort during extended use. The DSLR style handgrip is quite large (perhaps too large for small hands) to accommodate the massive 4360 mAh battery.

On paper the idea of an Android OS with a 4.8" LCD screen and a big APS-C sensor sounds great but I was sadly less than impressed.

Because of the Android OS startup time from fully off to ready to shoot is a very long 23 seconds. In standby mode the camera was ready to shoot in approx. 4 seconds. The camera runs warm, very warm, even just sitting idle on a cool 50 degree day. I would worry about overheating in the summer months.

Image quality was unimpressive especially in low light. Early morning, post sunrise, images with sky and clouds were extremely grainy and noisy. Performance in full light was better but not spectacular. Auto focus was run of the mill, often seeking excessively in low light situations. High ISO performance was exceedingly poor. Past ISO 800 images were rather noisier and grainy. In auto mode the camera seemed to make poor choices for ISO and shutter speeds.

Controls. Almost every setting is accessed via the large LCD screen.

There are over twenty pre-configured shooting modes. I used several of them while checking out this camera. These selections are made from a top to bottom scrolling 'carousel' where you scroll through until you find the option you want. I found it annoying to find and stop on the mode I wanted. You're going to miss shots trying to find the mode you want.

Continuous Shooting: burst mode. Surprisingly fast.
Kids Shot: the camera plays one of three sounds to attract a child's attention and then bursts five photos.
Macro: The Galaxy NX has a surprisingly short minimum focal distance with the kit lens and the macro photos I took were among the best results I was able to get from the camera.
Rich Tone: Samsung's HDR mode. Processing time was excessive.
Panorama: This is a sweep mode, smoothly move the camera (a tripod helps) to capture up to 180°'s of view. Disappointingly the camera reduces the image size significantly in Panorama mode.
Multi Exposure: combines two or more images into one.
Drama: combines several images of a moving subject into a single image. The camera was very picky about detecting moving objects. I encountered at least a 50% fail rate trying this mode. Additionally, as with the Panorama mode the image size is greatly reduced.

The camera can also be used in manual mode. Samsung calls it 'Expert Mode'. This gives you access to the standard PASM controls. The settings are controlled by three half-circle on screen dials that I found frustratingly hard to use. Try to change one and my thick fingers would spin the wrong dial. Using Shutter Priority mode I found the processing time of 30 second exposures was a disappointing additional 30 seconds.

There are some things I did like about this camera. It's not all bad. It can produce decent images and I honestly think the majority of the limitations I experienced were due to the cheap kit lens. The 4.8" LCD is gorgeous, in the right light, I recently went back to a camera with a beautiful 3" screen and it felt small. Some of the included shooting modes are fun to play with. Connectivity via WiFi was rock solid (I wasn't able to test the 3G/4G connectivity) even in parking lots of places that offered free WiFi. There were eleven gigs of free space in internal memory. That was plenty of room for a day's shooting and testing. I never did get around to installing an SD card.

In conclusion...
I'm not really sure who this camera is aimed at. They seem to be trying to attract smart phone users with the ability to access the internet almost anywhere and instantly share you photos. But do you really need an expensive, heavy and complex large-sensor camera to post photos to Facebook and Twitter?
On the flip side I just can't see this camera being attractive to professional photographers or high end photography enthusiasts. While the inclusion of the electronic viewfinder is nice I found the all on-screen controls to be distracting and bothersome and the image quality was for the most part lackluster.

A note about durability. As I was finishing up the testing of this camera I bobbled the camera due to nerve damage and it took a spill. The height was not great, less than three feet, and the initial impact was on soil and grass. The lens came apart into numerous pieces. I was able to put the lens back together but it appears to have suffered internal damage and will not focus either automatically or manually. I accept that I caused this damage but I am very unimpressed with the durability of such an expensive camera.

I really can't recommend this camera. Three stars but barely.

A side note about Samsung's technical support that isn't reflected in my rating of this camera. Calling Samsung's support line was a complete nightmare. Audio quality was atrocious. At the end I was practically screaming to be heard. I spent close to an hour and a half on the phone speaking with seven different people. Each person I spoke to had to be told all my information, the camera's information and the reason for my call. Four times I was transferred to 'the proper department.' In the end I had a supervisor tell me, first that the camera did not exist and then, that it must be a UK version and I'd have to start all over and call their UK support line. I then contacted Samsung through their Facebook support page. It's been almost a week and they still haven't decided what to do about the camera/lens.

{Edit}
It took nearly a month of back and forth and arguing to get Samsung to agree my camera was a US version, it was under warranty and they would issue a repair ticket for it. It was shipped off at their expense, repaired surprisingly quickly and shipped back. The camera's now in working order. Only one thing marred the process. When they returned the camera and lens the put a cap on the rear of the lens (I'd shipped it with the lens attached) but only put a piece of what looked like a Post-It across the body opening. I found it odd they wouldn't properly cap the body to protect the sensor though on the whole the packing job, bubble wrapped and foam peanuts was well done. Kudos to their repair facility but I'm still very put off by the whole experience with their support people.

The Gorillapod Video Tripod (Black/Blue) is a good idea on paper but in real life it just doesn't quite measure up.

The pan & tilt head is incredibly stiff which leads to jerky motion and bounce in your video. There also, on mine at least, appears to be a good bit of free play or slack in the vertical movement of the control arm. I've tried to tighten this down to no avail. The mounting screw seems to be a bit long. It wasn't bad mounting my RCA Small Wonder video camera but when I mounted my Kodak still camera the screw bottomed out and left the camera loose on the mount. The mount itself seems quite secure tight and sturdily attached to the tripod.

I like the adjustability of the legs but if you're not using the tripod on a metal surface for the magnetic feet to cling to it tends to just slide around when adjusting the pan or tilt. The magnets do appear to be strong for their size and will hold my RCA Small Wonder video camera fully horizontal on the 'fridge or door of my car. I tried this with my Kodak Z-650 still camera and it was too heavy for the magnets to support.

While on the subject of the magnetic feet I wanted to add a warning that if you're using an older CRT style monitor care should be taken to keep this tripod several feet away from your monitor. Even being more than a foot away from my 19" CRT cause distortion and image warping. There is the potential for damage to CRT monitors.

As a stationary camera mount this is a pretty cute product; easy to carry, lightweight with near infinitely adjustable legs. If you just want to plop down your camera so you don't have to hold it this product works fine. When you bring the flaws of the pan and tilt features into play the enjoyment goes downhill fast.

All in all it's not bad but it really isn't great.

Note: I would love to love this speaker set, but it has inconsistent performance with various devices. I received a review sample and was pleased by the sound when I plugged this into the phone port on my ThinkPad T61. The sound was clear and I could hear every note on the album that I use to test speakers (Miles Davis' [[ASIN:B000002ADT Kind of Blue]]). I use that album because the instruments in the ensemble cover low, mid and high range frequencies. The bass was a little thin, but with the speakers less than two feet away the sound was rich and I was happy.

Where I started to experience problems was when I plugged this into the 3.5mm port on my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 phone. There was static in the mix. The same with my [[ASIN:B00D029NNA Samsung Galaxy Tab 3 10.1 inch]] - static interfered with the music. My final test was to plug the 3.5mm cable end into an [[ASIN:B00AEJJRBK Avantree Cara Bluetooth 4.0 Handsfree stereo Car Kit with mic]] and connect via bluetooth. The sound was crystal clear.

I am not sure what conclusions to draw. It could be something wrong with the Samsung phone and tablet, although both work perfectly with headphones which I have directly plugged into their 3.5mm ports. It may be that the 3.5mm cable and interface on the input of this speaker is overly sensitive to impedance and the slightest deviation will induce static. I am not sure, but because I was unable to get the same quality consistently across all devices with which I tested these speakers I subtracted two stars.

Construction is exceptional, although I wish the design employed removable USB and 3.5mm cables instead of the fixed ones that provide power and signal inputs, and connect the two units. As it stands if a cable breaks it will take some skill to repair it. With removable, off-the-shelf cables a broken one can be rectified with a trip to an electronics store.

Overall, on the two devices that I tested with which these speakers worked the sound was spectacular. On the other two it was unlistenable. If you are connecting this to a bluetooth receiver it's probably a safe choice, but if you are connecting this to anything else I would proceed with caution.

First of all, the D-Link camera is relatively easy to set up - always the one to play with techie stuff first, my husband had it up and running in a flash (well almost a flash). Just attach the supplied cable to your computer, run the CD and follow the simple instructions and you're good to go. According to the instructions, you have two options to set up the camera: wirelessly or wired. Naturally, my husband tried the wireless option first, which didn't work because it claimed (spuriously, we believe) that it couldn't find the network, so he had to resort to the other method, which worked right away. We're using a Linksys wireless router.

The camera works quite well indoors where the intensity of the ambient light is generally much lower than outdoors. However, in the brighter outdoor light it is difficult to discern what you're looking at (is it a bird, is it a plane?). The colour is not the best, but then again, it ain't a Nikon 7000. There is some amount of adjustment that can be done online to change the settings, but you'll need to create an online account/register your camera first with D-Link at [...] This is also necessary if you want to view your camera remotely. Strange enough, whenever I try to access the camera online, I get a message telling me that the application needs an earlier version of Java. However, after hitting <Run> for the next three dialogue boxes or so that pop up, it will display the picture. I tried accessing the camera from outside my home network but was unable to do so. Maybe firewall issues?? (Too much effort required to check this). There is also an iPod app that is quite good, minus sound.

Night vision was surprisingly good too. In the dark, the images were shades of grey, but in brighter conditions, the colour returned. Four LED lights lit up whenever the night vision was activated (could be an issue if you wanted to place it somewhere discrete).

On the down side, the camera has to be plugged into an electrical socket to work, and the cord it came with is very short. This means you have to either place it near an electrical outlet or use an extension cord. This would obviously have limitations on where you can place it. It also has to be connected to your home network whether wired or wireless.

While in theory it could be used as a security camera, it has to be powered 24/7, so if you live in a country or area prone to an uneven power supply which could damage sensitive equipment, then you may want to consider that before getting it or you may need to install additional equipment such as line conditioners/UPS to protect your equipment.

The sound is not very good. In fact, after a few hours use it started to make a clicking sound in an endless loop.

Recommended for limited applications such as keeping an eye on kids (or pets, or pesky guests), or when you're avoiding (hiding from) certain people who come calling at your gate, but not as a dedicated security system.

Amanda Richards, June 29, 2011
Great product, cleaned my tv/cd player very well.  I liked the many steps it went through to make sure the sound and cleaning was precise.
All the electronics were alluring. But I didn't know what I know now. Does not come Bluetooth accessible. Sound is poor quality.

My original Echo, purchased when the first invitations were sent out, was much beloved for years. She finally began to have performance problems last month. Stuttering, failing to perform tasks and simply not hearing her name anymore. Definitely time for an upgrade.

I like this Echo Plus, but I'm not thrilled with the short, fat, squatty shape over the tall, slender original Echo. This one doesn't fit in the same spot and just looks like any generic, knockoff speaker rather than Alexa. However, the sound quality of music and Audible books is superior and can be clearly heard at lower volumes than my old Echo.

I will say the coordination/communication between the physical Plus and the Alexa app is spotty and slow. In particular when using the Plus's built in temperature monitor. I had hoped specifically to use this to monitor our RV temperature when traveling for the safety of our dogs. Alexa does tell me the temperature has reached the preset warning level - an HOUR later!!! That's useless. I ended up spending more money to but a dedicated Wifi temperature/humidity monitor that alerts my phone via text and email literally within 90 seconds of the preset parameters. I love Alexa in general and we have 3 Dots, the Auto and this Plus, so we're fully integrated in the ecosystem, but this Plus isn't as good as the original, 1st generation Echo.

This is one of those products where I really like the gadget itself, but absolutely hate the company and policies behind it. Enough so that I would never actually do business with or trust the Canary company with my personal financial information.

The camera itself is sleek and easy to use and set up. It connected via Bluetooth and wifi in minutes and upgraded its own software immediately. You have to have the app going first to get the camera online and running. There are blue, yellow, white and red lights on the bottom that sort of tell you what the status is - it's actually a pretty solid copy cat of the way the Alexa Echo devices do things.

I've been impressed with the clarity and detail in the camera both live streaming and the short recordings. The night vision is remarkably good - that alone warrants a five star review if the policies didn't ruin everything else. Setting up the app and camera to determine Home, Away and Night modes is ok, but doesn't always work. Right now Canary is alerting me that a person has been detected - IT IS ME! I set it to home mode, but the camera just doesn't believe it. I was able to connect the Canary with Alexa in the Alexa App Skills and watch live streaming of our living room on the bedroom television via the Firestick - completely painless.

Here's my problem. The so called three month free trial of the Canary membership requires a full credit card input BEFORE you can use the free trial. Umm.....no. I don't know this company, there's zero information in the app about exactly how they secure our info and if after the trial is over, you want to cancel, there aren't clear directions and a single step CANCEL button. It's about as sketchy as can be. All the features you might buy this camera for are locked unless you pony up that membership fee. Honestly, I'm just sick to death of being nickled and dined every month. This camera should include a SD card slot and it doesn't. Bottom line is that I have no idea if the microphone works or the downloading of recordings because the free trial isn't actually available unless I give them credit card access - never going to happen.

Slower than the 5 year old name brand cables from my ancient Blackberry and slower than the Amazon basics cables from last year. This cable works and it does charge my cell phone in the car, but when used with the same car charger as the other two cables mentioned above, my phone charges much more slowly. I noticed the same problem when using this cable plugged directly into the USB outlet in my truck vs using the other two cables. I am charging a two month old LG V10 phone in the truck normally. This morning I switched things up and tried with a brand new (2 days) Sony Xperia X phone - exact same issue - very slow charging.

My LG typically gains a 10% bump in the truck in the time it takes me to drive from Starbucks to the horse barn every morning - this is while it plays my audio book via blue tooth at the same time. Yesterday with this StarTech cable my LG gained went from 83% on the battery to 86% under the exact same conditions. Bottom line for me is that this cable does work, but at a glacially slow pace and at best it's an emergency back up and nothing more.

I wanted to wait and use it a while before leaving a review.

it grunts at me while using it, much like my old dying hard drive did, so that does worry me a little bit.

Well, they do play music - for a while.

The TV is lightweight. The picture is pretty good for a $130 TV. I like that it has both RCA audio out jacks and a headphone jack. If you really want a small size TV, this is certainly one to consider.

I bought my pair of Bluez 2S directly from AfterShokz company, and not via Amazon. Just like with so many things there are aspects to like and aspects to not like.

I will start with the negatives. If you are in a noisy environment, such as working out in an exercise room, the volume just is not loud enough or satisfactory at all. You need earplugs in the ears to get the satisfactory volume. Yes, earplugs. Of course, that defeats the whole purpose of buying headphones that do not go inside or cover your ears.

You can test this out by simply putting a finger in each ear and then you'll hear the remarkable level of volume change.

Because of the lack of loudness one can achieve in a noisy environment, I cannot recommend these (unless you want to buy earplugs and wear them at the same time).

The only other negative for me personally is the lack of a way to go back to a previous song, or repeat the currently playing song. (You can skip forward to the next song, but you cannot go back.)

The positives: These are comfortable to wear and very lightweight. The Bluez 2S offers the ability for decent call quality when using them to make calls. Microphones seem good (I have only tried this indoors, and not outdoors, so I cannot comment further on this particular subject.)

The Bluez 2S are very easy to operate.

In a quiet environment, volume is fine, and music quality is acceptable for this price point. (Of course you will not get the level of music quality or bass you'd get with a more expensive name brand headphones that go directly over the ear.)

So, for specific purposes such as cell phone calls where you want to keep both ears free, these are quite good indeed, offering good voice quality for both parties. (Pairing with my iPhone 5 and 6S went flawlessly.)

I got mine for $248 plus sales tax with the immediate $50 reduction in price if one has Amazon Prime. I think that is a fair price for this Soundbar.

There is a lot to like about this Soundbar. You will love its easy ability to program in your TV's remote control, or any IR remote, to control the volume and mute. Very convenient.

The volume on the Soundbar can get plenty loud. The sound is quite clear.

Vizio includes all possible cables you might need.

The Soundbar is heavy and appears solidly built.

Programming features via the Vizio remote are very nice and easy to understand and figure out.

The negative: I applaud Vizio for trying to include bass speakers into the Soundbar so you won't need a separate bass speaker, but sadly they have failed. I did lots of testing on various TV feeds, from Music Choice stations to movies to local newscasts to regular network TV shows. I did adjustments to the bass via the remote on all TV feeds. The bass level is not there yet to satisfy.

I plugged in an 8" Energy brand powered bass speaker (this is not a large bass speaker), and let me tell you the difference is remarkable with all the TV feeds.

I will strongly suggest that if you consider buying this Soundbar you accept that for the most satisfying sound you really need and should have an external bass speaker. You will not be sorry at all.

One day a company might be able to invent a Soundbar with built-in bass speakers that truly deliver. Vizio has not succeeded with this model. But again, excluding the bass aspect, the rest of the Soundbar does deliver the quality.

First, a warning for you about the warranty. This Speaker Tower is very, very heavy. Should it break during the one-year warranty, as expected you will have to pay to ship it to Pyle. (I am OK with this.) But along with the item you must include a $50 money order to pay Pyle Audio to send the item back to you.

Most companies work by you pay to ship the broken item to them, they pay to ship the fixed item back to you under the warranty period.

OK, now to the product review:

Overall, I am disappointed with the quality of the audio and I do not recommend this item to people who want the best audio quality and I would not ever purchase it again.

If anyone out there paid even close to the full retail list price of $433.99, you have my sympathy.

This tower does have some positives. The ability to play either FM radio, an iOS device, or other music source (you will need a 3.5mm to dual RCA male cable if wanting to play directly from the headphone jack of an MP3 player, etc.). It would have been nice if they had included a 3.5mm input jack as well, especially at this price.

Some songs sound pretty good, but others sound muffled or muddy. Not crystal clear like you would expect at this weight and price, and from Pyle Audio. If you compare your songs through this tower and then through the $300+ Dr. Dre Original Model Beatbox as one wild example, you will hear the difference in clarity and quality from the speakers immediately.

But again, some songs do sound quite decent, and with that I can see why some give this tower a great review. But if you are like me and you want and recognize the best quality sound, you might be disappointed with this tower.

The instruction manual is very disappointing, as well. I, and most can figure things out eventually, but there will be some folks who might need to ask for help.

The FM antenna is a small hard wired wire. You cannot add your own antenna.

I got the black matte model, and it does look nice in the room.

I think this deserves 3 stars because I think there are some people who will enjoy this tower and its features and its small footprint and its look for the $171 price.

I use a $100 external sound card when DJ'ing because I want better sound than what the built-in laptop sound card offers. I notice a big difference.

I then was doing more research and read how the makers of these way more expensive USB cables claim they offer superior sound. So, I took the plunge and spent $50 for this Pangea Audio solid silver USB cable.

I seriously could not hear any difference between this USB cable and the $10 short USB cable I was using. For $50, I expected a perceptible difference, even if it was just a small difference.

I had others also judge...and they agreed with me.

From looking at and holding the cable, it does indeed come across as a quality cable. But again, I heard no difference in the sound...and I tested it with different genres of songs.

I would not recommend this cable. If you indeed have a great (and expensive) external sound card or a great DAC, my guess is you do not need to buy one of these $50 (or even more expensive) USB cables.

I give the cable 5 stars for build quality and 1 star for its inability to cause the sound from your laptop to either an external sound card or DAC to be noticeably improved. (So, I averaged it out to 3 stars.)

(I have not tested the much more expensive than this one USB cables, so maybe those do produce a perceptible difference?)

The specifications imply that this tablet is designed to accept a wireless sim card if the user decides to add an additional wireless telephone line. After spending half a day trying to register my purchase with Dell, I was told that, since Dell itself was not the seller, they are not bound to provide warranty coverage. So, Amazon Warehouse buyers might want to figure a Square Trade or other third-party warranty into the purchase price for this Dell. When I asked about the fact that a card slot for a wireless phone sim card is engineered into the Dell Venue, the Dell rep informed me that the Dell engineers originally designed a separate card slot for this purpose, but "in recent models it has been DISCONNECTED!" Which is just about the most nonsensical thing I've heard in a long time.

Several years ago, I worked as a technical telephone support person for Denon home theater systems, and realized at that time that audio and telecommunications engineers frequently make completely mystifying. unnecessarily complicated design decisions, so this was not news to me ....It WAS however, a disappointment that cost the Dell Venue 8 two stars on this review.

That said, the 2GHz processor and Jelly Bean OS are wicked fast for simple gaming, texting (with "My SMS" or other texting apps from Google Play, synched to your Android phone), etc. It can be synchronized via Wi-Fi, USB tether or Bluetooth. It's a nice size (although a little heavy), and makes a very good Kindle-type unit for reading news, books, online magazines, etc. I've decided I like the tablet very much, but would be a LOT happier with if I could get Dell updates and downloads or install a wireless phone card.

I just received this Sanjean RCR-10 and set it up. The good news is that the sound is wonderfully rich and balanced for a little radio. First bedside table clock radio I've ever had that sounds good enough to crank up loud to fill my whole apartment with music. I'm impressed, and I'm not easily impressed.

On the other hand, it seems that, the more sophisticated these digital electronics get, the more challenging and puzzling they are to set up. It could well be that these companies need to shell out a little more money for decent technical writers to produce more thorough step-by-step setup instructions. OR, they could simply design the units so they're easier to set up for those of us who are not geeks or electronics engineers. It's not all that terribly frustrating; just be ready for several minutes of trial and error ...and pray you don't have a power outage! (The unit also offers a back-up batteries feature, so I wouldn't forget to do that.)

The RCR-10 is solid, substantial (not flimsy or lightweight) and attractive. The display also includes basic metadata indicating station and artist. The only thing missing for me --since I use an Android phone as my personal music player-- would be a little close-able cover for the empty iPod docking slot. It's going to be a dust collector in my house.

UPDATE: I'm revising my five star review down to three stars, because after a couple of months' use, I've realized this thing is REALLY a pain in the butt to re-progam. Even turning the alarm pre-set volume down a notch requires that you go through a big long procedure, as if you were setting the alarm for the first time. The same thing is true if you think you'd like to awaken to some other type of music station. Hard to do anything on the fly; if you need to make a change, be prepared to sit down for twenty minutes with the OM open for reference to accomplish even the most simple adjustment. Sanjean needs to make these beautiful radios MORE USER FRIENDLY!

I went on the search for a set of ear buds that would stay in my ears better than my Airpod Pros but with the same level of Noise cancellation. It seemed like the Sony WF-1000XM4 and Bose Quietcomfort earbuds were the top picks in this space. After a lot of research i went with the Sony earbuds. Besides their sound and level of ANC. i liked the fact the Sony earbuds still had a lot of playback control available from the earbuds and you can use either earbud individually. I also felt like the fact that they sit in your ear canal rather than on the outside would contribute to the noise cancellation.

The earbuds felt and sound good and the accompanying app was nice but the case had a cheap, almost cardboard feel. My main issues were, although the earbuds never actually fell out of my ear, I think their top-heavy design made them feel like they were always about to fall out. The bigger issue i had, which won't apply to everyone, is how much effort went into getting them to sit correctly in my ear. Even with twisting, and pushing, I could never get the right earbud to fit securely in my ear like the left one did.

After a day of wearing the Sonys i decided to pick up a pair of Bose Quietcomfort ear buds as i already had a pair of Quietcomfort 35 over the ears that i loved, i figured I'd give Bose another shot. As soon as i opened the Bose, I immediately fell in love. Besides the unboxing and charging case feeling more premium, the earbuds went into my ear effortlessly and securely. I wore them the first day and they stayed in place all day and sounded great.

Although the Sony WF-1000XM4 is a great set of earbuds, The Bose earbuds have the same functionality, sound and ANC but are designed in a way to comfortably fit a wider array of ear shapes and at a cheaper price. The Sonys are going back and the Bose are going to be my new day-to-day earbuds.

I've had a number of Bluetooth headphones and the overwhelming majority of them have an "audio interface" that makes sense - some bare bones, some quite pleasant. This interface is in the form of sounds the relate to each of the functions - power on/off, paring, etc. These headphones have a TERRIBLE interface. When you power them on an annoyingly loud series of tones blares in your ear. The tones rise in pitch. When you continue to hold the power button, to access the paring mode, all you hear is an extremely brief, muffled tone. Apparently, the makers thought this was enough of a signal to indicate you're in paring mode. Believe me, it is NOT obvious at all. When you power off the headphones, you hear the same annoying loud series of tones. In this case, the tones do not decrease in pitch, which one might expect.

By comparison, the audio interface of my other Bluetooth headphones are a joy - unfortunately, they do not have volume controls or skip and rewind. When powering them on, a pleasant female voice says, "Hello", and when you enter pairing mode, the same voice says, "Ready to pair." When pairing is established, the voice says, You're connected", then tells me how much charge I have - either full, medium or low. These Cootree headphones do none of that. You'll be lucky if you're able to tell if they've been turned off properly.

In terms of sound quality, they're okay - nothing exceptional. In terms of fit, they're okay as well. Again, nothing exceptional. To my knowledge, they do not have an active noise cancelling function, other than what little noise they may happen to muffle by covering your ears. I mention this only because the rating form asks about it.

I bought this to use with my LG TV and a couple of Anker Bluetooth speakers. Connecting the speakers to the transmitter was confusing because you have zero interface. Once I did get it connected, the latency was not good. The audio was not in sync at all - a god half to a full second behind the video. I'm returning this for a refund. If you're planning to use this with a TV and Bluetooth speakers, be sure they support the BT 5 aptx low latency codec.

EDIT

After returning the device, the manufacturer sent me a message. I almost deleted their email because it looked like spam, with emojis in the subject line. Anyway, they informed me that the problem I experienced was likely because the BT speakers (Upgraded, Anker Soundcore Boost) I used I paired with their device did not support the low latency aptx codec. This may have been the case, but I was unable to find specs for the speakers to confirm this.

I must say their customer support is extremely accommodating. In their email, they offered a number of options to make things right, including a gift card or a different BT transmitter. Unfortunately, I've already purchased wired speakers to replace the ones I had bought. Although I won't be taking advantage of their offers, I do give them high marks for service and have changed my rating from 2 stars to 4 stars.

For the price, this device is okay, but the user interface is pathetic. The touch interface is annoying because it only applies to half the screen. What's worse is when the device screen goes blank (to save battery life), you have to touch the screen - which performs one of the functions, like play or pause. It's quite annoying. The buttons of the touch screen are at the bottom and you can only navigate the interface by tapping up/down/left/right. So doing things on the device is a chore

I bought this for a friend and didn't spend much time with it - only to set it up. So I don't have an opinion of the sound quality or the build quality. However ... one comment on the latter. I've seen a number of reviews for this and similar products which reference the weight of the device and correlation it to the quality of the build. The 2 don't always to hand in hand. The Chinese have been known to add lead weights to devices to make them heavier so that people will believe it's better build quality or material than it really is. I don't know this to be the case with this device - just wanted to point out that weight may not be the telltale people think it is

Let me start by saying I don't use the cell phone features of these headphones, so this review is not all encompassing.

That said, I was a little disappointed in these headphones. Although the sound quality is good, the build quality and attention to detail in design could be better. The control buttons on the right ear are difficult to use as you can't easily feel with your finger where one starts and another begins, You just have to press in the general area, which is not very reassuring. The buttons themselves have no raised symbols or any physical element you can touch to let you know you're on a button, let alone the correct one.

The build quality is not the best. The control buttons fit together less tightly than other Bluetooth headphones I've used. The main play/pause/on/off/pairing button, located in the center of the right earphone in particular seems loose and misaligned.

The functions of the buttons work well enough. However, with some functions, there is no audio feedback. Having used other headsets that provide a short beep each time a button is pressed, I was a little confused when I first tried these - I'd press pause and the audio would just stop, with no beep. I suppose some users would find this preferable though. Some of the button functions, such as play/pause, are not instantaneous. There's a slight delay (about a second) between the time you press it and the time the audio actually plays or pauses. I've experienced this with other Bluetooth headsets and it seems to be a common annoyance.

Because the fit is somewhat tight, getting the earphones on requires a little manipulation. I often find I have to guide the tip of my ear into the space between the neckband (the part that holds the earpieces and wraps around your neck) and the earpiece.This is mainly due to the padding on the earpieces. Once the headphones are on though, they've not uncomfortable. However, a little more space between the neckband and the top of the earpieces would be an improvement. Wearing the headphones lying down or with your head against the back of a seat is not uncomfortable for the most part.

The charging port is has a rubber cover. Although it serves a purpose and some might find this helpful, I find it just gets in the way and will likely fall off. The charging cable is VERY short - about 3 feet, and it comes with no AC adapter, so you'll need to plug it into a USB port for charging - or acquire an adapter so you can use an electrical outlet. Due to the shortness of the cord, it will likely be inconvenient for use with some outlets.

Attaching the charging cord is somewhat difficult. This is to be expected, I guess, due to the micro-USB size of the plug that goes into the ear piece. The end of the cord that plugs into the ear piece is tapered on one side, so there's some visual indication of which way it should go in, but it's always a pain trying to insert these kinds of plugs, no matter what the device. I haven't used the headphones for any great length of time, so I can't comment on the battery life at this time.

The fact that these headphones can fold up to a fairly small size is nice and may be helpful to some when traveling. Typically, I wear them while walking or taking public transportation, so no real advantage for me.

I purchased 2 pair of these - 1 for myself and one as a gift. The ones I bought for myself were to replace a pair of Motorola Bluetooth headphones I thought were malfunctioning. Whenever I wore them, if I turned my heard too far to the right, the sound would cut out or it would seem to skip slightly. The first time I tried the Kinivo BTH240 headphones, they did the exact same thing. Is this something common to Bluetooth devices?

All in all, I suppose the negatives I've noted are minor and are likely more personal, but they still prevent me from rating these higher than 3 stars.

It would be nice if the battery were user replaceable, so all that plastic and electronics didn't have to end up in a landfill.

So, as I mentioned, I like the product and would have rated it higher if not for the flaws I've noted.
