[[VIDEOID:121051b82f50880623cdf0499f74c575]] THE GOOD:
--------------
* 1080P native and extremely small, so it's very portable. The size is the whole reason I got this. It's for traveling and being able to project bigger screens in hotel walls.
* 300 ansi lumens, ALPD laser tech.
* 25000 hrs lamp life.
* Airplay, Miracast thru wi-fi.
* Aesthetically, very nice minimalist design.
* Picture quality is good, but I'm not a videophile. I do have a more serious Vava UST 4k projector in my living room, so all these portable projectors will never compare. They serve as a traveling device for me, and will not be the go-to video source at home.
* Very nice case is included to hold everything.

THE BAD:
------------
* Onboard 1W speakers are very weak to say the least. You will definitely want to hook up a portable speaker. It has a headphone jack, which is basically the same as an aux out jack. I hooked it up to a cheap little speaker and the sound improved drastically. Watch my video.
* No remote.
* No smart OS, so I have a chromecast connected in my video demo, and I just cast from my phone.
* No Bluetooth, so you must use aux if connecting a speaker.
* No mounting solution or tripod included. Depending on your situation, you might not even need it. Just set it on a coffee table and you're good.
* No built in battery.
* Lastly, the price. There are so many features lacking, so I do not understand the price point. If you're willing to spend $600, then check out the Nebula Capsule Max that's less than $500. It is also compact, the size of a coke can. It has a built in battery, 8w speakers, smart interface, bluetooth, and remote. The only thing it doesn't have is native 1080p, it is native 720p. But it's hard to even tell the difference with these little projectors anyway. So I am not sure that paying more money, and having less features is worth that 1080p. And if you have to also lug around an external speaker, a chromecast or fire TV, then it really defeats the purpose of being completely portable. With the Nebula, everything you need is inside a device the size of a coke can.

In conclusion, this is a neat little barebones projector, but the onboard speakers are so bad, you'll need to carry around a portable speaker as well, so it's no longer as portable as I anticipated. At its price point, I assume they're saying it's a premium to have a projector at this size that is 1080p.. But again, that size feature is almost negated by the need to bring along external speakers, and smart devices like a Fire TV stick. And if the Nebula Capsule products doesn't exist, then I guess this price point is justified, but the Nebula does exist, and it's a much better buy. I'm going 3-Stars.

Very easy to use this- I set it up in like a minute without even reading the instructions thanks to the on screen prompts. It was very painless.

Picture quality is so so- it's decent looking but basically, you have to be standing somewhere in front of it to see full color- the image and color is distorted if you look at it from the side or any other angle. But other than that- it does look pretty good and the picture is very usable and nice looking.

Sound- it calls the speakers "loud speakers" but some videos I can BARELY hear sound, others I can hear it if everything around me is quiet and that's with the frame's volume turned up to max! Nothing "loud" about this and sadly it doesn't have bluetooth or amy sound output. I guess if you want sound, your best bet is the play music with some other device along with this.

Overall this is a fairly nice, easy-to-use frame. I loaded pictures and videos on it with ease. The speakers need major improvement. The only other complaint is the price point but these frames all seem to be higher priced than a tv which seems silly. You can get a 24 inch tv with a usb slot cheaper than this 15" screen and it'd probably have better picture. For the price, It should have much better viewing angles/ better video quality.

So the first flatter tvs had HORRIBLE speakers and thus the soundbar was born. The newer tvs however often have great speakers, much better than the soundbars you can add to them. I have a basic $700 LG 70" tv I got here on Amazon and their built in speakers are louder and better than this soundbar. SO I ditched the soundbar pretty quickly and went right back to the built in speakers. Kind of disappointed in this for the price point honestly, I remember buying giant stereos back in the day for cheaper than this that produced a lot more sound. I'd skip this one and go with some bigger speakers maybe if you need a decent amount of sound.

Shipped quickly and efficiently. Sound quality not the best and external power supply not included which is not a good idea. Complete packages are available for about the same price and with better quality sound
Found this item to not be the quality expected low volume along with poor sound quality makes this item usable as a light but not as a quality speaker for extending tv sound

I bought this for my 7 year old daughter. Not sure why radios like this are so pricey nowadays, especially those that use string or bands on the inside (analog tuners) to tune radio stations, gives it a cheap feel, one without durability. The selector switches feel cheap, not sure how long the switches and tuning knob will last, they are probably the weakness on this radio. Overall it is just ok, the sound is not as tinny as some competitor models, which is nice. In the end this is for my 7 year old daughter, just feel a product like this should be priced at about $25.00 - $35.00, not it's current price.

Okay, so this tracker had me intrigued because it can be taken out and used as an earbud. I mean, that's pretty cool, cause you can be at the gym and it'd still be recording all the steps and stuff but also use it to listen to music and stuff. Well, it wasn't as cool as I thought and while the sound is okay, it isn't as good as the normal earbuds I use when I am out at the gym. I also don't feel it really is able to keep up when it's in my ear and I am doing stuff compared to when it's on my wrist and I am doing something. I don't know, I feel like my wrist tracker is hands-down better compared to this tracker. As for receiving phone calls, it works pretty well and it's cool to just pop it out and talk but I can do all that with my normal earbuds too and as I said before, they sound a whole lot better. So, yeah, these are all right but I doubt I will use it anymore just to be honest.
The headphones at the bottom or a little plastic look a little weak and you can't really adjust the size for a small child but the sound does work so

Overall, the keyboard works.  The keys are a good size, they sound fine, and they feel good to press.  But the layout isn't as good, the volume button doesn't spin well, and there aren't enough programmable buttons for my tastes.

Okay, there are three types of devices which are this size. One is an ebook reader. If that's all you want, get a Paperwhite. Seriously, try reading on the Fire's screen for half an hour and it will be like reading on a computer screen (not so good for the eyes). Especially in low light!

The second is a tablet, if that's what you want then get a Galaxy Tab. I have a Toshiba Thrive, which is similar to the Tab (one step down in some respects, the same in others) and that blows this out of the water in terms of what it can do and how it does it. But it isn't the best at playing back movies. eBook capabilities are similar and screen is similar, so if you aren't going to watch movies on it then DO NOT BUY A FIRE HD!!!

The third type of device I call a portable media device. And here is where the Kindle Fire really shines. The screen is currently the best screen available on a 7" device. And the sound is great. Using the built in application, I can play movies ripped from DVDs with great sound and video. On my Thrive I have trouble with this, getting jittery video and low sound most of the time and no consistency. A free program will convert your videos over to Kindle Fire screen size and save them in a format that the Fire can open (search for them, there are many and lots of free options so don't pay for that).

The negatives are, however, many. The Kindle Fire HD sports the UGLIEST user interface I have ever seen. Some replacements are available, and I'm debating them just like I am debating rooting the device to get the Play store. Note that if you have an Android phone, without rooting you can not get your paid apps on the Fire. Also, you can access only a few thousand of the half a million apps that other Android devices offer. This is just because Amazon wants to reduce piracy by restricting apps that may get around protections, but it costs hundreds of thousands of legitimate apps. Also, Google apps are not present (except gmail), so you can't get Google Maps or Voice or the like without sideloading or rooting. I'm not sure why Amazon hates Google, since Google gave them the framework for this tablet! I got the $25 screen protector and I don't like the feel, but that isn't the tablet's fault.

If you have kids, Amazon's kidtime app is great. Other similar apps are available for other devices, and if you want any content this one costs $2.99/month for a one child license, but it is a good app and they did a great job of integrating it so there are no bugs which could cause your kid to find their way out accidentally (or on purpose for those smarter kids out there). If the service was free for Prime members, or if a limited version was free for Prime members, I would rate this app as 5 stars and perhaps raise the entire Kindle Fire HD up a star since that would add one great use which I currently am not taking advantage of.

Oh, and there is no SD slot, no USB slot for external drives, and no IR port so it can't be a remote control (all very disappointing).

Having said all of that, I am keeping mine for movie playback and occasional reading when on a plane or in a doctor's office. I have a 10" tablet which I love and wouldn't trade in for this Kindle if they paid me. But since I can have both (thanks mostly to putting several people together to buy me one present together), this is worth keeping.

I've purchased quite a few compact computers previously and all of them have little quirks that I have to deal with but in the end, I'm able to set them up with the necessary drivers and use them without issues. This Kamrui CK 10, though...

On paper, the specs of this computer is impressive. A 10th generation i7 processor with the integrated Intel graphics which I already knew wouldn't be winning any awards in the gaming department but that's expected. With 16 GB of ram and 512GB of nvme storage, this computer is a good starting point for anyone who needs a fairly powerful PC in a compact package.

Regarding the ram: I've disassembled this computer and found that the ram is soldered to the motherboard, as is the CPU. This means there is no way to upgrade the ram.

Regarding the storage: There is good news here. There are two M.2 slots supporting NVME so SSD storage is quite expandable. I installed another 512gb ssd in the secondary slot.

The operating system that was included was a vanilla Windows 11 Pro with absolutely no additional bloatware aside from what Microsoft has already included. This is good. All drivers were installed and the machine booted fine.

So in my case, it is customary for me to install Windows from scratch when I buy a new computer. It's just something I do. I don't trust that there are no hidden software in the preinstalled systems. As such, I needed to locate the necessary drivers for this computer.

As expected, Windows will successfully detect the graphics, wifi and bluetooth hardware. Also as expected, the Intel chipset drivers needed to be installed manually. All standard so far. With all of this done, there were three pieces of hardware that were unidentifiable. These were the sound drivers.

Scouring the search engines, I couldn't find the drivers for the CK 10. I finally located Kamrui's facebook page, which led to a linktree that then led me to their forums. In the forums, I searched and found a set of drivers for the CK 10. Unfortunately, that seems to be for the CK 10 with an i5 cpu. It did not contain the correct drivers for the sound card.

I resorted to searching for the drivers by device id. From there, I pieced together the necessary drivers to get sound working. I had to use drivers from three different driver sets from HP.

I did reach out to Kamrui's support email. They responded two days later but rather than read what I wrote, they responded with a canned form for me to list my product, serial, purchase date, etc.

So what else is wrong? Well, at least twice per day, this computer freezes without warning. It could be caused by the sound drivers that I had to piece together but how would I know? I don't can't actually get the right drivers for it.

I use an HDMI KVM to control multiple computers. This KVM has an optical output which extracts the audio channel from the HDMI port. I use this optical connection to connect to the 1Mii bluetooth transmitter.

The 1Mii Bluetooth 5.2 Transmitter for TV to 2 Wireless Headphones is a transmitter with an optical and a 3.5mm headphone jack inputs. On the output side, this device transmits through bluetooth 5.2 and supports various bluetooth audio standards such as APTX. You can connect up to 2 bluetooth devices to this transmitter and both will be able to hear the audio.

I picked up this transmitter to replace another transmitter because the 1mii has volume controls that is missing from the other transmitter and dedicated buttons to pair headset 1 and 2. After the replacement, I found that the audio coming from the 1mii was not as loud as my old transmitter. To address this, I actually had to install a volume plugin for Chrome which will boost youtube audio by over 200%. Unfortunately, I can't do the same for my other applications. This is a glaring problem that you will face every day when using this device.

To clarify this a little bit. I pair this device with an open ear bone conduction headset so that I can hear my surroundings while having the computer audio also in my ears. I can certainly put in an earplug to get better sound, it would defeat the purpose of using the open ear design when working at my computer.

Bone conduction headphones have become quite popular and because of this, there are many to choose from. This specific model is quite minimalist. A thin metal frame with the vibration units and electronics hanging off it.

In terms of comfort, there is no adjustability to the metal frame so it may take some getting used to because the frame may feel like they are too big or too small depending on your head size. For me it felt a little bit loose but I came to realize that it actually stayed where you place it and it really wasn't a problem.

For sound quality, this bone conduction headphone will never match a nice pair of over-ear headphones but that really isn't what it's for. By leaving the ears open, one is still able to stay aware of the surroundings, making it great for cycling and jogging where hearing the traffic is essential for safety reasons.

A pair of earplugs are included with this product and with one or both in, one can really appreciate the difference between regular headphones and bone conduction. You can still hear the music (or in my case, audiobook) through the earplugs because of the bone vibration but all outside sound is cut off. This means that you'd be able to listen to music over the sound of a loud machine.

I have tried a few different pairs of bone conduction headphones and these are the ones that I have stuck with so far. The buttons maybe be somewhat limited (just two buttons that control volume and power), but they are easily reachable and not hard to press and the IPX6 means it's water resistant against rain and sweat.

These bone conduction headphones are waterproof (IP68) and come with 16GB of storage so that they would work while swimming (bluetooth will not work well under water and really doesn't have the distance to cover a pool). They can be fairly loud and can be heard even with (especially with) earplugs.

The advantages of an open-ear, bone conduction headphone is that you can hear everything going on around you while still being able to listen to your music or audiobook. Put earplugs in your ear and you can retreat into a more private listening experience.

The disadvantage is that the sound quality is just not going to be as good as headphones that cover your ears. That is especially true for this pair of headphones.

The sound quality from these headphones is not good. The lows are barely audible most of the time and when you turn up the volume to try and hear more of the lower tones (including human voices), the higher tones are already too loud. This is alleviated by putting in earplugs. The plugs will block most of the higher tones as those come out of the speakers themselves while the low tones come in through the vibrations.

Another issue I have is that the buttons are horrible. They are made of a single piece of rubber on the outside and the buttons themselves are recessed pretty far in. This means that I have to push quite far before actually hitting the button and there is just no tactile response to know that I've actually pressed it. This makes everyday use of these headphones a chore.

The last problem I have with it is the custom charging cable. I really do not like devices that do this. Not only do you have to remember to bring the cable with you if you need to charge in your car or elsewhere, if it breaks, you're pretty much screwed.

For the price they are charging (more than Aftershokz Titanium), this really isn't worth it.

The NexHT 1080P Pan Digital Tilt / 8X Zoom Indoor Smart Camera has all of the features that one would want from a wifi camera. Panning, recording, remote viewing, infrared night vision and two-way audio. It is also very small. Designed to look like the Wyze cam, it is actually much smaller at 1.5" wide and 3" tall. While cloud storage services are available, there is a microsd port for local recording.

If one just needs a basic camera at a low price to monitor the home, this camera will serve well. To compare to products such as Wyze, this camera comes up a little bit short. The title of the product is carefully worded to show that the tilt function is "digital", which really means that the camera records with a wide-angled lens and when the phone is held in landscape mode, one can drag the image up and down. When held in portrait mode, the entire height of the image can be seen and there is actually no tilt function. Even so, in both modes, the camera image is squeezed together and not at the correct aspect ratio (I guess this depends on your phone's aspect ratio because the programmers chose not to maintain aspect ratio of the picture).

The recording function is fairly basic. It works like a dashcam in that the camera is always recording and will loop back over itself once the storage is filled.

As with any other wifi home automation product, a separate account needs to be created to log in to the app -- an app one must trust to not send any sensitive information back to the mothership. Personally, I plug this camera into a smart switch that I can turn on only when I'm out so that at least the camera isn't on when I'm at home.

So this camera will do what it advertises but it there really isn't anything that sets it apart from the large number of products out there. Wyze, while being a little bit bigger, costs only $30 and has actual tilt function.

I had this for 6 months, then went to put them on one morning and the right side, inside the sliding part, broke all the way off.  Not repairable. So I’ve used duct tape to hold it together. I’d give the duct tape a perfect score. The sound quality, noise canceling, etc is excellent. The plastic is cheap and doesn’t hold up.
The mic works great.  My only problem is that it cuts out your ipod Touch speaker.  Good for record only mode.  Not good for using with an app that has talk and sound (like Talkatone).

I tried these last night for a little. They plug into the same port as your charger so that kind of rules out using them at night while your phone is charging. I was hoping to use them for music at bedtime but unless I change the time I charge my phone that's a no go. Shame Samsung couldn't have left that regular plug alone on this model. Sound seems to be OK in them.

Let me preface this review with saying that I love the Spectrum Noir markers. Have had both generations and recommend them to everyone. They are easy to use and a good value. On the other hand, I am not so "gobsmacked" about the new line of pencils. I bought the complete set because I am an illustrator and I like to have full sets of the tools I use. First off I was put off by the fact that there are 5 tins to sort through to find a color. I'm sure they did this, so folks could buy a tin at a time, but it easy to keep flipping open lids and looking around for just the right color you want. The pencils also fit very snuggly in the boxes and it is difficult to get them out sometimes.
As for the "creaminess" of said pencils, I would say there are some inconsistencies in that as well. Some of the Floral colors are really soft and creamy, some of the browns and grays are hard and scratchy and then there are some that are just so waxy you can't lay down two colors on top of each other.
If you are a rubber stamper or crafter that plans to use them, you will probably be fine with these. They seem to be geared more to that kind of audience. The price is right for what you get. I had no trouble sharpening the few I used. No breakage like I have encountered with the Prismacolor set I've had for 10 years. The blending solution I suspect is just Gamsol which most stampers already have if they've been using pencils before. I was able to achieve the same results using the Prismacolor pencils I had over the markers.
I will say their customer service rocks because they are going to allow me to send these back. This is a great company to deal with, I just think they kind of missed the mark with these.

Handsome, easy to read display.  Functionality is largely intuitive and easy to understand and learn.  Very good sound and picture quality.  My only reservation was that while I could easily transfer music files from my old iPod that were recorded from CD's, this unit would not allow me to transfer music files that I'd downloaded from the iTunes Library.  (I will concede that it's possible I missed something, but it seemed not to work.)  Overall, though, a very impressive unit.

So one of the reasons I bought this was to be able to charge phones etc since it had such amazing battery storage. Well I was duped.. The outlets only work while the unit is plugged in, yeah pretty dumb. I mean if I have an outlet to plug the unit in to... You guessed it I probably don't need to use the outlets on the unit. But other than that it's a great speaker for the price. Good sound, very durable, easy to use.

Finally I found a device that worked so I could plug my VHS tape player into my PC and use software to create digital files from our old tapes.

When I began this project I really didn’t think it would be near as difficult as it ended up being. I tested a couple similar devices with minimal success - I could achieve video transfer but no audio.

Even with this device I struggled and finally found the only way for audio to transfer was for me to toggle the switch on the side to 16:9 - theoretically this should have nothing to do with sound but in the 4:3 setting I have no sound transfer.

The single sheet of instructions are abysmal. Set up is relatively straightforward unless it doesn’t work. The first thing I would try is switching that toggle switch on the side.

If you are looking to transfer analog VHS tapes to digital using your PC, I recommend downloading OBS Studio (free software) via obsproject.

This device does get warm during use. Since I only used it for limited amounts of time for my specific purpose it wasn’t an issue. If this was to be used long term for connecting a game system to a TV I would question its longevity.

While this worked for my purposes it is a bit glitchy. I got it to work with time thankfully and was able to accomplish what I set out to do.

This is an ok product but not outstanding.

The built in camera and apps on the iPhone allow for so much more creative work than most of us lovers of photography ever dreamed possible - there is no reason not to enjoy that technology. Years ago I never would have dreamed of shooting photos with my phone rather than my DSLR but that is, in fact, often the case.

This has led me to testing, evaluating and reviewing many accessories that make creative shooting with the phone even more versatile than it is natively.

I’ve reviewed a few similar lens kits. This one comes with macro, wide angle and zoom lenses, a mini tripod for the zoom lens, the adapters needed to attach the lenses to the phone and a case for it all.

The wide angle and macro lenses are both decent quality - not professional quality but adequate for hobby enthusiasts. Of the three lenses the macro is the best. The wide angle causes photos focus to get soft towards the edges.

Unfortunately the zoom lens is sub par. While I can get it to work images are consistently below average. Zoom lenses work by utilizing a series of lenses that must be perfectly aligned to capture an accurate, crisp image. While I use excellent photography apps on my iPhone X and worked adjusting the zoom lens I never could get photos near as crisp as with other sets.

This is a mediocre set - I’ve reviewed much worse and a few better, although they were at higher price points. At this price point this is not a bad deal but I certainly wouldn’t rave about this set.

Thanks for reading my review. I enjoy writing them as I value reading other’s reviews when I’m making a buying decision. I regularly update my reviews to reflect any changes I may discover and to include helpful tips you may need if you purchase the product. I will always make every effort to answer any questions I can as it is my pleasure to help.

Being both an audiophile and a lover of all new tech when I first read about this technology coming out a few years ago I started looking forward to testing it.

So what are the potential advantages of bone conduction earphones? I’m glad you asked. When properly adjusted they allow the user to enjoy listening to whatever they choose while not blocking external noises, thus allowing the user to react to ambient noises. This should make them safe to use while driving or doing other activities that require hearing ambient noise in order to conduct safely.

Unfortunately these R9 headphones allow for very little fine adjustment. In order for this type of headphones to work properly and provide the highest sound quality they should rest flat, or almost flat against the skin between the front of the ear and the rear part of the cheek bone. When adjusting the speaker it is clear when the speaker is properly adjusted. The adjustment that I was able to do came from working the rubber casing and sliding the speaker further onto the arm that wraps around the back of the head. By twisting the speaker inward I was able to get the speaker closer to the proper location but not exactly correct. Due to this, sound quality is not optimal and surrounding people are able to hear what the listener is playing.

In terms of design choices I find it odd that while it’s estimated between 70-95% of the population of any ethnicity is right handed this manufacturer chose to place the controls on the left side. This makes controlling them both awkward and difficult. While the buttons operate in a standard press and double press pattern it is awkward reaching across and doing it on the left side.

In terms of operation these headphones maintain a solid connection for the full 33 feet they are rated for and the batteries lasted approximately 6.25 hours on the first full charge cycle. Sound quality is middle of the road especially due to not allowing for fine adjusting of the speakers.

With a couple of minor changes these headphones would be a much better product. If the speakers are held in the correct positions it is much better - if an adjustment system were added these could potentially have much higher sound quality. In addition, obviously the controls should be placed on the right side for ease and regularity of access.

This is a great technology with a lot of potential. These headphones while not capable of fine adjustments would probably fit someone with an average sized head better. My head is a bit smaller than average which made these fit a bit too large for me.

At least it is REALLY water proof. The rest claim to be weather proof but warns you to cover in rain and snow
This unit like all the others I've tried WILL NOT pick up a loud talking voice further than 7' away. This one is 2' further in distance but still no where near as good as the built in mic on cameras you can buy. The over all sound is very clear and the back ground noise is by far the best out of the others sold on amazon. For the price you get what you pay for.

This is the best one that amazon sells for under 30$. If your just needing something for an enclosed porch or small room, this unit will be perfect. If your trying to use in an open area or outside I would suggest finding a unit 2x or 3x the money. It will not meet the advertising claims of distance. But it is weather proof. Has already survived a 3 day rain storm 2 days of sleet n ice and now 6" snow with temps 14 degrees at night. Unit is working like it would on a clear sunny day.
At least they arent lying about those claims like the other.

These headphones were good for a while- they held their charge like they were supposed to in the beginning and they worked really well. Great sound and mic quality- especially for being on the cheaper end of Bluetooth headphones. Though, after a couple of weeks of use, the left headphone specifically would altogether stop charging. I would be able to have it on for maybe 2-8 minutes, then it would notify me that it was at low battery. I'm not exactly sure what happened here, but the left headphone because practically useless. I was able to return them though and got a full refund. I'm sad they didn't work out- they were really cute headphones!

I had hoped this would work well with my new TV, I bought it because of the bluetooth feature. The bluetooth only works for pairing with phones to listen to music - it does NOT connect to your TV via bluetooth. The ironic part is that the connector that comes with it doesn't fit most TVs. Awesome. I had to go buy other parts to make it work. The GIGANTIC remote it comes with now only controls the volume and nothing else and my regular remotes will not work on the volume at all.
Everything about these gets a “c” on the report card. They are okay comfortable, they sound okay and they only lasted about 9 months. I would not order these again.

These lose the charge SUPER FAST. Once you figure out how to turn them on, off and connect with device, they sound amazing. I listened to Soundgarden,  Tame Impala and Led Zeppelin through them to get a feel for sound nuances, once again proving that music is literally the best invention in the world! Super comfortable to wear too so I want to use them all the time. But when I reach for them, they are always dead. Even when they had a charge left in them from previous use. I hate always leaving things on a charger, but I guess I have to with these.

The biggest difference between this projector & the much more expensive projectors in professional settings is the bulb. This one does a fine job in low light or with back light but will completely wash out with light around or over the screen. I ordered this primarily to do presentations & show videos at my club meetings. It performed well but we did have to fiddle a bit with the lights in the room & the position of the projector.

The usefulness of this projector is its portability & low cost. It is lightweight & compact & fairly easy to set up. I would have appreciated a padded carry case for the projector but the box it comes in works pretty well. It has foam that surrounds the projector, it holds all the cords, it has a handle & it is easily sturdy enough to set the projector on for more height.

It helps a lot with the focus & clarity if the projector is nearly horizontal. That means that if the projection screen is to be 4' over the ground then the projector also needs to be 4' off the ground which is generally going to be much higher than a table. The focus ring around the lens works very well to dial in the clarity. There is a foot that unscrews from the bottom front to angle the projector up. I tried propping something under the front to angle it higher but the image distorts & loses clarity the more it is tilted.

The biggest issue I have had with the projector is the image source. I can't get either of my laptop computers to recognize the projector as an external screen with the HDMI cable but the HDMI works on a DVD player. The IOS control works pretty well with my iPad. My Pixel phone doesn't support the built-in Miracast. The Bluetooth only recognizes my Samsung TV & none of my phones, computers or tablets sees the projector's Bluetooth signal. It has a YouTube app built into the device software but it is un-useable due to a cumbersome search process that doesn't return any results. I ended up using it with a USB thumb drive which works well & the menu is easy enough to navigate but takes some learning. I did not try the AV cable inputs or the SD memory slot.

This actually fits my needs pretty well, I just wanted a BT speaker for my daughter to use to practice her routines instead of turning the speakers all the way up on her iPhone. The sound is generated by a single-cone speaker, about 4" diameter & the enclosure doesn't do much to improve the sound. It probably won't sound as good as the device it's hooked to but it is louder & without distortion.
Bluetooth setup is easy but it will only link to one device at a time, I have to "forget" it from another device before linking to another. I haven't used it with USB, or micro SD (or even the audio jack) but since it doesn't have any kind of display I think it would be a pain to play anything but a pre-arranged set list or track albums. I have never run the battery all the way down so I don't know how long it lasts but it lasts a while.

These sound excellent though they aren't as dynamic as other earbuds I have tried & are a little light on bass. They are very comfortable, stay in the ear very well & I like that they grip the inner ear instead of going around the ear. Only having the inner ear clamps also makes the charger smaller. The earbuds charge in a small box that has a battery of it's own so they can recharge in a pocket.

When we first got these they set up easily & quickly. After about 2 weeks they quit pairing each other. Now, each earbud will connect individually with a phone but not with each other. I would drop a star but my daughter still uses them, one at a time & still likes them.

The good news is that it DOES work, and sounds pretty decent for a cheap no-name brand. If you've installed a double din stereo before, it should be pretty familiar and straight forward.
But let's just jump right into the odd design. Why is there an "external mic" option that is RIGHT NEXT to the internal mic? Usually an external mic is supposed to be mounted somewhere closer to the driver's mouth (up by the visor or mirror, or over the dash by the steering wheel, etc). The purpose is to get better sound, and either having the internal one as a backup if you don't want to mount one, or using it to pick up ambient background noise for NR filtering. Having an external nub right next to the internal one makes ZERO sense at all! Why even have one?! If anything, making it lower than the internal one seems like it would get WORSE sound, and if the position were so good, why not make THAT where the internal one is? Not to mention it looks weird as heck.
The features seem to be functional at least, but it has a pretty noticeable lag to the user interface. If you're expecting an OEM style menu experience, you might be disappointed. This feels like an old-school web browser loading pages when you open up a feature. Compared to modern units like, for example an Atoto F7, this feels like something a generation older at least.
I want to give this at least 3 stars for functional purposes, but the truth is I know that you get a much better unit for not a lot of money more. I can't really recommend it unless it is on an extreme sale.

I'm very conflicted writing this review. As music listening and noise cancellation devices, they are wonderful! You can wear this in a noisy environment and get lost in your own tunes or just hear yourself think. Also, it has a similar functional design as Air Pods that allows air in to make it comfortable to wear without the vacuum "under water" seal effect that other ear buds have. So out of the box, color me impressed- comfortable and sounds great, what could be better, right?
Well, the reason I wanted to try Jabra over other brands is their commitment to call quality. Back in the early days of Bluetooth, Jabra was one of the kings if you wanted to ensure a clear 2-way conversation on a call. A lot of portable audio devices these days overlook mic quality and put all their effort into music / playback, with Apple, Sony, and some other big brands being the exception.
Sadly, these Jabras don't seem to deliver in that regard. People we call constantly complain they can't hear us, that we sound far away, under water or over-compressed / missing parts of our voice. In quiet environments it seems to work ok, but maybe the noise cancellation bit is working overtime? I don't know. All I know is I'm so disappointed with the call quality, I can't rely on these if I want the other party to hear me clearly. Yes, the ANC is awesome. Yes, the music sounds good. Yes they are comfortable. But if you need to switch to another headset to make a phone call, these are silly. I really wish it wasn't so.

I wanted to upgrade my 04 Solara stock radio to one with bluetooth and a backup camera, but the car has a JBL factory amp and I wanted to keep this install as simple as possible (especially including steering wheel controls). Crutchfield recommended this model to make that happen, but it was out of stock so I ordered it here instead.
Well, for starters it only supports control over L+R, fading from front front to rear isn't an option as it just sends both front and back speakers the same signal. That's fine for a limitation, I did read that from the description here so I wasn't surprised, but it was just the first sign of a product that seems half baked. Next up, the steering wheel controls DID NOT WORK. I have an Atoto head unit, and none of the dip switch SWC settings worked. You have to set the buttons on the Atoto, but no matter what switch settings I used, I only got SOME of the buttons working and not others. Like, sometimes only vol + but not vol -, or a different setting gave me just mode and track down, but never all of them at once. I reached out to customer support and it took several tries to get a response, after which they gave me a different set of switch settings to try (not one from the manual) which still didn't work.
In the end, I cut the SWC wires from the harness and fed them directly to SW1 and SW2 on the Atoto harness directly, and got them ALL to show up and set correctly! So basically, buying the model with SWC retention was a waste of extra money as it didn't even work.
Then I had some ground loop noise I was trying to troubleshoot. To be fair, it could have been the radio, so I tried wiring it directly to speakers to see if the output from the radio had it... it did not. Another weird issue is that I noticed a faint hiss coming from the speakers EVEN WHEN THE RADIO WAS POWERED OFF. As in, I'm not playing anything and want the car to be dead silent, but the adapter still turned on the amp even if the head unit is off! It was more pronounced when I had ground loop noise, but now that I've mostly fixed that, there is still an obvious hum like there is power going to the amp and it is waiting for sound. This should power it off if my radio is off, but that is not happening. I reached out to Crux again, multiple times, explaining the problem and got no response. I reached out again and asked if I could just buy another wire harness in case there is something wonky about the one I have (the swc issue I later realized might have been one of the wires not communicating to the adapter, since connecting only sw1 or sw2 at a time made it act the way it did before with only half the buttons working at a time- but obviously my wire to the car was working as was the headunit because different settings switched around which buttons were active... so the fault must have been in the adapter or harness). No response. It was too late to return it so I tried troubleshooting on my own.

I'm living with the faint hiss for now, when the car is on it isn't a big deal and usually I'm listening to something anyway so that's fine. The fade from front to back is fine because its a coupe and not like there's a lot of difference between the front and rear of the car. The SWC buttons are working because I bypassed the faulty operation of the Crux unit, so it's mostly fine now. But I feel like I overpaid for something that under delivered. I wish I had gone with a different interfacing adapter and/or bypassed my factory amp. This was supposed to make the installation EASY and it ended up causing me more grief instead.
Also? Crux customer support has been terrible. When they did finally respond, it seemed like they didn't want to help because I didn't buy it from one of their authorized retailers and I wasn't a professional installer. Their website also went down for weeks in the middle and I feared they went out of business due to the pandemic. They have since responded so I know they are still around, but were not really helpful. The technical team at Atoto was worlds more helpful (they wanted it to work and were trying everything to see if the problem was on their side). It seems the problem was with Crux's adapter and their lack of support.

[[VIDEOID:2212eb120f801d8851a76eb4e94985a0]] This is a really cool way to make your head unit act like a tablet. If you have Android Auto in your dash, you already know that it is pretty cool but a watered down experience of the full blown OS on your phone. It also relies on your phone being plugged in. This device eliminates that by having its own complete Android operating system on a stick that appears on your display, completely independent of your phone. Complete with play store and streaming apps! It is a very cool concept and pretty useful, but sadly I hit some snags along the user experience:
1) You have to wait 30 seconds for it to boot every time you start the car.
2) Unlike Android Auto on your phone, you need to supply an internet connection (you can use your phone as a hotspot if your plan allows and you have enough data, but it is extra steps involved every time you boot if you want to connect)
3) There is no shutdown/sleep. When you turn off the car, the device abruptly dies and has to start fresh again each time. Aside from the long boot up each time, this leads to two potential problems:
3a)The time/date resets every time you turn the ignition. If you don't have a network connection for it to grab the correct time, it will default to thinking it is Dec 31st and 7am. Every. Single. Boot.
3b) Anyone who knows how operating systems work can vouch that if you are in the middle of a write operation (saving a file, updating an app, etc) storage could become corrupted if power is immediately shut without warning to the device. There is no warning to the device, it's either on while the car is, or dead when the ignition is cut. Heck, even if you leave the ignition in the acc position so it remains powered on, if you turn to the ignition position, that momentary cut to the power while the car starts means another 30 second reboot and the time reset to 7am. Very annoying.
4) There is no pinch to zoom option, which some apps (like maps) assume is available for the user experience.
5) Bluetooth support from a phone is very poor. The unit can tell you that a call is coming in, but you can't answer or initiate the call without exiting the UI and either going back to the head unit menu, or controlling it from the phone. Also, no phone audio (A2DP) is played from the phone because the MStick is using the Bluetooth profile for its own audio.

In a nutshell, a lot of these caveats could be worked around with some design changes. The stick could be built with a small internal battery much like a phone or tablet, so that it can sleep when the power is shut off and wait for the user to turn the car back on without rebooting from scratch. This would also solve the time reset issue.
The same way that there is a button on the nav bar to pull down the notification shade, there could be a button to enable pinch zooming within apps that require it.

There could also be a built in way to attach another display, perhaps mirror to a phone or remote desktop in so that you can set up all your apps, etc, at home in the comfort of your wifi instead of doing all of this outside in the car. Everytime I wanted to try something, I had to tinker outside in my driveway and run down my car's battery and/or waste fuel keeping it running for no reason. Little things like that would make a HUGE difference in the end user experience. This product seems like more hassle than it is worth for the average user, but is an excellent proof of concept if you want to, for example, have Torque running on your car display but not upgrade the whole stereo to an Android powered one.
BUT, then again, it sort of begs to wonder why not just get an Android tablet or old phone and mount it on the dash and leave the radio to connect with your phone? The user experience might be better than working around the caveats that this introduces.

These are great for removing the clutter that comes from traditional PC speakers. Personally, I'm tired of the mess that my home editing/gaming PC speakers take: A right and left speaker with a cable connecting them, a cable with a 3.5mm jack to go into the back of the computer case, and then another cable to go into the outlet for power. It's just a mess of wires and really makes me miss my old Macintosh from the early 90s that had integrated speakers inside the case.
I was thinking about trying to wire up a DIY dynamic speaker inside my case, when I discovered this listing on Amazon. It essentially is a USB sound card built into a small stereo speaker array. All powered off the USB port. So you need one, single USB cable, no multiple wires back and forth, and no more giant wall adapter on my power strip! It actually is pretty cute on my desk, doesn't take up a lot of space, and has an integrated volume dial. Awesome!
The only catch? The sound isn't so great. And when that's the purpose of the product, you have to be a little upset about it. I have portable Bluetooth speakers that sound much clearer than this. It's not that it doesn't get loud (it totally can), but the clarity is lacking, as is the bass (in a major way). It's hard to describe- it's louder than a phone, but still has that tin sounding quality I'd expect from a speakerphone. Not exactly high quality. I wouldn't watch a movie or use it for atmospheric game soundscapes, but if you have a home PC and don't want to wear headphones or clutter up your desk with lots of wires, the single USB connection is pretty nice.

[[VIDEOID:2e1e48afafe7261f888f4fa063c2dbdd]] I really like the fact that this is a larger display than the 7 inchers you usually find in car radio replacements. That's what initially attracted me to trying this unit, since my Toyota Solara's double din dash kit has tons of unused space to the right and left of the faceplate. The problem?
It's *slightly* too large vertically, and is centered instead of starting at the bottom. To explain: I measured my dashboard and realized it would stick up past the top and partially cover the bottom of my hazard button as well as the vents, but that's livable. I don't use the hazard button very often, and the vents can be adjusted away from it. The problem is, it sticks out both top AND bottom, with the middle double-din sized part being centered in the display. That downward part concerns me because of my ability to turn the knobs for the climate control underneath. I wish that the unit started at the bottom of the double-din space and only went UP only. That's what I was expecting it to do, the way modern car radios have displays that stick out vertically but are flush with the dash underneath. I'm not ok with it rubbing against the climate knobs.
I took a video of trying to install it on my dash kit before I gave up and put it back in the box. I DID hook it up to 12v power just to see it turn on and make sure everything works, and I have to say it's a shame because this LOOKS really cool. I love that it runs Android and has all the customization I'd crave from a system like that. Android Auto is a treat too. I didn't hook up any speakers so I can't vouch for sound quality and I can't vouch for the longevity of the unit since I didn't actually keep it in my car, but it looks like a pretty good value for the money if this fits your dash layout.

I listen to lectures on headphones when doing chores around the house and often can't hear people trying to get my attention. I've seen neck speakers before, and I thought it would be a very cool option for me as my family gets kind of annoyed that I can't hear them and they can't tell if I'm currently listening to something.
But I'll be honest, after trying these, I'm not really loving them. I had a pair of sunglasses speakers that aimed sound towards my ears, but this sort of blasts sound out and around me. Like, not even towards my ears. Basically, it seems just as loud to someone else in the room with me as it does to me, which then begs the question of why not just use an external speaker at that point? The call quality was just OK as well. The one thing I can say is that the build quality seems quite good. It feels really durable and made with premium feeling materials. But I just can't shake the feeling that for the asking price, I'm missing the point of these. Shouldn't the speakers be facing upwards towards my ears instead of blasting at each other in front of my Adam's Apple? Seems like a weird design that might be missing the mark.

This has so much potential, but just barely falls short of what I want in a media center remote. I have a fire stick 4k attached to a TV, and while the stock IR remote it came with is close to everything I need (can do TV's volume and power thanks to pre-programmed IR), it lacks a keyboard and programmable buttons (my stereo system isn't in the Fire TV's list so it can't control it, and I use that for surround sound). I have a USB host adapter that allows me to use media keyboard combos like this one on the stick, so I could have my QWERTY but traditionally then I'd give up the Alexa mic and IR controls of the stock remote since they usually don't have that. Whats amazing about this is that on paper I should still have everything I love- a QWERTY on one side, nav pad and plenty of shortcut buttons on the flip side, programmable IR buttons (YES!), and even a voice assistant mic button!
Seems too good to be true, because it sort of it. The mic button doesn't seem to work on Fire stick or even on my old Chinese Android player box. In Windows it seems to launch Cortana but I don't use that. Maybe it does something on Apple TV like invoke Siri, but I don't have one to test. The button in my case, is useless. Also, the programmable IR buttons? I was able to train the buttons to my TV for power and vol + and -. but not the stereo system. Sometimes it would seem to work and remember one side (either volume up or down) but never both together. I'd clear the buttons to default and start over, and then the TV ones wouldn't work either (commence tearing out hair). After a few cycles attempted to learn my IR codes, I got the TV working again but never the entire stereo system. What stinks is that I can already do that on my stock Firestick remote, and at least there I also get working Alexa voice command via the same remote. This didn't do that properly. Also on the firestick, system android volume settings don't effect anything. So I really wanted to reprogram the vol up and down buttons to the IR codes, but I could only do that on one of the 4 programmable buttons.

The air mouse function is really useful, and having the full keyboard is cool and good to have, but sadly this isn't that much better than the cheaper standard USB or BT keyboards you could already hook up and lose the voice input and IR control. You still need both, and in my case also the remote for the surround sound. I was hoping to consolidate all of those into one unit, and this really COULD have been the one to bring them all together if it was designed better.

I wanted to use these to replace some older bookshelf speakers in our living room, currently connected to a streaming Alexa-enabled player. I like that these have two auxiliary inputs so technically I can attach it to our audio system and ALSO something like our home theater receiver, and occasionally use Bluetooth to connect to a phone when needed. These are much nicer looking and sound really good compared to my old speakers, however I'm rather annoyed that everytime they power up it defaults to Bluetooth again. My audio system gets shut off at night and turned back on in the morning via a switch. I really wish the speakers would go back to the last setting used, or perhaps have a way to change the default. As it is right now, every morning we have to find the remote and press Line 1 to hear the music, despite the player trying to play. Even worse, if we can't find the remote, there's NO WAY to change settings on speaker itself. This just seems like an unnecessary extra step and it has made some of my family members prefer the old speakers instead, sadly.
It is very unfortunate because these otherwise have the potential to be so incredible! But this is a usability fail. It should at the very least recall the last mode used.
These headphones lasted approx. 3 months. The wires were super thin and just using them when I walked, the tiny wires inside disconnected & broke and no longer any sound.

They come with small, medium, and large earbud nubs to properly fit into your ear.  The main thing I don't like about these earbuds is the sound quality isn't the greatest. Not bad for the price. Maximum volume is lower than I'd hoped, but I suppose I should've expected that from a small speaker like this. My biggest annoyance is that there isn't any way to skip forward/back using the controls on the speaker. I suppose you get what you pay for.

These are very similar to many of the other cheaper kids headphones.

This affordable radio is perfect for my needs. Yet, I miss the quality from the higher end Sony portable.  Sorry, the sound is a bit tinny.  Yet, I am a fan of the controls, display and design.  Good value.

Unlike Coke Cola company, which continues to produce exceptional products, Sony has thrown in the towel when it comes to it WALKMAN market share, and loyal customers. While millions of hard working adults and millions of dillegent students have turned to Sony Walkman for their music while at the gym or out in the sports field, Sony has turned its back on them. This D-NF340 will be one of the last walkmans, as its quality has continuously diminished, and Sony has lost its willpower to make leading edge MUSIC.

First, the FM Tuner does a poor job in getting a good reception. I mostly get static on my machine. So, what happened SONY? Where is the quality?

Second, the CD Style is outdated, as so many are moving into SD cards, micro SD cards, and internal memory to play the music. Sony should have continued with their ATRAC-3 technology, and onto memory stick, rather than throw in the towel to just MP3. Yet, something could be said about going MP3, which makes sense. But, not providing a SPORTS walkman, now that is bad news. It is like Coke Cola saying to Pepsi, "ok, you win." Now, wait a minute. Both Coke Cola and Pepsi continue to make advancements, and both continue to make sales and keep business going. So, what happened Sony. Is this the end for Sony? The CD style is also very bulky. There is no need to carry such a bulky physical CD anymore. But, another version of the Walkman should have been created. Shame on you, Sony.

Third, the knobs and controls are good, yet they could be better served on a digital walkman. There is something nice by having knobs and buttons, controls and sliding switches. The controls of such nature blend well with humans who are sweating, running, exercising, stretching, pulling, pushing, bumping, etc. The digital up/down arrows, push etc. just are not controling enough for this person. Maybe it is the same with driving a car. Manual transmission, putting the hand on the stick shift knob, feeling the car going from first to second, from second to third, and so on. That feel is part of being human. Not sure why a sports version of a digital mp3 player by the GREATEST CREATOR of WALKMAN cannot put together such a product. Knobs, oh how they provide controlable pleasure.

Fourth, the sports thing. This CD player, along with its many many prior versions failed the drop test. Oh, so many start loosing a function, like the loss of one side audio, or loss of display, etc. after one drop on the ground. And, because they are heavy, what can you expect. Ahh Punka, Bash, Blop, Clunk!, Dah Pinga, Dah Dong, Blip, Ding, Dong, Crash, Kaput. Even the sports version was heavy. Eh. So, yeah SONY WALKMAN designers, make the MP3 version with digital memory, in the light weight version, please. Sweat resistant, slightly water resistant (for the rain,) unlike this one. Dah? Where have you been Sony? And, call it the Walkman, MAN!!

Now, for all the poor people who just do not want to hurt their eyes, make the display FONT size a good bit larger. Give your loyal customers a break. Large enough so it can be seen in various environments - lighted room, darken street, etc. Some of us JOG at night, and can use the larger font size.

Until then, this product is a "don't buy." It is not a sports version, It is not supported by Sony software, it is not MP3 and ATRAC3, it is not light weight, it is not water resistant, ... what it is ... OLD FASHION.

These started out great. If you can find a way to protect and waterproof the outlet these need to plug into (yes, they're battery powered as well but it's useless) these worked really well at first. The wireless channel connected quickly and I could play my iPod through them clearly in my backyard and could even adjust their volume from my iPod alone. But after having these live in their new outdoor home their quality slowly degraded and then the right speaker starting disconnecting constantly and just buzzing loudly. Over time the speakers began sounding tinny and harsh until finally the right speaker stopped connecting entirely.

There are very similar style speakers to these on the market which work better. These are cheap and poorly made.

Pros: these are comfortable headphones with great noise isolation and noise canceling.

Cons: I was shocked by how poor the sound quality was considering the price tag. The sound was nothing special. They sounded less crisp than the 10 year old non brand name $15 earbuds I was using up to this point.

I feel like these are worth buying only if you value the noise cancelling feature and don’t care much about how the actual music sounds.

I returned these, bought the Sennheiser 598s, and was very happy with those.

Sound is ok unless you want it louder (about 60-70% of the volume control range) , then you can clearly hear a distortion on the middle and high frequency. It holds the lower range pretty good. The volume control knob is small, tight and slippery. It's hard to turn or rotate it without holding the speaker. Price/quality ratio is good, that's why 3 stars.
There's no output for headphones.

The headband is lightweight, but unfortunately it has stretched out enough that it wanders as I sleep, which then moves speakers. The sound is good if I can get them adjusted to the right spot, but there is no way to secure them in that spot , so it is a constant placement challenge. I WISH they were wireless!  Speakers are just too labile, Very annoying. And now one speaker seems to be much quieter than the other. May return because of this issue.

I had a TDK A33 and bought this one to get a louder speaker with better battery life. The sound of the Big Jambox should be WAY richer for the price, I was disappointed.

The TDK A33 sounds WAY better than this speaker, it's water proof and it's less than half the price, but its battery sucks... :(

I need a better product.

The Bose SoundSports have a nice, clear sound, but they are VERY large! I purchased the Samsung Earbuds after these, and all I ever use are the Samsung's. The Bose SS HAVE to be used with at LEAST the Right bud everytime. Cannot be used independently. The Samsung's can. And I LOVE THAT.

Samsung earbuds are tiny and fit so well in my ears. I wanted these Bose SS's for over 3 years, and FINALLY got them on sale, but was disappointed. Sound quality is good, but still overall chose the Samsung's for size and independent usage. Battery life is better in Samsung's too.
The sound quality is average. One ear bud stopped working after three days.Returned the item

I've had this camera a few months. The install went pretty well. I had to reboot a few times to pick the camera up, but once it was recognized, that has worked well. The camera does not clamp securely onto my external monitor. I fixed that problem by getting a separate flexible arm that clamps onto my desk and holds the camara. I love the physical lens cover so I can easily control when the camera is capturing an image. The picture quality is great. I love having an external camera instead of relying on the one on my laptop so my laptop can stay connected to the docking station and I don't have to try to get it moved over to the center of my desk every time I have a videoconference. Unfortnately there there are two remaining problems that are making me now decide to look for another camera:

1. Echos: When using this camera, is it causes an echo on videoconferencing that others can hear. I cannot hear it. It is so annoying to others that immediately people start talking about it and asking if the call can be done using some other audio. It definitely happens on Microsoft Teams calls as others have said in the Questions section for this product on Amazon. I can't remember if it happened on Webex videocalls also. Others have said switching the audio source solves that problem.

2. Wide View: This may be standard on these cameras. I'll find out when I shop for a new one, but the view is much wider than my native laptop camera. I can't find any way on the camera to "crop" it so that it shows only the person during videoconference and not a lot of what is to the right and left of the person. I solved that problem by installing OBS Studio and the OBS virtual camera. OBS allows me to crop the picture and then uses that video as the "camera" in Microsoft Teams. That works very well to get a good cropped video, however, the image quality went way down and it freezes up sometimes, so it is not a great solution because I end up not having smooth starts to videoconferences with all the troubleshooting I have to do to get OBS, the webcam, and the conferecing software to all work together.

I hope I can find a camera that works seemlessly so that the now much more frequent videoconferences, thanks to the pandemic, will go more smoothly.

The sound is pretty good with these headphones - gets very loud.  They are not so good for activities because they easily fall out of my ears and are not very comfortable.  These are probably fine if you are sitting at a desk and not moving around.

Overall these are not bad. Sound quality is good overall and the volume has a nice range. The size of them is not bad and doesn't bother my ears if I wear them for hours. The only problem I have is that every now and then there is some random static.

Annoying hum when volume is past 50%

I’m on the fence. I’ve got another week before I can no longer return these, and it’s been a bittersweet experience. I love this tablet and, if it weren't for the battery life and how long it takes to recharge, I would give it 5 stars. The tablet itself is beautiful, thin, lightweight and works beautifully. I have had mine since the beginning of September 2014, and I have only had to reboot it twice since then (due to errors, I mean). The display is beautiful. The sound is quite good, for a tablet. And now that Samsung has allowed it to upgrade to Lollipop, I can run most of my new apps from my 32 gb SD Card and this leaves me a lot less nervous about running out of memory. Though, I still find the 16 GB HD a bit on the tight side overall.

My previous tablet was a Toshiba Excite AT305T16. It was my first tablet, but I still could tell how slow it was. And it constantly needed to be rebooted. Everything kept getting bound up on it. Not so with this Samsung. It is quick, it stays fresh, and it just plain performs. Which is all we ask for, right? I will be buying more Samsung products in the future, I think. Those guys really know and deliver quality. Now, if they could just improve the battery and be a bit more generous with the on-board memory.

UPDATE: I have downgraded my review by one star. I have owned this tablet since August of 2014. And, although I still enjoy it, I am now running out of memory and, even though I have a 64gb sd card attached, I am finding it increasingly challenging and frustrating to manage the remaining space. While many of the apps can be moved to the SD card, most of them can't. And the apps themselves are becoming larger and larger overall. And, to make matters worse, suddenly, I can no longer update many of my apps residing on the SD card, unless I move them back to the internal storage first. This is too laborious and time consuming and I haven't found a fix for it yet. Also, suddenly I can no longer move PDF files onto the SD card either. Other types of files can be moved as before, but not the PDF files. Wondering if the tablet performed some sort of automatic system upgrade that may have triggered these issues. When I "upgraded" (and I use that term lightly, with tongue in cheek) from Kitkat to Lollipop, the tablet lost some very useful functions. So now I have to wonder why these problems are suddenly cropping up?

I had a keyboard die when I spilled liquid on it so I grabbed the first one I saw available without looking at the details. When I opened the box and found that this was a backlit keyboard with large print keys, I was intrigued. As an old, retired guy, I spend hours a day at the computer gaming, streaming videos, and staying in touch with a far-flung network of family and friends via social media. This keyboard is particularly nice for the gaming. The white backlight against the black keyboard, as well as the large print keys make it very easy for me to hit the right keys when my eyes are bouncing back and forth between the screen and the keyboard while my hands are handling the both the keyboard and the mouse. This keyboard makes my responses faster and more accurate, which I very much appreciate as an older gamer.

There are those irritating glitches though. One of the worse is that the backspace key constantly sticks. Thankfully, I don't use that key in my gaming, or this keyboard would be totally unusable for me. When typing things like this review though, or posts on social media, that sticky key is very frustrating. Every time I have to backspace to clear a mistake I have to hit that key repeatedly, like I had to do three times while typing this sentence. What makes it even worse is that there is no telling how many hits it takes to move back the necessary amount of spaces. So it is very easy to backspace too far, causing even more mistakes.

Another glitch is that the keys seem bigger than on my last keyboard. I don't notice that in gaming, but when typing more than a few sentences of text, my hands and fingers begin to feel some strain. There are some minor glitches too. The volume control on my speakers is in an awkward place to reach. My last keyboard had separate volume control keys, making it easy to adjust the volume from the keyboard. This one also has volume controls but they are on the function keys, requiring two buttons to be pressed to raise or lower the volume. That sounds like a small thing but every time I adjust the volume,it is a bit irritating to have to hit two keys instead of one. And finally, this keyboard bills itself as "quiet". Hah! It's probably the nosiest, clackity clack typing I've done in a long, long time.

All in all, this keyboard feels like a cheaper knockoff of a higher quality one. For now I'll use this one, because I need it. As soon as I find that higher quality keyboard though, this one is getting tossed out.

As an old, retired guy I spend a lot of time online gaming, streaming videos, and dabbling on social media. Over the last few months I've tried out a variety of keyboards and mice, some of them high end gaming gear. As soon as you take this keyboard and mouse out of the box it's clear that this is a low end rig. It just doesn't have the solid heft of more expensive equipment. That's not necessarily a bad thing though as I've used some excellent, inexpensive keyboards and mice. Sadly, this product is not of that caliber either.

The compact size makes the keyboard feel cramped when typing. Even as I'm writing this, my fingers are feeling strained from the cramped tightness. The manufacturer makes the 12 function/F key combos seem like a big deal. To me those combos just seem like an unnecessary complication. There are other, more standard ways of doing all those things without having to learn a whole new set of keys. The six "hot keys" seem to be just a set of video controls that duplicate functionality already available on any computer with a standard video player.

The mouse is particularly disappointing for anyone who does gaming. Now I'm just a casual gamer, by no means a hard core one, and even I find this mouse to be a handicap. In my main game you move your character forward by holding down both the left and right mouse buttons simultaneously. With other mice that is no big deal. With this mouse there is a perceptible hesitation or stutter before moving when holding down the buttons like that. That may not sound like a big deal to a non-gamer but that kind of stuttering can quickly get your character killed in a gaming battle. Also, it seems to take some effort to hold those buttons down. My fingers feel a strain in holding these mouse buttons down, a strain I haven't felt with other mice. And yes, I did try the suggested solutions for mouse problems offered in the "Manual" that came with this product (one tiny sheet printed on both sides). They didn't help.

So if you are mostly watching videos and reading Facebook on your computer, you will probably be okay with this gear. Any more serious use than that and you will want to pass on this stuff.

My first thought when I initially saw the Motorola Sphere 2-in-1Bluetooth Speaker with Over-Ear Headphones was, wow. It is extremely attractive and would definitely appeal to the young folks. Ironically, our house is full of loud, music playing teenagers who have very clear ideas about what sounds good and which products they prefer to use. They like speakers and headphones that offer clear sound quality with bass. We have a Bose Soundlink speaker, and VModa or Sennheiser earphones. So unfortunately when I reviewed these, I was comparing them with others that I have used. While this product might look good (definitely a 5), it needs to sound good. And this is where I am disappointed – in the sound quality.
In a nutshell:

Attractiveness – The Motorola Sphere is attractive. It is black and looks like a head with headphones.The system looks nice on a bookshelf, desk or dresser in a dorm room, bedroom, etc.. I do love the look.

Set up – The directions for setting up the device are easy to follow. Once you pair the headphones and the sphere (separately) to your phone (via Bluetooth), it is pretty easy to use. There is sometimes a lag when you disconnect or switch between the sphere and the headphones. You might have to press the button on the headphones to make the sound switch between the two devices.

Headphones – They are adjustable and the sound quality is good via the headphones.

Sound Quality – The sound quality is not good thru the speaker. I’d give it 2.5 at the most. To me the frequency response seemed a little high, which is why the sound thru the speaker is hollow or missing something, no matter the genre (i.e., classic, jazz, rap, rock) played. But a plus is that the quality of the sound thru the headphones is better, it is more balanced and therefore rates 3.5-4 (although the bass is still not heavy).

In conclusion, while I love the look and concept (2 in 1 – speaker and headphones) of the Motorola, I wouldn’t recommend it. I would instead suggest investing a little more money and getting a better more quality speaker.

Slept two nights with these headphones in their stock configuration and decided I could create something far superior.
For several years I’ve owned and extensively used a pair of the original wired SleepPhones. They are extremely comfortable. The drivers are only 2-3mm thick and sandwiched between two layers of felt. The fleece headband stayed in place without feeling constrictive. It was also easy to wash - open the hook and loop closure on the back, pulled out the speakers and wires, wash, dry, re-install.
By contrast, MusiCozy uses thicker drivers (granted, the frequency response is better than the SleepPhone drivers) then adds a rubber cover, then covers that with a thin jersey fabric. The headband was painfully tight, and I don’t have a big head (22.5”). After the first night, I stretched the headband over a small throw pillow for a day and that helped a bit. But the second night, the thick drivers hurt my ears so bad I took the whole thing off. I mostly sleep on my side and stomach. It’s also tricky to charge because the port is only accessible if you line up the slit in the jersey fabric just right. Some simple product testing would have identified these issues. But for $20, I couldn’t be happier….. why?
SleepPhoness wants $100 for their bluetooth units. I’m sure they are top-notch but I didn’t want to spend that much. Here’s my solutions: The entire MuziCozy headband was disassembled….all two components. The bluetooth receiver / battery compartment and speakers come out easily enough. The fake ‘control panel’ on the front isn’t needed. The speakers have a rubber cover that is not needed. Once that is removed, the speakers are only 3-4mm thick, which is good. I disassembled the wired SleepPhones as well. The felt driver covers were re-used with the MuziCozy drivers, then the whole thing was re-installed into the SleepPhone headband.
This is the best setup - the headband is comfortable, I can still use it to cover my eyes, the sound quality is improved, and the MuziCozy charge port is easier to access thanks to the large velcro opening on the back of the headband.
My girlfriend, by contrast, likes absolute silence while sleeping so she uses the MuziCozy headband to make sure her earplugs don’t fall out and to cover her eyes.
So the entire unit has gone to good use, just not in the way it was delivered. I’m happy with the results but the original product need some redesign.

I really wanted to love this keyboard. Having a wireless keyboard to type on a propped up laptop while studying was my solution to really bad back pains. And for the first 2 days I loved this keyboard. The keys don't jiggle when typing, everything about the look/design/feel is sleek and smooth. The integration with my macbook and my iphone was seamless. The keys fought off dust and crumbs for a week.

HOWEVER:

1) Please be wary of the fragility of some of the keys. I had only been using the keyboard for the first day or so when I noticed that my "-" (dash key) was loose. Upon further investigation with a magnifying glass, a small piece of plastic had been broken, which was why I couldn't snap the key back into place. I don't bang keys loudly or carelessly when I typed, and given that I hadn't had the keyboard for very long, I assumed it the product arrived with a defective key. After a few days, I looked at my F2 key (bluetooth key)- I touched this key maybe ONCE while connecting to my iPhone- and found it LOOSE! I can't snap it back into place because of the same broken plastic issue.

2) Logitech does not have/provide spare keys: When I called Logitech to inquire about spare board keys (rather than returning the entire keyboard to Amazon, because I did really love it besides this key popping problem), the customer service representative offered to replace the entire keyboard, which is great, but he also made mention of the fact they they DID NOT MAKE/PROVIDE spare keys for this model. This means that in the future, if just one key becomes problematic, the customer will have to go through the struggles of shipping out the entire keyboard, etc. I confirmed with the customer service representative that they did IN FACT not make spare keys (I was shocked), but perhaps I had spoken with a particularly new/tired/unversed representative.

All that being said, I am awaiting for a replacement from Amazon (I figured the shipping would be faster w/Amazon's superb customer service), and will see whether the new keyboard presents with problematic keys.
Hope the above two caveats help.
