(WARNING- This is an IN DEPTH review of this stereo to help anyone interested in making an informed buying decision. If you prefer a more brief summary, see section marked THE BOTTOM LINE)
------------
In my house there is a variety of quality of audio items. There are those who really don’t seem to care what kind of quality, as long as it is not too bad. Then there are those who really want to hear definition of sound but they can tolerate lower quality. Then there are those who are so sensitive to audio that they will go on in great depth to analyze and evaluate anything related to stereos whether it is the CD player, bluetooth player, headphones, speakers, and fine tuning of sound.

This stereo system was picked to replace a very old Onkyo which is hanging on, but not for long. Let’s see how this measures up.

WHAT IS THIS STEREO LIKE?
First of all, the write up when I had the opportunity to get this stereo said it was a mini stereo system (different than it is now). I expected it to fit where my other stereo system is which was also a condensed system. Boy was I surprised. This system is a LOT bigger than I expected it to be, but still will fit where I wanted to put it although much tighter than I thought it would.

This system has a CD/bluetooth base to it. There is a dial which is rather large on the front that deals with volume. The CD player has the usual controls on it and there is only an FM radio, no AM. There is an infrared remote which has all of the controls you would need to run the stereo.

LIST OF CONNECTORS
FM Antenna terminal
Line 1 and 2 terminals
Speaker light terminal
Speaker out terminal
USB input on front
Headphone jack on front

MEASUREMENTS
Receiver: 11 x 11 13/16 x 5 5/8
Speakers: 12 x 10 3/4 x 16 5/16
Speaker cords approx 2 ft

HOW DOES THIS UNIT PERFORM?
The CD drawer in the bottom right corner operates about average as far as loading and reading. When playing a CD there were not any problems. As far as the equalizer goes, there are only five functions (one is flat- ewww). For this price there should have been more or customizable options.

The equalizer options sound okay, but the two that we choose most often for a variety of music is jazz and rock. Pop, flat, classic seem lack luster for all of the CDs we tried including classical, rock, country, jazz, hip hop, etc.

Despite limitations, the sound did separate well on one of our CDs which has very muffled and quiet background noise at the beginning of a song that we have never heard clearly before.

SOUND QUALITY
The highs come through pretty well, due to the two tweeters per speaker. The mids and lows depend on the music. They tend to suffer more. It booms but not overly clearly. This is more of a mediocre sound that is designed to pump at very high volumes such as for a party. This is not high fidelity sound if that is what you are looking for.

SPEAKER LIGHTS
Although they are interesting at first, the lights seem kind of odd. For the price, it should have had better options. You can choose colors that stay on and do not blink or change out of seven choices. You can choose to have it flash and change color continuously, or you can choose to have the lights flash fast and change continuously, or you can flash the light in white. None of the settings go in time with the music.

You can also opt for no lights on as well. The lights do connect to the speakers by a second wire- it is not in with the speaker connector.

BLUETOOTH
The bluetooth took a while to recognize on the phone. We used android. Once it was paired, many types of music from old to new tracks, and older songs were not as clear or loud as newer tracks. As far as decoding from the bluetooth, it sounded pretty good and did not drop once.

RADIO
The FM sound on this was good and no complaints. Reception was pretty standard, nothing remarkable, but not horrible either.

REMOTE
Remote has to be pointed directly at the receiver. There were a few times where we had to press buttons twice because it would not pick up the signals. The remote itself is black and very small, which makes it easy to misplace. Marking it with neon paint is something we are going to do to make it harder to lose.

PROS
Nice and loud
Picks up highs very well
Bluetooth and CD player in one both work well
Two tweeters per speaker is nice

CONS
Remote very small
Lights sometimes are annoying
Wires are way too short- speakers can not be separated to put in corners of room
Speaker wires are proprietary to the receiver with special attachment (can not use other speakers)

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you want to have a good middle of the road stereo with nice separation of highs and decent sound, you might like this one. The lights and loud capacity also make this a great party unit if you like to fill up a large room or house with sound. Remote works okay , but speakers can not be separated very far. Due to proprietary speaker connections, the only way to change that would be to splice the wires if you are good at electronics.

RATING
This stereo is rather high priced for what you get. It does not have any bass boost, or customizing options for the equalizer. The sound is loud, but not overly high quality. Although this is not a bad unit, it really is not jaw dropping either. I want to give this THREE AND A HALF STARS due to the price and what you get for it. Unfortunately there is only a choice between four and three stars.

Several of my family have been into taking photos for a long time. We have been through quite a few cameras, although not top of the line, still not inexpensive by any means. $500 is usually the price range of cameras we have purchased.

The Fujifilm FinePix S1 is a contradiction of sorts. You might say there is a love-hate relationship with it.

WHAT WE LIKE
Camera lightweight for what is in it
Easy grip- to hang on to and hold
Great neck strap
Macro and Supermacro capabilities are good
Durable
WiFi feature works great with tablet (android OS)
50X zoom works great (have to have very steady hand for that)
Great movies for what it is
Mini HDMI port works for TV or monitor
Photos with flash turn out well consistently
Left and right zoom buttons come in VERY handy
Takes decent self portraits, although a bit clumsy at times to hold
Timer worked well

WHAT WE DON'T LIKE
Navigation can be frustrating
Directional pad can be frustrating
Light sensor is unstable
Automatic settings very unstable and inconsistent
Photos look better on LCD pad than they actually are
Sometimes photos look flat and/or grainy (not 3D looking or clear)

THE BOTTOM LINE

THE LIGHT PROBLEM
We tested this camera extensively inside, outside, at night, in indirect light and with sunlight and found that the light sensor in this camera is way too inconsistent for satisfying picture taking. Sometimes the colors captured were exquisite and better than any other camera I have ever used. I didn't have to do any adjusting at all. Other times they were abyssmal.

For instance, in taking 10 pictures in a row, changing absolutely nothing, it was virtually impossible to have two pictures turn out alike. They were all vastly different. Sometimes they were dark, sometimes way too light, sometimes perfect. That is a lot of effort to capture the perfect picture.

On the flip side, one night in absolute frustration not being able to capture anything decent at all, I turned out all of the lights so that the room was pitch black. I held my camera up to my fish tanks and snapped a few pictures. Besides traumatizing my fish from the sudden light, I was shocked to see some of the most beautiful photos I had taken all evening. Perfect colors, clarity and definition consistently.

It appears that when you use the flash, that the color calibration kicks into high gear and you get pretty darned good photos.

You can not live your life taking flash photos unfortunately.

PHOTO QUALITY
I found that by using various settings and experimenting, I could get pretty nice photos- but I had to use a lot of effort. The menu is not easy to navigate, nor is it forgiving if you take too long to decipher it- it shuts off on you and you have to go through it again.

I did find that sometimes I was taking what I thought were fantastic photos (from the LCD screen) only to upload them to my photo editing program and seeing that they were grainy or blurry or just plain flat and un-dimensional. On the LCD screen they looked amazing. On the other hand, sometimes they turned out blah on my LCD screen, but great on the SD card.

Once in a while, I have problems with my Canon with color. I love bright colors and my photography focus is often color oriented. Canon often understates color way too much for me and I have to spend some time to get it to look accurate in photo editing. With the FinePix S1, however, once in a while, I could capture color that was so gorgeous and realistic that I would gasp and be very excited.

The problem is that it is not always predictable and that was frustrating. Like the proverbial carrot on the string in front of the horse, I find myself reaching for this camera when frustrated with my others to capture colors that don't seem to do well on any other camera. Once in a while the effort is worth it so I come back for more frustration.

FINAL COMMENTS
As I said at the beginning, I have a bit of a love hate relationship with this camera. On the one hand it is a lot of work to get decent photos, but on the other hand, when you do manage to get one, it is amazing. Rare, but amazing.

If Fujifilm would fix the issues with depth in photos, consistency in the light sensor, and quality issues on automatic settings, this camera would be a MUST buy. As it is now, however, I can only give it three stars because of the inconsistency in quality of photos and the effort I have to go through to get a good one. I gave it three stars because once in a while it does capture photos with brilliant colors that none of my other cameras will capture, despite the slightly lower quality at times. The videos are great- sound excellent and clarity nice. The flash is great. Out of the way when you don't want it- and nice photos. It has potential to be a fantastic camera.

As it is now, until they correct a few things, it is only average.

I can not believe how much I love and hate this thing at the same time!

There are some very nice features to these buds, and I do intend to keep them. (Another reviewer was about to return them.) But there are some things that just aren't as good as I had hoped. I'll try to be as detailed as possible.

First, the out-of-box experience is kinda nice, but not fabuous. The smallish box presents the much smaller charger box that the buds live in, and a tiny box that contains a charger cable. Wait -- are there really no instructions? And I thought there were interchangable ear thingies to accommodate ears of different sizes. Ok, so the very brief instruction book clings to the top of the box because it's too big not to fall out on its own. And the ear thingies are hiding in the box where the charging cable is. I seem to be ok with the default ear thingies that are already installed on the buds. (Note, you have to use your own charger with the charging cable. You probably already have too many of those.)

You'll need to download and install the Galaxy Wearable app (on Android, a different one is available for iOS). The app helps you connect to the buds, pretty easy, and is reasonably fully functional. There are numerous options you can play with.

The fit -- quite comfortable actually. Looking at the peculiar shape, I wondered whether these would stay in my ears, and whether they would be uncomfortable. Yes, they stay put, even when walking around, and no, not uncomfortable. This was a pleasant surprise; Samsung really got this part right. I feel as though I could wear these at the office all day and not get ear fatigue. Much, much better than a clumsy pair of headphones slipping off my head when I'm walking around. When wearing the buds, you can hear outside sounds/conversations very well, and perhaps that's the whole idea of these buds. I like this.

There's an equalizer section on the app's main screen. The equalizer options are sort of ok, but not wonderful. I don't know why there's no option for a 10-band graphic equalizer. I just settled on the default after not liking the other choices any better.

You can turn on and off the ANC (active noise cancellation). I have a pair of conventional headphones (not Bose) with ANC that works really well. You feel like you're in a cocoon. These buds have ANC that you can barely tell is working. It sounds a little different, maybe even a little bit of an improvement, but it doesn't seem like it's getting rid of any particular noise. So the ANC is sort of a bust.

Now let's talk about sound quality. As I say, I really wanted to love these little guys. The sound quality is good but not great. Maybe I'm expecting too much. My pair of $250 conventional headphones sound spectacular, and I can listen to music for hours with them. These buds aren't that impressive. The sound quality is ok -- just ok. It's not "bad" in any way at all, but it's not great. I listened to an entire CD that I know well and like. The experience was pleasant, but at the end I really wanted to listen to it on the stereo instead. As I say, maybe I'm expecting too much. The sound quality is probably good enough to listen to at work all day. I had the volume up a little too high, and when my test CD was finished and I took the buds out of my ears, I felt that my ears were ringing a little bit. Next time I'll set the volume lower.

As an interesting aside, I'll compare the sound quality to another wearable that I just got, the Bose Frames (audio sunglasses, a weirdly interesting product). The sound from the Bose Frames is "smooth" in a very wonderful way -- much better than the buds. However, the Bose Frames have absolutely no lower end -- no bass sounds at all. The sounds they do have are great. By contrast, these buds are full range, with pretty good bass. But the sound just isn't smooth.

I didn't try to take a phone call., so I don't know how seamless this works. Considering it's Samsung, and I have a Galaxy S9, I bet this works well enough. I'm not very fussy about sound quality on calls -- I just need to be able to understand what's being said. So "good enough" for me is probably not hard to achieve.

There's a "button" on the buds that you press to skip a track, answer a call, etc. It's not a real button, it's just a touch-sensitive area on the outside of the bud. I haven't been able to get this touch point to work reliably. I don't think there's necessarily anything wrong with the bud, probably just my fat fingers.

Bottom line? I think I'll have a use for these, most likely when I want to listen to my own music without disturbing others, and without the very wonderful but cumbersome conventional earphones. When I'm walking out and about, the smooth sound from the Bose Frames is better. So it's a toss-up with the Galaxy Buds Live. They're good enough, but unfortunately not better than that.

If you have TV Ears, you'll need to keep replacing the tips. These are the official tips, but the price is pretty steep for 10 little pieces of foam. I find the TV Ears product in general unsatisfying (mono sound, not very comfortable to wear), but my mom likes it pretty well.

I ordered the 'Malektronic Interstellar Premium Wireless Noise Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones' for review and would like to share my thoughts.

So I am no audiophile, but I do love a good quality headphone that is built well and sound good. Sounding good or even great is really subjective depending on personal preference. For the going retail price of these Malektronic Interstellar Premium Wireless Noise Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones, I really expected much more than what I personally find these to be. I'll break my experience and thoughts into a few main points that stood out to me.

Comfort - These are comfortable but they don't fit as snug as I would have liked. I have a small head for a 54yro male, and even on the smallest adjustment setting, they just don't hug my ears like I would have hoped for such an expensive set of headphones.

Noise Cancelling - yea this is a big one for me right hear (see what I did there). I am not at all impressed with the Noise Cancelling in these headphones for the price. I mean it's OK, but I have ANC wireless earbuds that do a much better job for about the same price. There are only two settings. ANC On and ANC Off. For me, It's really hard to tell whether I've turned it on or off. There is no indicator like others I have that would either beep or greet you with some kind of prompt letting you know which mode you are in (there are voice prompts when you turn them on or off so why not anything for ANC modes). In fact the only way I can truly tell that it's on or off, is to pause the song and push the ANC button at which point it's pretty clear. However, and with that said, I do notice that when it's on, the music almost sounds more heavy on the Bass. It's almost like the Bass is supposed to give that "ANC" feel. Remember, I am no audiophile but this is just my observation.

Sound - Now I can say this, and that is that these do sound good until you get close to max volume. At which point they just don't hold up to the volume. Not that they get really loud but if you have the ANC on and you are listening to a heavy Bass song, they tend to bottom out just a tad. It's not bad but again for this price point, I would have expected better. The highs are nice but even better when ANC is off. Mids are there and probably sound good in either mode really. Another thing I noticed is that if you take these off while the music is still playing at full volume, they sound like they are rattling and sound a bit distorted. However when you put them back on, there is no distortion like I noticed with them off. That was kind of strange.

Micro USB charging - I always have to point this out. It's 2020 companies and USB C should be the standard any more in my opinion. Just saying.

Build Quality - They aren't the worst I have seen or tried but at this price point they are not the best either. They are pretty much plastic although fairly solid.

Buttons - The buttons are hidden/covered near the edge of the ear pads and they took me a while to figure out where they are, but after using them for a while, I actually like the fact that they look to be buttonless.

Looks/design - These really do look nice both on and off. They don't look cheap which is nice, as I have some others that just look ugly and I refuse to wear haha. The design is well thought out and I do love how they fold flat and compact into the very nice hard case.

So with all that said, I do like these headphones. They sound pretty good. The ANC is meh but they are comfortable besides not fitting as snug as I would prefer. Build quality is decent and I do love they way they fold up and store nicely into the included hard case. Thank you for including this Maletronics! Micro USB charging is a bummer but they also can be used wired with the included cable if you forget to get them charged up. Battery life is not bad. 30hrs might be pushing it if you like to listen to them loud and are always using the ANC. I have yet to test that fully as the longest I generally go is maybe an hour at a time. So for me the battery life is fine.

Overall, I really want to love these, and I actually do like them a lot, but I am just not that "Wowed" at this price point. I have other brands at or around this price point that I like better. Now maybe I got a dud pair and that very well could be, but I don't dislike them. They are nice and I plan to keep them around as a back-up pair. I hope that this was helpful.

I ordered the 'Geeni, Sentry Floodlight Security Camera with Motion Sensor, Intruder Alarm and Audio Video Recording' for review and would like to share my thoughts.

So I have had this camera for a while now and finally got it installed a couple of weeks ago and I am ready to share my thoughts and experience so far. This camera requires hard wiring which is why it took so long to get it installed. In my old home it was going to require me to get an extension cord, drill through my wall in the garage and plug it in, in the garage. This was much more work than I had anticipated. Now the new home already had normal motion sensor lights installed on switches, which made this more feasible for me to install. I took one of the motion sensor lights down and had to retrofit a new mount out of a piece of wood to cover the original hole left by removing the old light. This wasn't to hard to do and the Geeni light mounted with ease. Once installed and I turned the light switch on, it was ready to set up which took some time to do. I had to reset the device several times to get the App to set it up properly which was a quite pain however.

The camera itself is very good but so far I am not happy with all the notifications that I get which seem to be false alerts. It seems that everything seems to trigger this thing with absolutely no control as to how sensitive you would like the sensor to be. This is truly my main con with this device. I ended up turning notifications off on my mobile device which kind of defeats the purpose really.

Then there is the App which has thus far been pretty buggy. It has crashed many times and it is not so easy to find the "actual" activity that it seems to detect. Of all the motion activity that it detects, I would say that only 40% of it is relative. I do have the App set to just record everything (continuous) on the 128gb SD card which makes more sense seeing as there are so many false readings.

As for the good of this Geeni device, the image quality both during daytime and nighttime recording and playback is great. There is very little lag when accessing the footage which is surprising as I have other WiFi cameras that are painfully slow to connect and playback footage. This is probably my favorite feature (when the App doesn't crash).

Overall I do like this motion sensor and think that there is absolute value to it. I am however, really hoping for a firmware update which might help with some of the issues and allow you to adjust the sensitivity of the motion detection. Also it would be nice to have an easier way to track down and view "actual" activity rather than having to try and find that exact moment of capture. It seems to just tag a portion of footage, and you need to watch several minutes before you can find what it detected. You are also able to save the footage via the App, but doing so can take several days for it to show up on your mobile device which is another downside to this device.

I hope that this was helpful.

I am reviewing the ‘TruSound TruWireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds | True Wireless Earbuds with Charging Case for Buds and Phone | Comfortable, Secure Fit | Immersive Stereo Sound, Deep Bass | Easy Touch Control Operation’.
Based on my experience thus far I would like to share my thoughts.

Pros:
1- The sound is decent but compared to other Wireless Earbuds that I have tried, these are pretty average.
2- The case is rechargeable via the included 18650 battery. This allows you to have extra 18650 batteries on hand which is an interesting feature.
3- It comes with extra ear tips.
4- It comes with a mini USB cable and even a USB type A to Mini USB adapter.
5- Aesthetically the earbuds look nice, feel comfortable and don’t protrude much when wearing them.
6- They stay in place quite well and do not randomly fall out.
7- Earbuds are held in place magnetically when in the case charging.
8- They pair up real fast and very easy. I have had no issues at all with pairing.

Cons:
1- I ordered these based on the description stating “active noise reduction is also a standout feature of TruSound ear buds, ensuring a distraction-free audio experience”. I took this as they had ANC or Active Noise Control. This is not the case. These “isolate” the outside sounds via the ear tip inserted into the ear canal. If you get the right tip fit, they do “isolate” the outside sounds but just not as expected.
2- No USB type C. In my opinion all new devices should have USB C charging.
3- The case is a bit bulky due to the fact that it uses the 18650 battery.
4- The case is plastic and uses two plastic tabs to snap the lid closed. The design makes it really hard to open the case once it’s snapped shut. I am worried that I will break the plastic tabs at which point I would need to use a rubber band to keep the lid closed.
5- The Stand-By time is not the greatest. I fully charged the 18650 battery with my own charger when I first got the Earbuds. I used the Earbuds briefly while initially testing them and when I went back a couple of weeks later to try them again, the battery was already dead. I have other earbuds that have this same issue. I should be able to fully charge my earbuds, keep them in my backpack for a few weeks and have them ready to go when I want to use them.
6- No IPX rating? Pretty much all of the newer Earbuds these days have some kind of waterproof rating. It’s not advertised so I am not really sure if they are.
7- No Bluetooth 5.0? These have Bluetooth 4.2+EDR which isn’t bad, but there are sync issues when watching YouTube, Netflix ect. It’s not bad, but it’s noticeable and I could not use these to watch videos for too long.

Overall these TruSound Earbuds are average, and I feel that compared to the flooded market of True Wireless Earbuds these are a bit overpriced. With that said, I do like these but, I do feel there could be some improvements made that would ultimately increase the value.

Disclaimer - I've only had these for about a week so far and these are the very first Truly Wireless Earbuds that I have ever owned.

I purchased these earbuds on a great sale while waiting for another more expensive brand to get restocked, and honestly didn't expect to much from these. First impressions were that they were quite cheap however after using them for a little while now, I've come to appreciate them even more. Even though these are my very first Truly Wireless Earbuds, I feel that after tons of research and watching reviews, I know what to look for in sound and quality. There are so many budget wireless earbuds on the market right now with so many more on Indigogo (which from comments and reviews I've seen and read, I will NEVER buy from). This makes it quite hard to know what to buy. For me, I have been waiting for that perfect very small and discreet Truly Wireless Earbud with amazing sound. The Iyesku YK-T02 TWS Sport Earbuds didn't hit that mark for me but at the price I paid, I honestly can't complain.
Pros:
1. Bluetooth 5.0 - This was one of my main requirements when searching and the YK-T02 has it.
2. Easy to pair (I am using the Samsung Note 8) and pairing was very easy. Once the buds are initially paired, they connect super fast once you pull them out of the charging case.
3. No loss of connectivity to either earbud. I've seen a bunch of reviews where this is an issue with MANY other wireless earbuds on the market. Even some of the more spendy ones.
4. Fit is very comfortable and seem to be very secure though I have not put them through the test of running nor exercise. However I don't think this would be an issue at all.
5. Sound quality is decent. More about this in the Cons.
6. Tons of ear tip options. Most earbuds come with a few extra sizes but these come with a plethora, for that perfect custom fit.
7. Quite small and discreet.
8. Small pocketable charging case.

Cons:
1. Sound. As I stated in the Pros these sound "good" (for the money) but the Highs are quite loud (Mids and Bass are not) and almost hurt when the volume is turned all the way up. Mids are not to bad but the bass is nearly non existent which was a huge let down. HOWEVER let me say, once I played with the ear tips and found the right fit, Highs, Mids, and Bass are much better, but still not what I would have hoped for but again these aren't "High end" earbuds right?
2. Because the volume of these buds are quite low, Audio books are hard to hear when in a loud environment.
3. No satisfying magnet to hold the buds in the charging case like many others on the market. (The case does click shut to ensure the buds wont be falling out.)
4. Speaking of the case, my first impression was that the case felt very nice and lightweight, but it does feel cheap.

Final thoughts:
Like I said earlier in this review, if you can get these from Amazon on a lightning deal or with a coupon, I would say grab you a pair, but just don't expect these to compete with higher end buds. These would be great for the kids and anyone that just wants a good pair of Truly Wireless Earbuds that wont break the bank.

Update: After 16 months the right ear went out. Bummer. Took off a star.

Gorgeous sound coming from these but I don't like the clips. They're clunky in that they don't allow the speaker to sit firmly against my ear so I'm not getting the full sound I could be getting. Come on, Koss, offer these with a headband please.

Cons

This product is just OKAY. They are really onto a good concept, they just need to refine it a bit. I wouldn't say it is great or horrible... just average. I have a Phillips docking station that has incredible speaker sound for its size. I was very disappointed in the speakers on this unit. My favorite part is that it can rotate. This makes it nice if you are laying in bed and want to watch a movie while it is docked and charging. You have to use a USB cable and then use your Apply power supply for it to work. This is unlike the other docking stations I have. So, would I purchase it... only if I just had to have a horizontal docking station with slightly more audible sound. Pros:

Cons:

First, let me say I purchased the Powershot 510 and the Powershot 310. The 510 is a much more solid camera and a lot less plastic than the 310. I think my two largest complaints and frustration comes with the touch screen and the 12 power zoom. The touch screen drains the battery faster than my other Canon Powershot cameras and the zoom is incredibly difficult to get stable when at full 12 power and my pictures haven't turned out as well as I would like at that distance. Overall, I really didn't like the Canon Powershot 310, so I am on the fence as to whether or not I will keep this one. I have a few more days to think about it. For now... here is a more detailed list of pros and cons:

Pros:
- Takes incredibly good photos with regard to color.
- Easy to use.
- The vivid setting is great for flowers and fall colors.
- I love the fisheye effect without having to carry around my Canon DSLR camera and lenses. I also love having the wide angle.
- The miniature setting is kind of fun to use.
- Feels incredibly heavy and solid, unlike the new 310.
- Fits easily in my purse and pocket.

Cons:

Not sure what to order if I send this one back. So, I am still on the fence, as I am partial to Canon cameras over Nikons. The red color is not as it is shown in the picture. It is more of a rust/burgandy color of red... it has a bit more brown to it, but I actually like it.

UPDATE: 12/12/2011 - I ended up sending this one back and kept the Canon 310. I am really glad I did. I get a great battery life and when I compared the photos on this camera vs. the 510, the photos had better color and looked a lot more crisp from the 310. I am happy with my decision.
They’re ok…sound is great! They unfortunately don’t stay in my ear and they don’t last more than four hours…good for when my others die out and I need a quick, temporary earpiece. Meh….

I've had this head unit installed for 2 weeks now. Great concept that was poorly executed especially for its price. Installation was easy enough despite the directions not being too helpful. YouTube videos saved the day once again. Device setup wasn't too bad since it's Android based. Bought all the peripherals - the steering wheel controls because the stereo interfaced with my factory controls flawlessly.
Radio was installed into a 2006 F-350.

After 2 weeks of daily use and several hundred miles here are my complaints: volume and sound quality are terrible compared to the stock system--only the head unit was removed. A good amp may correct this but I'm guessing it's the processor in the deck. Forget watching videos with the engine running. Can't hear it.

Like many other complaints, the unit does not like to pick up radio stations well. Only the strongest get through even though my 13 year old stock system had no problems before (the connection if fine).

The unit also doesn't like any internet connection I've tried. Slow as hell when it does work. Google play store crashes constantly making it extremely difficult download updates or new apps.

Frequently have to reboot system to get things to function again.

I'll probably add more later.

I'm regretting this purchase. Considering returning it.

Easy to setup and everything works flawlessly. But the sound really isn't any better than my old Vizio TVs built in sound. It might be an upgrade for a computer system or something, but an extra piece of hardware on my TV with no improvement in sound is not worth messing with.

Very easy to setup and use. It's a great idea for keys, remote, etc - my only complaint is that it's not very loud. There's 2 volume settings in the app, but even the louder of the two would not be loud enough if your keys were in the next room or buried in the laundry. Otherwise, it works great.

These a are decent ear buds... not great, but decent. I didnt have and problem pairing them to my phone and the sound was clear, but they didnt seem to have as much low end as I would have liked. They sound just a little thin.

Today, I put them on for a routine on my elliptical. They did okay, but again, I felt they were lacking in the low end. When I started sweating, they started slipping and I struggled to keep them in my ear. They come with extra earpieces of different sizes, but the ones I had on felt comfortable before I started. Perhaps I need to experiment with those for awhile.

As for function, the charging port is a standard one like a typical phone and it charged reasonably quick. Near the end of my workout, it seemed as though I was losing volume. So the length of service was only moderate. The real concern for new, though, was the charging port's cover. It's a tiny rubber piece with an incredibly small "nib" that needs to be grasped to reveal the port. The only way is with your fingernails (my nails are not very long - this was not easy). Then there was the controls... 3 side by side buttons that are positioned on a piece that's out of view (when wearing them). So you have to feel for the buttons.

Also, a case would have been a nice addition.
Not a bad antennae. In rural areas, still have a little static. Unfortunately; compared with the slightly longer antennae; 5”; the quality is slightly less efficient.
Volume could be louder for a large room/area.  Had to hold a microphone up to the speaker.  Connected well to bluetooth.  Like the size.

So I have several large speaker Alexa devices, but due to scalpers, those aren't available currently. So I bought this instead. The sound quality is crackly and awful. It's not very loud either. The sound is very tinny and just sounds bad. Anyway, it was only $20 so I'm not too mad about it.
Not a $600 sound quality IMHO.  Heavy on the head as well.  I returned them.

This cable runs from my server room to the next room by going through the wall and attic. Tested this cable before hand for a couple days before running the cable through the house and worked fine. After the install it worked fine for about 3 months and then stopped working. I checked the PSU that came with the cable and it appears to be dead.

I was able to use a powered hub that seems to be enough to power a keyboard, mouse and audio card without using a PSU on the cable end itself.

The sound is fine. It's what I would expect from quality tweeters and a reasonable size woofer with a decent driver. It does not compare to a decent set of bookshelf type monitors like the JBL LSR series but the price is far lower so I guess they're ok for PC speakers.

But the excellence ends at the sound. The speakers do not have an analog signal input from the computer (there is one at the puck for a MP3 player or whatever). Instead, the signal comes via USB. The problem is the speakers do not come with any drivers. Bose assumes you have the drivers already on your Windows installation. That's a very bad assumption as many people do not have the drivers (just do a google search on Bose Companion 5 drivers to see). There's no help from Bose here. The drivers cannot be downloaded from their web site. I called Bose's tech support and after half and hour they were not able to solve the problem. I eventually solved the problem myself on my Windows 7 Pro 64-bit install but I think it's terribly lame that Bose cannot provide the driver for their product. If I wasn't using the pre-load install of Windows they assume everyone uses, then I would be screwed.

So exactly what do I get for this odd USB input in lieu of a standard audio input? Nothing except incompatibility and the inability to use the speakers apart from a full blown PC. The audio quality and features are not improved by USB audio input. Period.

Room mode correction should be a straightforward feaure on speakers like these. It is not. Although my sound card supports it, the Bose speakers do not have the DSP to do it independently. The lack of sound-card independent RMC doesn't justify the high cost of these speakers. If it were included, the price would look a little better.

I installed the Companion 5 system on an Ergotron cart. The two speakers fit perfectly under the monitor the way I wanted (I removed the stands). The acoustimass is bulkier than I would have liked but I think it's fair to say a smaller module would not perform as well and for most under-desk installs it would be fine. What I do think it's fair to complain about is the poor design of the acoustimass module case. Despite being very heavy, it features a plastic rear end-cap that is fragile. Come-on. For the price, give me painted steel not brittle plastic. The case is also oddly shaped with curves that prevent anything but a bottom-down mount position. The case is not designed to be mounted in a down-firing position, up-firing or on it's side or upside down. The case is also not equipped or rated to be flown or ceiling mounted (it could fall apart and drop parts on people below). Bose should know these are all viable positions. Not everyone can have this thing on the floor with like six wires running out for people to trip over -- seriously, that is totally not acceptable in a public space.

Bose has a habit of not publishing Watts RMS specifications for their amplifiers or speaker handling abilities. I sort of understand not wanting to confuse consumers who don't understand driver efficiencies, but at least give us some max. 1 meter SPL's so we have some clue how loud these things are. As it is, the Companion 5 is loud enough for a PC system in a fairly live medium-sized residential room. It's much louder than my Wave system which proved way more anemic than it was made out to be. The Wave is useless except in the smallest bedroom. I use the Companion 5 primarily in my kitchen (on the Ergotron cart). The kitchen is fairly live but has some acoustic paneling to tame some of the reverberations. If I were putting this system in a small classroom, I would think twice. As a PC system for someone who sits right in front of it, it's obviously perfectly good. I probably wouldn't even use it at half-volume sitting that close.

The wide angle lens is wonderful. The field of view and the speed (light gathering ability) of the lens can only be rivaled by high end camera and lens combinations costing six to ten times as much (admittedly those are superior in many other ways as well). Still, the point is that no other compact point and shoot camera can rival the field of view and speed of this one. Nevertheless, some things come up short of fair on the LX3.

The shutter lag is terrible. I am a very instinctive shooter that is quite capable in photojournalist style candids but I am almost always defeated by this camera.

I am not a photophile or electronic gadget spec sheet bench racer. I've done wonderful 8x10 prints with a 6MP camera and 10MP is enough to get prints after substantial cropping. I have huge film scans when I need them but I cannot realistically show dozens of megapixels on screen or in print for more than a handful of images. I also shoot in .jpg and it's great. I can't imagine the agony of terabytes of raw data jamming my PC.

I love the LX3 video quality for movies. It's ideal for Youtube and even Youtube HD. I do not like the Quicktime .MOV format or the weak compression algorithm. I wish it had H.264 and wrote an .MPG type format. It still beats the data format from a DVD camcorder though.

The audio quality for movies is terrible. Again, I'm not talking audiophile critique here. For comparison, my Sony DSC T9 (ultra compact point and shoot) has far better sound.

I hate the manual aspect ratio slider. If I shoot movies I want 16:9 but for stills I want 3:2 (of course). The LX3 requires that I remember to both turn the dial and slide the switch or I will end up shooting 16:9 stills.

Overall, it's a great camera. I hope they get the rest sorted out by the time I expect to buy another one in about 3 or 4 years.

Meh. Too expensive for what you get which is mediocre sound and mediocre charging ability. However, living in San Francisco I bought it for an earthquake kit. I use it to listen to podcasts and it's fine for that and it does charge my cellphone, but is not powerful enough to charge an iPad. It isn't exactly light either so not something I'd want to take backpacking.

OK for the discounted price. They squish my ears because the earpad is too small.  After a couple of hours it's pretty uncomfortable and yor ears get sweaty.  These are fine for plugging in at work and working for shorter periods of time. The ear cushion area would fit an elf but not an adult of any kind. I'm a 5 foot 3 female and was hoping these would cover my ears more rather than sit ON them.  Perhaps I'll get used to them and for watching a movie on an airplane for a couple hours they are fine but I'm not sure I can stand to wear them too long.  The sound is decent, and they were only $23, which is the only reason I gave them 3 stars.

These are kind of fragile, but work. Bass isn't good, not the greatest sound replication, but for the price there's no complaining. Except I also bought a pair off Amazon that cost a whopping $3 and they work the same. Same sound, same quality. Skullcandy is the one to beat, but I don't like using those where they might get wet or destroyed.

I have had my cherry M50s for a little over a year and use them extensively for listening to radio, music from CD and iPod and movies.

In a nutshell these are beautiful furniture quality speakers that pass that most important 'will my wife like to have them in the living room' test, however the sound is not what it could be for a large floor speaker. The sound is actually pretty good, but tolerable is the word I would prefer. I found them to be a bit harsh in the highs and lacking depth until I bi-wired them. They are hungry for power and bi-wired with 105 watts per channel watts they sound better, but still lack crispness and punch.

The point is that the case and build quality suggests that these are going to be in my living room for a good ten years, during which they will look nice but I will also feel like I compromised on having just 'OK' sound. Go ahead and buy them as your first set of floor speakers - but know that you will likely want to upgrade in the future. But I strongly suggest that you not upgrade to these, hold on to what you have and save a few more bucks for a pair of RTi A5, A7 or A9s.

For me I will buy a pair of cherry RTi A7s to match (when they come down in price) and use the M50s as rears. Like I said, I'm sure that these will be in my living room for a good ten years...

Pros:
* Amazing industrial design as always
* Great processing power although I wish the 7700 was offered
* Speakers are the best built-ins I've heard
* The Touch Bar is pleasant to use and customizable enough
* Having only usb-c isn't a major constraint day to day in my opinion.

Cons:

* [Moderately annoying] The low travel keyboard is feels cheap. It was not worth shaving 1mm off the machine's depth for this unsatisfying keyboard.
* [Minor] The Touch Bar needs a lot more 3rd party integration. If you only use OS X built-in apps then you'll be happy, but 3rd party integration is very low aside from some designer-oriented apps.
* [Minor] I've had some issues with the usb-c interface trying to output sound to my external monitors that don't have built-in speakers
* [Minor] The lip to open the shell has been reduced, but the resistance to opening has been increase. This make opening the machine somewhat annoying.

I agree with people who said you get what you pay for. The sound quality was pretty good for the price but these lasted me less than a year. I did use them almost everyday for at least an hour and was very careful with how I stored them. Still, I expected better longevity. Not happy considering I could've bought a similar pair that lasted me 3-4x as long for $20 more. Oh well, you live and learn.

These will do the job, but it's immediately obvious how much thinner and flimsier these are than the usual cd cases you get with audio or software cds. I very carefully opened the back on one just to try it, and was worried that it would break something during this process. It didn't, but I wasn't left with a great feeling of comfort, either.

So I think they're ok for a cheap replacement case, but if you want something sturdy, keep looking.

The one good thing is that they were packed nicely in a robust cardboard box, and were not at all damaged in transit.

(Revised & re-rated.)

I wanted to upgrade my office music setup: I had a Chromecast Audio connected (through a line booster) to a stereo amp playing to a nice pair of Aperion "bookshelf" (medium size) speakers. I decided to replace the Chromecast with this Grace Link player, hooked up to an external DAC, with output going into the stereo amp.

The problem is this: the Grace Link limits the digital output to 48kb, which doesn't support the "high quality" from streaming music services like Youtube Music and Amazon Music, let alone the high-resolution streams you can get (if you pay more). The old Chromecast Audio does better, especially if you use an optical cable and pipe it through a decent DAC.

I returned it, and am kicking myself for not reading the fine print more closely. I'll look for a better streaming audio receiver (which will of course cost more), but until I find something I'll go back to my Chromecast Audio.

It does the job, and I have a fairly powerful and functional computer, but on consideration I think I should have considered some of the alternatives instead.

The most frustrating problem has been unaccounted for behavior with Windows 7, apparently related to the mobo. For instance, wake from sleep consistently crashes the computer (I checked the dumps to verify that it was definitely a wake-related crash), and there is (as yet) no bios or driver update to fix it. Ok, sleep isn't that important, I can live without it. But sometimes a simple reboot will hang, apparently in the same place, right when Windows should be booting up. A forced shutdown (holding the power button for several seconds) and restart fixes that problem. But neither of these is really expected, or acceptable.

A lesser problem is the sound -- somehow it's tinny, sounds worse than the audio on my 5-year old mid-range computer. I'm probably going to buy an audio card, which shouldn't have been necessary.

The onboard networking is just fine, I haven't had any problems with it. The onboard video is ok as well, but I didn't test that too much since I added a separate video card.

I think I should have gone with MSI or Asus instead, and that's what I'm going to look at when my son & I build a mid-price gaming rig for him later this fall.

This case was recommended in several build guides, and seemed to be highly rated on Amazon, but I must say I'm quite disappointed.

Pros:
(1) It does the job. It's roomy -- in fact, it's really big. There's room for a really big graphics card without taking out any drive cages.
(2) Comes with four quiet fans (2 intakes in front, one large intake on the side, one exhaust on the back), and room to add more on the top.
(3) Having a couple of usb3 ports and audio/mike ports in the front is very convenient. Having the power supply at the bottom (in the back) also worked well for me.
(4) All the bits come apart and back together without too much trouble.

Cons:
(1) I had a lot of trouble getting my EVGA power supply to install, because the screw holes didn't line up nicely. Finally managed it by using a combination of power and adapting to what the case gave me.
(2) The 5.25 drive bays go in the conventional way, with the backs near the mobo for easy connections. But the 2.5/3.5 drive bays go in sideways, which might seem convenient at first, but now you have their connectors on the other side of the box -- so you're threading your power and sata cables around, and creating a bulge of cables etc. And that extra wiring room that the case promises? It doesn't extend all the way to the front, apparently the artists overcame the engineers (or they fought and the users lost). This arrangement also means that it's harder to share your sata power cables, depending on what you're trying to do with your setup.
(3) As others have pointed out, those nice intake fans aren't standard, they would be hard to replace individually. I'd have to replace all of them with standard case fans, I think.
(4) I wasn't as impressed with the cable management as many others were -- while it was useful to be able to run some wires on the back, that also made some of the shorter ones trickier to connect. Also, I find it easiest to place the box down on the side to work on the inside. Having to flip it over or keep it standing vertical wasn't my idea of convenience during assembly, and it made things really tricky when I wanted to add another hdd.

Neutral:
(1) An inexpensive mini-speaker (for POST beeps) would have been a good idea to include with the box.

All in all, I'm not unhappy enough to curse it, but I'm also far from recommending it. I'd look around more the next time, so 3* seems about right.

They're ok for basic use perhaps.  Perhaps.  But they're really quite tinny sounding, and I quickly find it painful to listen to music playing through these speakers. To be clear, I'm not expecting the performance of my home stereo, I'm just comparing them to my other computer speakers -- they're much better.  So if you have a sensitive ear, you might wish to spend a bit more money and get a nicer pair.

Unfortunately, not all coax cable splitters are the same. The frequency range supported does matter, since cable companies are now using higher frequencies in their signals.

This one specifies 5-900MHz, which is likely to cause problems with your HD channels. Most frequently, some channels won't come through, or you may see a lot of "digital noise". (I've seen the problems, and verified that the splitter is the culprit, by removing the splitter.)

You may want to get a splitter with a wider frequency range ...

I've had this headset for about a year now; I use it with a Razr. It's a fine headset from a technical perspective: the sound is fine, it's easy to pair and use, etc. I haven't run into any problems using it in a car, or out of doors.

However, it's really not very comfortable: the hook that goes over the ear is just a bit too stiff and edgy, I wouldn't want to wear it for a long call (more than 15-20min say).

For comfort and performance, consider the Plantronics Voyager 510 (around $50 at Amazon); I've had one of those (now used by my son), and it is excellent. If you're into new gadgets, check out the Jawbone sets -- I haven't used one, but a colleague swears by the one he's been using for a couple of months.

This is a very basic cover for your Kindle Fire HD (4th generation) that will offer some protection if you're going to carry it about - the price isn't too bad, but there are better, more functional covers out there (of course, you'll pay more for them, so it's a give and take).
First, though I was offered a red cover, a black one arrived. That was a bit perplexing and made me double-check what I clicked on. Nope, order said red. All right. Second, when you slide the Kindle Fire into the cover, it's basically held into place by a tab/molded frame on one end and elastic tabs on the other. You don't slide it in completely like with some cases, or snap it all in with others so it's completely secure. Second, there's no 'sleep' mode with this case, so you have to make sure you power it off or on when you close the case or else you'll drain your battery (as I said, very basic). Also, it only has an easel/landscape viewing mode - you flip the case open and stand it up that way to read or view the Kindle, there's no tab or folding capabilities with the back flap, no stand other than the cover flipping back.
You close the Kindle and 'seal' it with an elastic band. That's not uncommon with a lot of covers. The case is nice and slim, which means that you can fit it easily in a purse or a bag, which is nice. The case has a 'leather' look to it, and has the necessary holes cut out so you can access power, sound, etc. It's not a bad case, it's just if you are going to be traveling a lot with your Kindle and do want to use it to for apps or movies, or to set it down to read, I'd spend a little more money for an origami case or something with a little more features.

When my much more expensive Bluetooth on-ear headphones broke I was a bit frustrated and decided to go back to something cheaper. As expected, this product is less comfortable and clearly uses cheaper materials and construction, but I can't really complain given the price. The sound quality is fine as far as I can tell. The battery life is decent but noticeably shorter than my previous headphones. Also, the low battery warning is a very annoying loud series of beeps that repeats periodically until you charge it. So if you just want to listen for 5 more minutes or get through the last couple of minutes of that video and then charge it, well too bad, because the beeps are going to annoy the **** out of you until you charge it. Also, the pictures in the instructions were not clear to me at all, and it took me a while to find the charging port (you have to tilt one of the earphones to reveal the port which is otherwise hidden behind the headband).

Also, unlike my previous headphones, this one does not work well with my tablet's media volume sync (when the headphones are turned on they always revert to a default volume, they don't remember the last volume used), so I had to turn sync off to avoid constantly having to recalibrate the volume of the headset relative to the tablet.

In terms of audio performance these seem good. They are a bit uncomfortable to wear for longer periods of time, e.g. more than say 45 minutes (rough approximation) and they start to hurt my ears a bit. I do have asymmetrical ears, one has a larger fold on the top than the other, this could be a factor in the comfort (along with possibly other head/ear size/shape differences among people). As a result of this discomfort alone it is hard for me to give them more than 3 stars. I found the best way for me to wear them when I am not on the move is in reverse, with the neck bar over my chin. There is enough tension to keep them on as long as I am basically just lying back or reclining, and in that configuration they don't hurt my ears.

Another con is the type-C USB connector. Yes it is mentioned down in the wall of text of the product page so perhaps it is my fault for not noticing. But to me there is no excuse for any product of this nature not to use a standard micro-USB connector. Now I have to make sure I keep track of this cable for this device which is the only one of this type that I have, since all the other use micro-USB. I can't just plug it in to all the other micro-USB cables I have lying around my apartment.

I'm also not getting any kind of audible low battery warning, which other similar headsets always had.

The other functions such as the equalizer and locator app are fine/nice, though honestly I don't really use them.

This is my first sound bar, so I was expecting a lot from the reviews I read. It is definitely an improvement for the TV speakers however for the price I paid, I expected more. The subwoffer doesn't make a major difference either. My friend has a sound bar, paid half the price, and I can't tell the difference. It was very easy to install, that was a plus.
Again, it's okay but I could have gone with lesser quality/price.

The MHBT0545W is a simple blah, as much as you might expect, given the kind of reviews, number consumer responses, manufacture details-specs, and the retailers you would generally find these at. While trying to understand what market these are aimed towards, given the MSRP, you would think Memorex or the OEM would have given these more respect.

Packaging aside, what you find them here on Amazon, price wise is really what they are worth, or a bit less. So with that I am not that impressed. The shrink wrap is not every sophisticated and they very well might have been rewrapped. The sleeve cover slides off and reveals front flap to the headphones which sit in a velvety plastic tray. Under neath is a gold tipped red flat wire aux cable, which reminds me of the cable on the Sony MDR-V55 head phones. Also included is a micro USB charging cable. Although I had expected it, there was no carrying pouch. While doing my research I was under the impression a pouch was included. There is a 90 day warranty card, and a fold out instruction sheet, in both English and Spanish. The headphones seem to have been fully charged, as they powered up out of the box, and when I charged them they stopped charging very quickly.

They sound okay. A bit too bass for me and not clear at that. However because they have an adjustable equalizer, I prefer the treble boost setting, the most. They are not "over the ear" but more or less on the ear for me. They do well at isolating sound, the cups are soft, but the headphones keep my ears and the surrounding area warm or hot. The band has a nice plushy cushion over the head, and the cups are quite tight on my ears. I will have to see what I can do about that. The buttons are labeled well, but until I get used to them I have to take the phones off and look. So with that in mind, they are not intuitive. The lower cost model of Memorex headphones have touch controls in obvious locations on the outside ear cup - for comparisons sake, I am wondering what is up with that? These are $70 ear phones and more difficult to use.

I was able to pair them with my laptop and phone, and while connected at the same time, will switch to the source of the audio, automatically. They will not auto connect to your second device, only to the first one - which is the last device you used or paired, then you have to go to the second one and manually select connect. There is a slight gap in audio, as it detects and plays the source of sound, or start your source.

There are no voice prompts that I have noticed. The headphones have basic alert tones which do not seem very loud. Some customers will understand and appreciate what I am writing here. I will have to come back to this part and update as I get more use out of them.

Double clicking the play/pause/power button activates SIRI. However SIRI does not understand anything I say and when she speaks it's the worst quality I have ever heard. This is not particularly important, as SIRI is not an advertised feature. I will get back to this in a moment.

Conclusion, these headphones are using circuitry and a chipset, meant for $80+ headphones. Although not mentioned, they are using a CSR 8645 chipset which by specification, can multi-point connect to two phones or other combination of bluetooth audio sources. They do not advertise what codecs are supported but again by definition the chipset is meant to support Apt-X, Low Latency, and ACC, please see [...] for reference. I am led to believe, they use the chip for it's most basic features, Bluetooth 4.1, half of the available slots meant for equalizer settings, and nothing else. SIRI sounding as bad as she does, is a victim of this basic configuration, and I am surprised she actually does anything at all.

The phones look good, sound okay and worth the amount of money I paid for them. However I will be buying something else at some future date, as the bluetooth headphone market matures.

The computer itself is fine. It was originally sold to a university in California, and half the warranty had been used while it sat on a shelf. The box was slightly worn, and the cables were dirty even though the box was sealed. I made the mistake of thinking it had a screen protector on it and tried to pull it off. Y'all, it was part of the screen. The seller refunded me the difference in price between a new item and a like new item. Since this already had a registered owner in Dell's system and it was some trouble to transfer over, I'd say it was conceivably like new but not new. I used that difference in price to pay for the repair. [Note: they did initially not want to make up the difference until I provided pictures of dirty cords, etc, and offered to escalate it to Amazon's customer service. But they did eventually grant the refund in difference. But it took weeks to get the difference in price and then to have the warranty transferred to me. I was *this close* to going through Amazon to try to return the whole shebang because of being misled. But they finally came through with a compromise I found acceptable. And I am otherwise happy with the computer.]

Here are my thoughts on the machine itself--unrelated to the seller:

PROS
- Terrific resolution. Much easier to read screen text.
- Lots of variety in color configurations for different light environments.
- 32 GB of memory really makes a difference over my previous 4-8GB.
- SSD is likewise fast and the whole system is quiet.
- This list of pros is short, but they are the most important things to me. Everything else is small beans.

CONS
- It is unbelievable how hard it is to get to the USB ports, etc, on the back! I literally have to use needle-nose pliers to plug or unplug USB devices--and a flashlight and contortions. I've read it's because the speakers didn't leave a lot of options for where to put these, but it just ridiculous.
- The sound is not as good as I expected. My last Dell AIO had JBL speakers and I don't think I realized how good those were. To be fair, the sound is fine, I was just expecting to be blown away by the six speakers on the bottom.
- Poor webcam placement. It's on the bottom at a really weird angle. Will probably upgrade.
- Onboard mic is also worse than what was in the Inspiron 2320. Remedied by purchasing a separate mic. But on a system this expensive, the mic and webcam should be premium, not barely useable.
- The screen would buzz softly at anything less than 100% brightness. A workaround is to reduce brightness via Radeon Pro graphics board. SOLUTION: go through Dell community customer service boards to update the VBIOS.
- The color temperatures sometimes get really off after the monitor goes to sleep and wakes up. I put a shortcut to Dell Premier Color in the taskbar and just reapply the setting, and it's fine. Still shouldn't even be a thing that happens on a machine with this price tag.
- Not a fan of the included wired mouse and keyboard, so I swapped out my own. I'm guessing this was originally meant for a computer lab where you wouldn't want someone to walk away with the peripherals.

OVERALL VERDICT
It took a while to get everything sorted, some of which was my fault. But I did get it sorted. The lower price from the seller comes with the tradeoff of losing some of the warranty and it taking extra time to get the remaining warranty transferred to me. But it still cost thousands less via this route than it would have otherwise. So worth it, I guess, if you've got the time for shenanigans.

Battery life is pretty good.  Sound is reasonably good.  None of the ear cups fit my ears well enough to keep these from falling out, though.  And when I reach up to adjust one to keep it from falling out, barely brushing the button riggers it, which is hugely annoying, especially when I'm in the middle of a workout.  Would not buy it again.  Looking for an alternative.

The sound quality in these is pretty good.  The noise isolation is ... pretty good.  This is mechanical isolation, not electronic; the external noise is simply reduced by these acting as earplugs.  That's all I expected, so that's fine.  They stay on/in my ears pretty well, which was a principal feature that I wanted.  HOWEVER ... for appearance, I would have preferred a straight black without the silver decorative plate on each earpiece.  More importantly, one of the connections seems to be a touch flaky, and so I occasionally get static and pops or drop-outs in the sound.  These were a relatively inexpensive experiment, and I'll be trying something else.

The description on this headset is inaccurate, it states that it comes with in-line volume control, but it does not have any volume control at all. (Attaching screenshot of description at time of purchase in the event the description is changed to accurately reflect available features). The sound quality is good, the over-ear speakers are comfortable, and the mic works well but it is little on the soft side in terms of volume.

These were a cheap pair that in all honesty I got because it came with the mic/headphone y adapter. I needed a cheap pair for work from home and the computer required the adapter. I started to use the earbuds and was a bit underwhelmed, but understanding for how cheap they were.

Pros:
Usable and comfortable
Decent quality (For the Price)
The volume control is slider based and easy to use

Cons:
Sound is muffled
Audio quality is lower than earbuds only a little more expensive.

Not a pro or a con, just something to note:
The mic is at where the two headsets meet. Normally earbuds have it higher up and on the right or left side. It doesn't seem to effect audio quality of the mic, but I have heard it's a little quieter than my other earbuds that came with my phone.

Overall:
If you need everything from the headphones to the splitter, and don't expect incredible audio then the are a decent pair to buy. If you have a nice pair of earbuds and just need an adapter I would say just buy the adapter. If you don't need the adapter at all there are better earbuds for a little bit more. I will update this review if these break or I have other issues.

I last used binoculars on a trip to Alaska. I had inexpensive compact binoculars, which had a more limited range than these, and with less clarity. I was using them to look straight up the mountains to watch the amazing white goats. They were very light and my arms never became tired. Those are the ones I would take if I went again. These binoculars are superior, with the major exception being they are just not comfortable to hold. I couldn’t watch those goats for more than a few minutes, with these binoculars.

These will probably work great on a tripod, for a very muscular person, and certainly for viewing an object for a few minutes. If you have a stationary object to rest it on, that would help. Though one reviewer mentioned using a tripod, I wasn’t able to locate a place to screw in the tripod.

The price of these seems to fluctuate quite a bit. These can be a good buy for the right person.

Original review below.

I have been using the Logitech Z2300 that I purchased years ago. Connected to my computer and much appreciated when I listen to my apple subscription music. A real monster for a computer speaker. Thankfully, the Z 625 is decidedly smaller and fits on the bottom shelf of my 42 inch wood TV table with room to spare. There is also room left for my Amazon Echo and Braven wireless bluetooth speakers. The smaller size results in a much cleaner, more attractive package.

The dialog is much clearer than I expected. I have a ZVOX 450 on my main TV, so I do appreciate clear dialog.
I was disappointed that there is no bluetooth. The computer and Man Cave TV are on opposite sides of the same room, and having the Z2300 for music, and the Z625 for the TV is a bit too much. However, the problem was easily solved. On the Z625, I'm using the optical cable for the TV sound, and am using the enclosed jack to connect the speaker to my extra Iphone. As I type, I'm listening to Herman's Hermits through my Iphone to Z625 jack connection. The music is very soothing and suits my needs perfectly. No adjustments are needed when switching from the music through my smartphone via jack, or the TV sound through the optical cable. Automatic switching,

My TV test via optical was the opening of Game of Thrones. The subwoofer bass sounded great and added greatly to the enjoyment of watching the series. The galloping horses sounded thunderous.

Other considerations. I gave away my monstrous Polk system when we moved to our condo. Soundbars provide the cleanest look but really don't have any bass. My wife is picky. The soundbar is on the main TV for a cleaner appearance, while the Man Cave is a perfect home for this unit.

There was absolutely no documentation/instructions in the box, other than safety information. However hookup instructions were printed on the cardboard box. Don't destroy them opening it. Hooking up via optical was very intuitive and took minutes. I'd still like some instructions. For example, the power button is a push button. Does it shut off after inactivity? I'm doing it manually. Going by the Z2300, it probably won't make any difference. These are built to last.

I just returned this TV after 6 days.

Cons. Ranged from great picture, to all pink, to no picture at all on HDMI settings. When I changed to over the air, perfect picture. Back to HDMI, no picture.

As Vizio requires you to ship the TV to them in California, at your expense, for all warranty work on TVs under 32 inches, it wasn't worth keeping.

I returned this, and went next door to Sams Club and purchased the Vizio VO 320E for $ 338. This 32 inch size qualifies for in home service. I took Sams extended warranty. The quality is so much better than the 26 inch. Cable inputs are sensibly placed, not like the 26 inch model that requires you to perform acrobatics to hook up. Great picture and sound on this one. A Consumer Reports Best Buy.

Original review on Vizio 26.

I purchased this TV 2 days ago at Walmart, on sale at $248. Paid $ 19.99 to extend the warranty to 3 years. However, the Walmart warranty doesn't kick in until the Vizio warranty ends. Excellent PQ and VG sound. I expect to return the TV this week. Why? Vizio Warranty: With TVs less than 32 inches, Vizio requires the customer to ship the TV-at your expense- to some unidentified location. Not good. If they don't find a warrantied problem, you pay return shipping and probably the diagnostic cost.

On day one, the sound went out, and I had to pull the plug out, to reboot and get the sound back. On day 1, and day 2, the TV sometimes was all pink when turned on. More rebooting. Given the Vizio warranty terms, I don't want to take a chance and keep it. If there was a local authorized service center, I might take a chance.

OK, it's easy to use and works great!  Now, the rest of the story:  When you use it, it identifies itself as headphones.  Seems ok, but then you leave the house with your phone and you will miss every call and audible notation because it thinks it is still connected to headphones.  The solution is simple -- you must go into your phone settings and select bluetooth>Esinkin BT Adapter>Forget this Device.  That's right, every time you want to use it you have to pair it and then Forget it when done.  Simply "disconnecting" it only lasts a few seconds and your phone returns to headphone mode.  Now, if I am all wrong about this, please correct me and let everyone else know.  This would be great for a retired phone you use as your music box and stays connected to your sound system all the time.  But for an active phone, it's a PIA.

It's not plug in and use with Windows.  You have to go online and download a specific file to use it. It's hot to the touch and awkward for your laptop. The sound quality is very nice and clear with headphones but with this plugged in the sound on your computer will not work without them.

This worked after I copied the dvd (not large - in data size or physical size) to my desktop and installed it from there.

The program that captures audio is a pain. You have to read the manual to figure out simply how to record. After a few times I got it down though. It only saves in .wav file format. I had to save the wav file and bring it into to Audacity(free music editing program I got from internet) and then save it out as an mp3 file there. Fine as I was only using the Guitar Rig 2 program that came with the audio link cable to capture anyway. The Guitar Rig 2 program looks like it does a lot more so I'll be investigating that further.

I have now tried several things through this guitar link instead of just my guitar. If you have an instrument without a normal music jack, you can use an RCA mini stereo jack into what ever instrument you are using's headphone jack(which works as audio out) and it will record through the guitar link cable to the computer. Things I've tried even include the $13 dollar paper jamz drum kit and my Flanger(like a distortion pedal but fits right into the guitar's music jack), and my electric violins - one had a standard music jack and the other had the mini stero jack.

You should buy a cable that goes from mini stero to standard size music jack - to fit your head phones into the guitar link head phone slot. That head phone slot is for standard music cable, not mini stereo(the little head phone jack most head phones have.)

I've now tried it on Win 7 Starter and XP. I can use it on both.

This is for the “WiFi 6 Bluetooth YABER Pro V8 450 ANSI Lumen Native 1080P HD Projector” (more people should put their product in the review).

I really want to like this but I’m having a hard time.

First the positives….

It is lightweight. It doesn’t make much noise. The keystone adjustments are great. At about 8-10 feet from the screen it is really really good. It is a good value for the money.

Now the negatives…

It won’t connect to WiFi. At all. So I can’t update firmware or cast from my wireless devices.

I’m connected using Apple TV and I can’t get to the projector management screen to make any adjustments. I have to disconnect Apple TV and then I can access the projector menus. This is a real inconvenience.

8-10 feet seems to be the sweet spot. But I moved mine back to 16 feet so I could have it dead center to the screen. While I am still within the focal range, the focus does not seem crisp and the light appears slightly too dim. I read somewhere that a firmware update may help this… but I can’t connect the unit to the internet to get the update. This is almost a deal breaker for me. If I was still within my return window I would probably return it.

The lens cap can be difficult to remove and you can very easily touch the lens when removing the cap. It should be much easier or it should screw on.

Overall I would give this “good” but not great marks. Value for the money is good but not great if you can’t use all the features or suffer from mediocre focus and brightness. You may be happy. I’m almost regretting my choice.

I am, unfortunately, going to have to order a different headset. I had high hopes for this one, based on its reviews, but it is problematic for me. The controls would be convenient for many people, but they are not for me, which leads me to my major frustration with this headset: it is definitely not for glasses-wearers. I should have foreseen this, honestly, but I didn't. The piece that fits behind the ear is quite large, and even though I wear super thin, flexible glasses frames, there really isn't enough room for both the headset and my glasses behind my ear. It is next to impossible to put on this headset one-handed without my glasses on--with them, there's no chance, as far as I can tell. Trying to operate the controls makes my glasses move around on my face, which is definitely unpleasant while driving. I also find the rubber piece that fits in the ear uncomfortable. I switched to the small size option, but it still seems to be a little too large, and its shape is definitely less comfortable than that of my old Bose headset. One last comment--the packaging is terrible to get into, and you have to basically destroy it to open it, which means returning it is not really an option. I'm giving it 3 stars because I think it would be a fine headset for many people, even though it's a poor one for me.
