No codes to use with other universal remotes? Seems the Zvox people decided once it was hooked up no one would ever switch back to their TV sound for any functions. If it worked seamlessly with my remote I'd give it 4 stars. Easier to stick to their weird remote.

The little cow certainly can moo but she moo's even when no one is in the room (or directly outside, no breezes, no air conditioning, etc).

Either I have poltergeists or this cow moo's at her own free will. Either way, I can't count on her to moo accurately upon motion. The sound is pretty loud too, which I wanted.

Very disappointed. Product review does not tell you but this generation of Oontz angle 3 ultra is NOT compatible with any other earlier models. Purchased to replace a bad one of a pair and will have to return. Will not pair for L/R stereo or dual stereo to any previous models. Should be mentioned in LARGE letters in product description. Company basically told me tough luck. Otherwise, I have been a big fan of these speakers. They have a nice, balanced sound. This model also has to have the bass boosted one value to match the sound from previous versions and is able to be done in the app.

Picture quality is fine, so that's not issue. Enough reviews have covered that.

I have one major complaint, and though it seems petty it is frustrating: I only use the built in streaming services on this, and every time I turn the TV off it resets to the antenna input, with screeching static since there is no source. I've had to put my chromecast in an HDMI port to keep this from happening.

Also, the remote layout is not great, as the navigation buttons are right around major menu buttons. I often hit a menu button as I'm trying to navigate the streaming services, kicking me out of what I was doing.

If I could do it again I'd get a Vizio. The QWERTY keyboard on the back of the Vizio remote is genius, and it makes entering in account information for streaming services a breeze.

As far as sound quality, I was very impressed with the sound it produced despite being so affordable. I'd probably rate the sound at 4 stars for the price.

So, why three stars? Vizio isn't the largest brand in the world which means that this bar might not be able to be programmed into some remotes, which is the case with the AT&T Uverse remote, which of course means that you're likely going to have to keep the sound bar's remote handy. The remote is also pretty small, so the chances of losing it was pretty high.
It worked out of the box but only the channel and volume buttons light up. So  no good in the dark.

It works good. I had the s9-hd previously. That one seemed to be more comfortable and work better. But I do like this one also, nice sound.
It came on time also and the price was good

These are very tight against my ears causing discomfort. For JBLs these are not stellar. A bit thin with mids lacking. They’re inexpensive- I wasn’t expecting full rich sound, but JBL/Harmong Kardin make excellent small speakers with some of the best sound for the dollar. I got them to use/leave at work. I needed corded headphones to plug into the ridiculous pc for zoom. Having headphones on hand for lunch is useful and I am not interested in being expensive personal items to work. These will do, but boy they hurt. They’re light and not ugly.

Thin sound for JBL. Treble is dominant- little mid and very little bass.  From JBL, I expect much fuller sound. It's an odd little speaker. Because if it's shake some kart is always pointing at the surface on which it is sitting. It's heavy, but solid. Connects without any trouble - Just turn both devices on - no having to switch off and on to find each other. Doesn't drop off. Cable is solid. If Harmon/JBL has a bass device that connects/pairs I may pick it up. This jack if full sound grates on me.

I use this Tendak Gold-Plated Active HD 1080P HDMI to VGA Converter Adapter Dongle with 3.5mm Audio for Laptop PC Projector HDTV PS3 Xbox STB Blu-ray DVD with my Raspberry as a connection to a monitor that does not have the necessary connect cable.  I like it OK.

I review the package I purchased a while back and this keep popping up to be reviewed again.  The offering was for the 0 to 49$ product rating and I reviewed it favorably.  This extra review popping up for me to respond to is irratating and causes me grief.  So I am reviewing this plan as a result of it's effect of not being marketed such that the additional requests to review the product again, is reflected in this review.
This SF Cable, 3 RCA Male to 3 RCA Female Audio Video Extension Cable (10 Feet) allowed me to sit up a VHS tape player way away from my computer to make a digital file of an old Tape from years past.

These banana plugs are functional with one flaw.  The rubber gripping portion slided up on the bananna and can result in the prong not fully seating in the hole. Belkin should change the design to where the inside is wedged to not allow it to slide forward paste the face of the plug.  These do the job and the screw in the metal base to accomodate a good tight grip on the speaker wire is sound, if not a little more work.  Tighter than some other plugs that screw down on the wire after it is positioned out of a hole.  The gold coating on the bannana is a good sound fit, so for a home application it is OK.

I will use thePYLE-PRO PDMR5 - 5'' High Performance Midrange Drivers I purchased in a Center Channel speaker I am designing and building for my Living room.  I will provide enough volume combined with Tweeters and a couple of crossover arrangements to fill the area.  Backed up by a Powered Subwoofer, 15 Inch, behind the Theater System.

Its 50 bucks for a mic and mount - don't be expecting a 500 system.  Good starter rig but I can see already what I like and don't like and what I'll be swapping out or upgrading inside the year.  The arm is a bit light weight like something you'd get your kid.  Nothing stays exactly where you place it.  The arm can't actually handle the weight of the mic and the disc shield.  I'll probably grab a Walmart lamp on a similar but bigger arm and swap end hardware.  Double-check your PC hardware before writing off the mic.  I thought it was horrible when plugged directly to my laptop.  But when I put it through a USB hub it suddenly sounded pretty good. Probably on a different bus than all the hard-drive traffic. Its not magical: You have to put in the time to position it *just right*, and aim it *just so* and you can dial it in pretty good.  Speaking of dials - once the mic is in the shock mount you can use them, so just set the volume to 90% and do the rest on your PC.  Would have been nice if they included some zip ties for cable management. I have plenty but not include 4 zip ties is a sure sign of going as cheap as they could.

The bad first, the microphone is horrible, very scratchy to the point of unusable. The good news is it has a mounting screw adapter that fits my blue yeti microphone which I wanted to use in the first place. For the money the mount is worth it, but get your own microphone because the supplied one is very bad, I can’t stress how bad it is, don’t even try to use it.

Bought this to supplement my DSLR, size was right, handheld twilight mode was great (although colors were washed out), loved the compass and GPS features. Unfortunately I had to return this camera within two weeks of purchase - pictures were so noisy with a complete lack of sharpness. Yes I know it's not an SLR, but my wife's three year old canon point and shoot took higher quality photos! Even in bright mid-day shooting, under every possible camera setting, there's just no way to get a decently sharp picture. Just about every shot looked good thru the screen, but zoom in or transfer it to a computer screen and it looked grainier than old camera phone pics.

Replaced it with a Sony NEX-3, with dedicated lenses, yes the NEX-3 was more expensive, but then again it's worth it to be able to take wonderfully crisp photos!
The sound only works half of the time. Other wise it's a great tablet.
I liked it because the sound was pretty good.

This little earbuds have great battery life. They are a little clunky in your ear, and the sound isn't that great, but they lasted forever. The range on the bluetooth was also hit and miss with sometimes being less than a foot, and sometimes over 10 feet. Overall, a great set for kids or a cheap pair of headphones.

These are great as Bluetooth speakers but have a serious problem when you use the aux input: Delay. I wanted to be able to use these when I practice my bass using my headphone amp ( I no longer have headphones with a cord) but it doesn't work because of the delay issue.
Other than that, I'm delighted with their sound quality, the waterproof sturdy build, and silly light show... all great. But about half of what I use a Bluetooth speaker for is to practice my bass on the deck without having to lug my amp out and find an extension cord.
They keep popping off the wall. I got them so I wouldn't have to put nails in things but these are really not doing well.
Used for about a year, then had to get rid of it because the sound was so staticky. Not that great.

I am comparing this to a Logitech C910 HD 1080p webcam which I've been using almost daily since 2012.

I don't stream games but I stream my live DJ broadcasts. I use 4 webcams and a green screen. I use xSplit exclusively.

This C922x Pro Stream is for gamers so they can stream on Twitch or YouTube. The camera is supposed to automatically load a background removing program so you don't have to use a green screen. This special software, Personify ChromaCam, is free when have the C922. Installing is another matter entirely. Myself, like others, have older, but capable systems that cannot install this software. I checked on Personify's website and the PC requirements are: Processor: Intel 4th generation or higher Core CPU, or the AMD equivalent (Quad core AMD Phenom), OS: Windows 7, 8, 10, and Memory: 4GB+ RAM. My system, even though its 3 years old, meets all these specs but when installing I get a 'unable to install due to ABX or ADX" something.

The camera's clarity is not any better than my 4 year old C910. In fact, my C910 has Carl Zeiss, the new cam doesn't not. The colors appear washed out with too much brightness. I expected better, but the C922 regressed a bit in the lens department.

Now here's a kicker for you...you cannot, and I mean, cannot, view the camera while changing it's settings. Yes, you heard me right. Open the camera settings and you get a windowed box for changing the settings, but the webcam does not come on or is it viewable. So, am I supposed to change the settings, open the cam, close the cam, change the settings, open the cam...etc..etc?

The mount is sturdy and multi-positional. I like the added tripod adapter. At this price point there should be a privacy shield.

I had an issue getting the camera to initially turn on. The outer ring would flash but no camera picture. Then I realized that some webcams don't like being plugged into a USB hub. After adding an extension cord and plugging in directly to my PC the cam worked.

The big question...is this camera worth the $50 more than the entry level C920 series camera? For the money you get a ChromaCam program which may or may not work and you get 6 months free xSplit service. Hmmmmm...OBS, which is quite capable, is a free service.

Logitech has so many choices lately, each with increased pricing. Let's face it, it's all about the price. Do you really need your ugly mug put up in a live game? Probably not since it's going to use PC resources that would be better used for gaming. For the $50 extra you could get a couple decent games, or a new mouse, or a mouse pad, or a boat load of peanuts.

The choice is yours.

CD player stopped working after 3 months (just spit out cds) and the sound stopped 2 weeks later. Thus one star. Prior to that I was happy with it, so here's my review.
***UPDATE***: While it was past the Amazon return date, it was within the OEM 1yr warranty, so I sent it back and they replaced it. I had to pay shipping to them and round trip was 2 to 3 weeks without a radio. In general I do like the unit for the money, so long as this one isn't a dud.

Installation wasn't bad. I didn't need a trim kit as the one it came with was fine. I purchased a wire harness for my Nissan Frontier and crimp connectors made the connections easy. The hardest part was wiring up the backup camera. I had to find the wire to my reverse lights in a plug in the passenger foot rest and similarly I powered the backup camera by splicing into my backup light wire. That works fine, though the picture flickers occasionally. I suspect that's the wiring/ power and not a camera issue.

Sound quality was fine while it lasted. It does cut out the first second of each song when listening to my iPhone over Bluetooth, but that was only a minor annoyance. The touch screen interface worked fine for me. The interface isn't super intuitive but the icons are nice and big and the screen sensitivity was fine. It was great value for the money for the 3 months that it worked.
This is a lightweight unit, easy to use and delivers good sound quality - all for a very affordable price.

Initially I thought these headphones were Pokemon branded. The "ears" resemble Pikachu's tail. Although they have a Pokemon sounding name, "Volibolt", they are just capitalizing on people like me being mistaken.
The headphones are ok for sound quality, but the sound becomes distorted at higher volumes. They are not really large enough to fit kids older than ten. Both the expandable band and the ear covers are made for young children.

This camera feels a little rinky-dink. It is very lightweight and seems likely to break easily. That being said, it is not an expensive camera and might be what you need to use in a circumstance where you might not want to bring a more pricey model. The sound and image quality are ok, though nothing great. The screen is large enough that you can watch playback easily.
These speakers are of fair quality but don't hold a charge very well.  The sound quality is just middling. I also had some trouble getting the blue tooth set up with it. Not recommended.

I got these for my online courses for college. Unfortunately, they barely block out the surrounding noises. They initially star out comfortable when wearing them, but eventually they started hurting my ears. The sound and volume control were nice.

Our at least a rubber stopper. Otherwise you'll never get a good grip.

The hollow ball gets crushed so the swing arm just slips. I filled it with avrubber stopper. Problem solved. They need a better design.

It's near impossible to tell if there's anything behind my jeep. I wanted to be able to see behind me and I also wanted a forward camera to be able to record trail rides. I went with this mirror dash cam. I didn't even know these things existed until recently.

For recording, I'm using a samsung high endurance 64GB SD card. The built in formatting function is simple and quick. The video feeds for front and rear cameras are pretty clear. Going from one view to the other or both takes a a swipe.

I removed the OEM mirror and installed this as a full replacement. One thing about this mount vs the OEM, is that this one vibrates badly. Also, there's only one part that rotates behind the mirror. Whereas the OEM mirror rotates at the base and the mirror.

I stuck the reverse camera in the middle of spare tire mount. There was more than enough enough wire to run along the cage length of my jeep wrangler unlimited. I did not hook up the wire for the reverse lines, but the camera is live without it. It connects through a slim single plug from rear camera to mirror.

As for trying to use the rear camera full time instead of the mirror surface, there's still quite a bit of reflection. Even at full brightness. To cut down on the amount of reflection, you need to point the mirror at yourself instead of the towards the rear of the vehicle as you would do with a regular mirror. Which can be difficult since there's only that one pivot on this mirror.

One thing that was necessary for me, was to get the latest firmware. Out of the box, there's no way to turn off the loud music that plays when the mirror powers on and off. It'd be nice to have actual volume control even with the firmware, there's only on and off. There's no way I could have kept this mirror without being able to turn that sound off.

One other thing I'd like is a GPS module so I could overlay speed and even record trails overlays for off roading. There is an unused port labeled GPS, but the hole is covered.

It was not easy for me to tell what mode this thing is in. Too many variations of blinking lights.
The only way I knew that it worked was by popping out the sd card and plugging it into a computer.
Maybe if it at least had wifi while charging, you could check the status.
That being said, when I did check the video, the quality was quite clear.

I like that this connects to my BT sound bar, it gives my records a really rich sound and eliminated the need for a bulky pre/amp (I forget the word for the piece of equipment that used to act as the middle-man between my record player and speakers. It's been a while).

What I don't like is that it's very fickle. I thought my record was dusty, which would be impossible since it's been in the sleeve in a plastic bag for years, but after trying more records I got the same skippy results. The needle is sensitive or needs more weight to retain contact with the vinyl. This is frustrating since it's primary function is a record player. The FM feature works fine, but that's not what I bought a turntable for.

It's okay for casual playing, but frustrating when the main flaw is a part of it's main function.

The pros:
-The sound is immersive for a sound bar, it's rich and fills the room with realistic "layering" of sounds. It doesn't replace surround sound, but the highs and bass are all clear, the volume is great.
-There is a lot of control available for turning up and down different sounds in shows and movies
-It looks good, the casing is made of high quality materials. Even the packaging is well thought out!
-The wireless subwoofer is a big plus. The less cords the better, we have it about 5 feet from the sound bar and the connection between the two is reliable.

Cons:
-The HDMI output has trouble sending signal to the TV, it's really slow and we had to hook and unhook our devices many times. Finally we just used the digital/optical cable after three days of "no signal" frustration.

-The subwoofer does not have any lights to indicate if it is on. The soundbar itself also has no information screen which seems lacking for something of this cost. You just read the number of white lights that blink to get your information, this seems very dated and it's annoying. You can't see what input it's on or anything unless you hit the remote and count the lights.

I love mine! But, I don't like Alexa so I do like that I can keep her turned off. However, I have to turn her off after every update! That's a bit irritating. The other issue that I'm having is even though I have a large memory card inserted and have my audio books installed on it and there is more than plenty of room for all of them. I have to reinstalled them after every update. That is REALLY IRRITATING!!

This car stereo exceeded all of my expectations. True, those expectations were super low due to how inexpensive this is. But, my goodness, it was nice to get a good surprise for a change.

But then came the bad surprise: one night, we started the car, and the blue lights came on but the stereo did not. It wouldn't turn on. It wouldn't turn off. And when the car sat for a day, it drained the battery dry.

Which fixed it. It needed to have the power cut completely in order to reset. Your mileage may vary, but for me, that's a nonstarter. Get it? The husband thinks it's no big deal, at least not worth replacing until it quits entirely. He's the installer, so he wins.

The sound is perfectly serviceable. It gets loud, and all frequencies are clear. Bluetooth connection works great, though my husband prefers aux in for sound quality (Mr. Ears). It was an easy install in my 2004 Odyssey EX (I bought a wiring harness and a frame kit). Still, I would not buy it again.

Three and a half stars.

UPDATE: After a few months, I'm still fairly okay with the performance of the Orbi when it is working. However, there are a few things I wish I'd known ahead of time. For one, you won't get all the features if you have FIOS. You have to run the Orbi in bridge mode, which means no Circle. For another, the router does a poor-to-mediocre job of saving the names it lets you give your devices. I spent a day running down which MAC address went to which device. Next day, poof. Gone. A third issue is that the router needs to be reset every so often when it inexplicably slows down to dial-up speeds. Wouldn't be such a big deal if - IF - everything would just connect back up, but the Orbi doesn't play well with some devices. It HATES my Ecobee thermostat, which I have to assign a new static IP to with each reset, because the Orbi refuses to let it on dynamically and always gives the old static IP to another device. I wasn't looking for something so high maintenance when I forked over the money to buy these things.

Basically, this is a fast wifi network system that really does cover my whole house and is working well with a nighthawk EX7500 as an extender. It has some bugs and some limitations. It comes into a mostly Apple ecosystem and works fine with the computers and airport express extenders as well (but not airport extreme routers, because they will only bridge another airport extreme). The bugs are bad enough to knock it to three stars, but I like the speed so much that if the network stays up a week in a row, I will add a star.

I do not hate this at all. I bought the system because I was spending too much time on the phone with my ISP over an end-of-life router situation. There is no brand replacement coming for that router, at least not anytime soon, which is a bummer. I scoured the internet and settled on this.

I have set it up a couple of times now. The first time, it took all day to convince it to stay connected to its own satellite, worked a couple of days, and then would not connect to the internet. I called my ISP and got them to look at it through my modem (I don't know what it is they do or how they are able to "see" what router is connected to my modem). It went back up at screaming speed. This time it worked for about 24 hours before booting half of my smart devices. So, I set them up again, which took a while, since I now needed static IP addresses for some of them in order for Orbi to let them online. I do not know why.

I also tried to add a NetGear Nighthawk EX7000 extender so that I could have a remote disk via USB. So much nope. Even though it was in bridge mode, with no reason to exist except to make an external hard drive accessible on my network, the extender and Orbi were doubling IP addresses, so every so often people would get the "another computer is using your IP address" message. Pulled the extender and no more issues since then. It has only been about three days without an incident.

The good is great. I get coverage everywhere in my condo in an Edwardian building that has been added onto in strange and wonderful ways that make good wifi impossible upstairs. It works with an EX7500 extender (which is boss). I get well over 200Mpbs near the main router, and the lowest I get is 175 anywhere else. I am only paying for 200. As noted above, it also works with my Apple Airport Expresses, so I can have remote USB disks and printers.

I enabled Circle to stop my teenager from going on the internet in the middle of school nights without having to keep my husband, who works nights, from being able to check his email when he gets home. So far, that is rudimentary but okay. I am trying to figure out where QOS settings are. I think I found them on one of the router login places (there's the Orbi app, the Netgear Genie, the Orbi login page, and I think one other). So far, I think the only thing that works with Alexa are some very basic commands like pause the internet and when is my bedtime. I need to be able to tell it to pause the kid's internet. EDIT TO ADD: I can pause the kid's internet through IFTTT.

Bottom line: I'm okay with this, but I expected a smoother set up process for the money. If I'd known what it was going to entail, I probably would have waited to buy.

You really cannot beat the price on these. However, the sound is heavily compressed, and the wires are cheap. Nevertheless, I live in a house with a kitten and have a teenager who loses things. Therefore, I keep at least one of these earbud sets on hand, still in the packaging, at all times for when the kitten murders a better headset or for when the kid can't find headphones on the way out the door to school.

This is a tablet running a real operating system (Windows 10) hooked up to a small keyboard with a trackpad. And it's all right.

It's thicker and heavier but smaller than my 11 inch MacBook Air, which makes it more convenient in some respects and less convenient in others. The MacBook Air is a used 2012 model with a Core i5 and 4gb ram. It's snappy, but it didn't come with an SD slot, and used it cost about a hundred more than this. The quad core atom processor on the transformer book is pretty fast for a tablet, but it is definitely a lightweight compared to a core i5. Or even an i3.

My iPad Air runs iOS. Way less versatile than Windows 10 in terms of doing work-a-day things, having a browser respond the way you're used to having it respond, etc., but it's still pretty good. However, the keyboard experience is something of a pain, especially since there's no trackpad and you have to touch the tablet face to do the mouse-like things. And using the mail program is harder on the iPad than it is on a mac laptop or on the transformer book.

The transformer book is noticeably slower than either of the other devices, but I was able to do everything I set out to do on it. The Office apps are good and integrate seamlessly with the other Office installations on my other stuff. The screen is as nice as or nicer than my iPad Air. I had a MeMo for a year, and I loved the screen on that. This is very similar - excellent resolution, nice and bright, a bit wider aspect than what the iPad Air has.

The sound is about as good as one would expect. Which is to say, meh. But that's what headphones are for.

Cortano makes it easy to get set up. I asked it to find the apps I wanted. When I want something from the control panel, I ask for that. Since this is my first time with Windows 10, having the assistant helps a lot.

There do seem to be some battery issues. Charging takes a long time. There was an issue with the MeMos, as well, that I sort of resolved by fully cycling the battery a couple of times.

All things considered, I like this tablet/transformer book quite a bit. My only significant issue with it is weight. For my purposes, the ultralight notebook or the regular tablet will meet my needs on any given day. However, if you like your PC desktop and need, essentially, a shuttle craft, though. this is a pretty good compromise machine. It's a decent enough tablet. You can do business stuff, check email, surf the web, and watch movies. You won't be transcoding video or playing resource intense games, but this ultimately is a nice tablet with a keyboard. Not a desktop substitute. Maybe not even a laptop substitute, depending on your needs. But definitely a nice tablet.

UPDATE WITH USAGE ISSUES:

I was getting really annoyed with battery life/charging issues. My iPad Air will stand by for a couple of weeks, no problem, whereas this thing dies if I leave it off the charger a couple of days. It also needs its OEM charger if you intend to charge it within a few hours time, as opposed to overnight and then some. I was able to solve some of this by running task manager and disabling some of the high impact background apps (Microsoft OneDrive is a big offender). And, similar to my other Asus tablet, the battery charging problem seems to improve with conditioning. On the positive side, the more I use this, the better I like it.

The microphone doesn't work. Because there was no documentation for using the microphone, I thought there wasn't one. I guess it turns out that there IS one, but either it is broken or I don't know to which communication god I should make my sacrifice in order to get it to work.

UPDATE: I am not sure what I did, but the microphone works. I think it is because I removed a pair of bluetooth speakers from my device list. Not sure why they would interfere with the microphone, but I removed them, and now have audio input.

Compared to a similar camera made by Belkin, setting up the D-Link was kind of a pain. Not as much of a pain as setting up a Foscam F18918W - where you get directed to a third party domain name provider and get to learn the joys of port forwarding - but a relative hassle.

For the Belkin, I opened the box, plugged into my router, ran a set up program that took less than five minutes, downloaded an app, and I was up and running. While this is a very similar product in both look and function, it took over an hour - and two ethernet cables - to set it up. There is no Mac software on the installation cd. The box states that a Windows pc is required, but the website has a Mac download available. You have to scroll through the product photos, which aren't in alphanumeric order. Just keep looking until you find the DCS-930L - AFTER the 931L and the 932L and the 934L. Have faith. Keep going. It's there.

Once you get the program installed, it takes very little time to *find* the camera and teach it to log into your wireless network. And then you are back to the website to set up your account and view your camera. Except you are on a Mac, and the viewer requires you to install the Java Runtime Environment. JRE is a big old security vulnerability on Macs. So much so that Apple advises against using it. Mavericks lets you turn it on case by case - and, by default, it will ask you every time before running it. If you are on an OS below Mavericks, check the googles for setting your preferences so that you're not running JRE all the time.

Okay, so now you've got JRE going, and the first thing the program tells you is that you have to update your firmware AND you need to have the camera AND your computer ethernet-jacked right into your router. LOLWUT? I'm lucky. I am on a laptop, and I have an extra ethernet cable and an empty port. So, I did that, and there I was, up and running, about an hour, hour and a half, thereabouts, after I started.

Image quality is pretty good - not great. Audio is okay. The settings are very customizable. But the wifi receiver is very weak, and that limits the usefulness of this product.

The sound is average, nothing special, I was expecting more. The noise cancelling is disappointing and mine came with a problem in the left earphone, the noise cancel option sometimes turn off automatically. The ambient option is good and clear. The good thing is the connection stability with iPhone.
Seemly well made attractive CD player but the volume was so low, even on high. Had to return for that reason. No problems with the return.

Good fit but it’s the clarity was not there.
I thought for more money it would be at least passable, it wasn’t. Missed the return because we were moving. Hopefully I can save some folks the trouble.

Sounds are a little muffled, especially in the mid-range, but not enough to matter to most people.  I couldn't get Windows 7 to recognize the headset, which means I couldn't use the microphone. Unless there is a special driver for this, Windows 7 will not recognize anything that is simply plugged into the earphones hole.  Windows 7 (and most other versions) will simply power anything plugged into the external speaker plug as if they are all the same.  So that means no microphone will work without a driver.  But cups were comfortable, and I have listened to hours of music and movies with no discomfort at all.
The sound is terrible has a lot of feedback noise
Not nearly as durable as I had hoped (hollow aluminum rods and plastic crossbeam siding), and too much trouble to put together to be worthwhile compared to the myriad alternatives.

These headphones do have a more balanced sound than the horrible original Beats that were just too bass heavy. The Bluetooth pairing was quick and easy and battery life is decent. The case and accessories seem to be good quality. In all honesty though for the sound quality I'd never pay the retail asking price for these or recommend them to anyone. I got a used pair (yes they are real Beats) for half the price of new and at this price point I feel it's worth it. The noise canceling isn't anything to write home about and if it's a big reason why you're considering these I'd look to Bose or elsewhere where it's done much better. Another point with these is comfort. They're ok for an hour or so, but I'd not want these on pushing two or more. They tend to pinch at the ear cup level and you can see in various pics how the cups nearly touch when not on the head. So the farther you are pushing those cups out the more they are fighting to close so to speak. I don't have a large head, I don't expand the headband at all when wearing, and they get a little clampy after a bit. Another comfort issue is the interior depth of the ear cups. I don't have big ear or ones that stick out and I still feel my ears slightly pushing against the speaker. I couldn't imagine anyone with large ears being happy with these at all and if you fall into that category I'd definitely try on a pair in a store before buying. The cup pads are nice and it's too bad they didn't make them just a tad deeper.  So in summary these are good headphones if not great ones, but honestly not worth retail. The Bluetooth is nice, but you're obviously paying for image here.
It's not that loud and sound quality isn't the best
Was making beeping sound very often.

At this point, I have had the Sense 2 for 2 days and I know at least some of my issues will likely be fixed with later software updates. First, the good. I like the form factor. The case is thin and the watch, even with the supplied band, is comfortable. Speaking of the band, as a big guy, I was overjoyed to see the inclusion of a second band that actually fit. Also, changing bands is a snap.

Overall, it seems to be relatively high quality. The battery life, so far at least has been fantastic. I am on hour 42 of wearing it after a 99% charge and it is down to 70% battery left. The screen is fairly bright and crisp. An understated advantage of the Sense 2 (and one of the reasons I switched) is that is OS and phone brand agnostic. You can use it with Apple or Android and, unlike the Galaxy Watch, there are no features locked away if you are not using the correct brand of phone.

If you are coming from a Galaxy Watch where you could customize the watch face and all sorts of other things and that is important to you, then move along. This watch will not be for you. For now, at least, there is not really much substantive you can do to individualize your user experience. That's not so great.

Also not so great is the things that are missing. There is no Google Maps at launch. Also, despite being a Google company, no support for the Google Assistant (Alexa only sadly). There is also no interface to control music on your phone if that is important to you. I found it mildly annoying, but not a deal breaker. In addition, some people will be turned off by the fact that there are features that require a Fitbit paid subscription to get, even though you get six months for free.

The real reason I bought this watch was the ECG function. I have had A Fib for a couple of years and used to use (and still do) a Kardia XL to check my rhythm. The Galaxy Watch 4 was nice because it did a reasonable single lead reading and it meant not having to carry another gizmo with me. You simply held still and put a finger on each of the side buttons. Unfortunately, when I switched from a Galaxy phone to a Pixel, I lost the ability to do an ECG.

On the Sense 2, the ECG has not been impressive. First, I have big hands and contorting my right one to get my thumb and forefinger on the corner of the glass has been a challenge at time. It often takes several tries to get it right. Second, despite confirming on both my Kardia and my Galaxy Watch, the Sense 2 will never indicate that I am in A Fib. Apparently, if your pulse goes above 120 (which mine frequently does while in A Fib) then the Sense 2 just gives up and won't really check. Even in instances where it was below 120, the Sense will not confirm. I guess we get to settle for inconclusive results instead. Given this feature was the main reason I bought the watch, it may be a deal breaker for me and I may return it for that reason. If this feature is not that important to you, then it may still be a good option.

Overall though, it may be a good option for the right person. If you care primarily about health and fitness tracking and want a good battery life, then this is a good option. At the current $300 price point, I still feel like Fitbit may be asking a little too much given the features of the other higher end options on the market.

I had the older version on this amp, and I think it was better than this version.  I use these with Audio Technica ATH-M50x headphones and I noticed a difference, but I don't know that I would say it was better.  Louder certainly, but not as clear.  I am not an audiophile, so the only description I can give is that it seemed more muddy.  The highs didn't seem as clear and the bass was loud, but lacked any real punch in songs that normally would deliver it.

I think they are alright.  The sound quality is average for headphones in the price range.  The wires seem a little stiff to me, which I found more annoying than I probably should have.  All things considered, I would probably not buy them again.

In general, I would say that these are just sort of okay.  I have several other pairs of headphones that sound just as well, were cheaper, and were more comfortable.  Probably not a pair that I would repurchase.

I bought this system to replace my Yamaha YSP-500 and a fairly sizeable subwoofer. My issue was that we were doing a remodel of our living room to put in a wall with a fireplace and stonework where our existing entertainment center was. Because the Yamaha projector is fairly substantial, mounting it directly to the wall wasn't an option, so I would have had to build another shelf or do something else. I would have also had to relocate the sub which would have meant either buying some sort of wireless set up or running a cable under the floor and into the wall.

Since the Bose speaker is much slimmer and lighter, has an available wall bracket, and the sub is wireless I thought I had the solution to my problem. For that part, the Bose is great. It was easy to mount, is relatively unobtrusive, and having more flexibility with the placement of the sub is really nice. If you have space limitations or just don't want to mess with running speaker wire (or can't) then this is a good alternative.

This is also a good alternative for people that just want to plug something in and have it work. If you are technically challenged, or just don't want to invest the time in setting up a home theater then this is a usable solution. Most people could have this up and running (including configuration) in less than 20 minutes.

I thought the sound quality is pretty decent. I don't know that it is significantly better than the older (and cheaper) Yamaha Sound Projector that it replaced. Unlike some reviewers, I thought voices (at least on television shows) were clearer and easier to hear than what I was used to. The bass was crisp, but I haven't experienced the punch I am used to with my Yamaha sub. Granted the Bose Accoustimass module is a lot smaller, but there is a very noticeable difference.

There are two areas that I took a star away for each. One is obviously cost. At around $1000, I would say that this would be a better value. At its current price I think that you are not really getting what you pay for. For all the trade-offs, I think there are cheaper alternatives.

The second is the fact that it lacks any sort of display or ability to customize. You can't make any sort of sound profiles (movies, sports, etc), you don't have anything like a night mode, and there is no display whatsoever to indicate something as simple as volume level. Some people may like that, but to me it was rather annoying. For the price, I think you should be able to do a little more with it. Again, if you are the plug-and-play type, this probably won't bother you.

Overall, other than the size and wireless sub, this is not an improvement from my Yamaha Sound Projector. I think it's good, but if I had to do it over again I would probably look at other, cheaper options.

For the first two weeks, I really liked this alarm clock radio. It had good light; it had decent sound and reception; the buttons were responsive; and it did its basic functionality. The USB charging port was a bit iffy but that's not why I selected the item so that wasn't that important.

But after that two weeks, it started acting a little less responsive and the alarm would go off at odd times. I'd reset it and it would be fine for a bit but then act up again. After a recent black out, I tried to reset the time and the button for "time set" was not being responsive so I can no longer set the time.

So it worked well for awhile but then stopped working. Even the radio stopped getting a decent a reception so I'm not quite sure what happened. It is a little disappointing because it worked well for awhile and it looks good too.
These are the second pair of Midlands I have bought.  They are durable and have a good sound.  However, they use up battery power very quickly even in standby mode.
Amazing sound quality, but not very durable.
Not the best sound - a little high pitched without much bass and no ability to adjust or balance.  In hindsight, I should have ordered the set with the bass.

Nice little portable speaker. I bought this as a cheap alternative to a sound bar and I am impressed with the sound. My tv has down firing speakers, so this speaker gets the job done whether its sitting in front of the tv or next to me. It also has a 3.5mm jack of you want to plug in headphones. The instructions are pretty straightforward and it connects pretty easily.

The only thing I didn't like and why I took off a star, was because of the short charging cord that comes with it as it could stand to be a little longer (it also does not have a charging brick, but my rating does not reflect that, just to inform others if they want to know). The cord is about 6 inches long and I immediately changed it out with a 3ft cord I had to reach my extension plug by the tv.

Edit* Since owning this speaker a bit longer, I've noticed a ringing sound in the speaker when it's paired with my tv. While listening to music it's not as noticeable. I also learned the hard way that the 3.5mm jack is input only and not output when others had said you could use headphones with it. So if you want that option, it's a no go for this speaker.
The sound could have been louder but otherwise ok.

I own the TOZO T10, and I can't say enough great things about them, but alas, I stupidly left one where the puppy could get it, and now I have one ear that still performs, but the 'button' no longer works (amazing that it didn't break).

I probably should have bought another pair of the T10s, but the T6s had pretty amazing specs, so I took a chance.

First, the pros; AMAZING sound, noise isolation, fit, and sensitive fingerprint controls (no pressing). I have over ear Bose, and Beats, and these could stand against their sound quality any day.

Now the cons: you can't roam far from the phone, computer or iPad you're connected to, or the bluetooth will drop you. In fact, if a butterfly farts in the amazon, these earbuds will drop their connection to your bluetooth device. The other stand-out con is battery life. I don't know if mine were defective, but they NEVER had the battery that I enjoyed with the T10s, and they seem to be getting worse. The case will hold a charge when stored for well over a week, but the buds last about four hours with music playing in them. If you're just wearing them at the gym for an hour or two, they're fine, but if you're wearing them to drown out office noise, you're going to be out of luck after lunch.

I am considering handing these off to one of the younger people in my family who need a spare pair to use while their primary pair is charging. If TOZO comes out with a new model, I may wait to see if the folks reviewing it have the same issues. I'm actively looking for the old T10s in the meantime.

The sound pretty good for a cheaper pair of eat buds, but sadly, they don't last very long. The cords tend to snag quite a bit, and that definitely reduced their lifespan. Otherwise, they would be a nice alternative to expensive brands.

These headphones sound great, cancel noise completely, and are as comfortable as in-ear headphones can be, BUT, they separate at the noise cancelling rectangle no matter how gently you treat them. It's a flaw in the design that is just unavoidable. Since Bose does replace them, I would have deducted only one star, but they limit the number of times they will replace a single headset, but don't have a solution for the design flaw. One last complaint is about the coating on the wires. Bose continues to use a wire coating that has a tacky/sticky feel to them, and catches the wires on anything that they get close to. As a result, you will catch the wire on things as you walk by, and have the earbud jerked from your ear.

I would like to start out by saying this is my first bluetooth. The phone I am using it with is the Motorola Q Global (ATT). New law 7/1/08 so I was forced to get something.

My hair easily covers this headset and is completely hidden. I really like that feature. It is lightweight and when I call others they claim that the clarity is better than when I speak from cell phone. You get a really awesome carrying case which is also a charging base. The fit of this headset is also good, easy to put on with one hand and I wear glasses and it does not conflict at all.

However, the clarity for ME, especially if I am not in the car, is awful. And sometimes in the car is still not good. The volume is inadequate in the best situation.

For some reason the desk charger does not work the best. It is hard to get the headset positioned just right to be sure it is charging.

Battery life is mediocre nothing to write home about.

If Motorola fine tunes this bluetooth it stands to be the best. Looking for an new and improved version of this.

My daughter recommends that I buy the Jawbone II by Aliph, so I am going to try it also. But I am attached to the this one and hope that Motorola keeps the good the same and fixes the other issues.

Pros:
1) Small
2) Lightweight
3) Fit is great
4) Easy to put on
5) Nice charging options
6) Very Nice carrying case/charger
7) Nice adapter cable included

Cons
1) Very poor clarity (user/my end)
Static
Cutting in and out
Loudness inadequate
Tinny

2) Desk Charger: has to be positioned just right to charge

3) Battery life not the best
Sound quality is mediocre at best, and it doesn't get as loud as I'd hoped it would. But, it's portable and a cute red color and it beats the speakers on my phone, so, not bad.
The sound quality is terrible, and the interface is awful

The size alone is a huge limitation on this player because it takes a lot of futzing around to find the right controls.  Sound without earbuds is nearly non-existent, with earbuds, not bad.  Mostly it was a mistake on my part thinking that I was going to get more than I got.

Decent headphones, decent sound for my purposes which is to listen to audiobooks.  I don't like over-the-ear designs because they usually end up hurting if I wear them too long. Kind of pricey for what you get.
For keys it is ok but for my iphone and wallet  there is not enough volume

I like this small radio just fine.  I knew it was going to be small but it turned out to be smaller than I anticipated.  I keep it on a high shelf in my bathroom.  The sound quality is excellent.  There are two reasons why I rated it less than perfect.  First, the power button is located on the right side of radio.  When I reach up there to turn it off or on I often move the tuner wheel that is on the top.  This happens because I have to steady it on top as I turn it on/off.  This happens because it's so small…and I keep it high on a shelf.  Also, I've found it cutting out some times.  I'm not sure what's happening there.  I think the tuner had gone off station perhaps.  I'll have to watch this and see if it continues.  All in all, I can recommend this radio.  If you're looking for a small radio with excellent sound then you'll like this radio.

This can only hook up to ONE first gen echo. Or TWO of the beer generations. When playing on the everywhere group it’s just ok. I think for the price and size there should be more functionality. I’m not impressed. There has got to be someway to make Alexa thump. This just isn’t it. It should be. But it’s not. Debating on sending it back.

Set up was a little tricky. It doesn’t connect to Bluetooth. The sound quality is so so. I was hoping to shake the floor or at least fill my bar with some good sound. This helps but it’s not the answer

The sound is awesome. Perfect for my car with the stereo that doesn't work. However, Not even a a full day passed before one of the little latches that locks the unit down to make it compact broke off. So now it won't close.

So, I love how portable this player is and I love how long the batteries last, but I'm rating it lower, because the sound is very noticably garbled and the over all sound quality is pretty poor.  I love listening to music, so I like to have good quality players.  Granted, I didn't pay much for this player, so I didn't expect much, but I was still a little disappointed.  It seems hardy though and it will serve its purpose for a bathroom music player.  I also dance, and sometimes need a portable music player to practice routines or dancing in general in different little studios on my college campus, so this will work well for that too.  It can play quite loud.

Okay, For a pair of headphones that cost me less than 10 bucks, I didn't expect anything that great anyways. You get what you pay for, they're not bad, but they're not that great either. This is why: Sound quality is pretty weak, it's not just flat, but a bit tinny, on the trebles and the bass is pretty weak. The fit is unergonomic, it's just this generic round shape that runs a little big, so if you have small ears, the fit will be awkward. I've only had it for a week so, so far there are no problems with the durability. I like how the plug end is flexible, so I know int he future the wires aren't gonna fray and break. The cable is pretty flexible too, I don;t anticipate any crimping. The plastic housing on the wires and ear pieces themselves are alright for the price. I bought these cause I wanted some cheap disposable in ears for cycling. I can still hear what's going on outside while wearing these. They're a bit quieter than my regular in ear headphones. The bottom line is, if you want cheap earphones that work decently, these are fine. If you're used to better sound quality, these may jar you.
I also want to compare these to the earbuds that came with my zune player. The Zune earbuds are much better in sound quality and fit. After using it for two years, they broke so I bought these as a replacement. For around the same price, under 10 dollars, the zune ones are better.

They sound great, but I didn't like how they fit.  They felt loose around my head.  If I looked down or moved my head forward or back they would just fall off.  There was no tension in keeping them on my head.

Decent sound quality and comfortable.  Great plus in that they can work as external speaker in addition to headphones.  The external speaker sound quality average, not as good as when used as headphones, but very acceptable and volume is fine indoors or out.  These are not earthshakingly loud, but they are not superquiet as other reviewers have posted.  The convenience to cart them around and use that way but use less space is a plus.  Only drawback I had was an issue with the charge port.  After a while I had trouble getting a good connection with the USB--like it developed too much "give".  This made maintaining a good charging contact difficult.  Have not yet resolved this challenge.

My company bought these for me to help me telecommute. I really wanted to like them. On the pro side, the sound is quite good, it connects to two devices and thru a USB dongle. The range for both connection modes is quite good. It is reasonably comfortable to wear all day, and the noise cancellation is also pretty good. For the price, however, I find it to be only OK.
On the negative side: it charges with micro USB... this should absolutely be USB C; it has LEDs for the noise cancellation and open phone call, but not a simple on/off LED, so I end up turning it on and off and listening to the audio message to verify the state. I think the on/off button is overloaded as it is also for answering/ending phone calls. Finally, even with 3 inner and 3 outer earpiece selections, I can't really keep these in if I go for a hike. Wearing them in the office is OK, but as soon as I start moving, they just work their way loose - not great from a practicality standpoint.
I'm happy to use these since my company paid for them, but I'd be pissed if I dropped my own hard-earned cash on this set only to have it cause bush-league problems.

Put these in the rear doors to supplement a front component set. They don't get too loud and distort with any amount of bass. I can't expect much out of speakers this small, but they distort low bass at half the RMS these are rated for. Gave them 3 stars still because I expect it...4 inchers
There is no way this is an "original replacement."  The sound is muffled; lacks clarity.  The wire is made of cheap plastic.
Well made,beutifull wood, nice cables...but the sound is mediocre for me.The bass is week.My Skulcandy wich cost 20$ at BestBuy are way better regarding performance.

I purchased these several months ago and have found myself reaching for them less and less because of their inconsistent behavior. They'll pair with my phone (Samsung Galaxy S9) just fine with no issue, but the phone has to be in a particular spot for the connection to remain stable. I had it in my inner jacket pocket while snowblowing recently, and if I turned my head too far to the right, the earbuds dropped connection momentarily and skipped my song a bit. If I put them in my snowpants pocket near my waist, it would continually cut out so I couldn't enjoy a full song. I don't have a pacemaker or any other electronic device on my person or near me, and the snowblower is a mechanical gas-powered device without bluetooth, so there's no real reason why the earbuds would be acting oddly under these circumstances. I can't wear them while mowing the lawn on my (gas-powered) riding lawnmower because they cut out all the time. Can't wear them while cleaning in my basement unless I am always in direct line-of-sight to my phone at all times. I haven't even tried using them while exercising but I anticipate another frustrating experience. It's too bad because they fit well, the sound is good, and the charging case is super well-designed and convenient. But I can't rely on them to deliver good sound continuously. I'll probably only use these at my desk (if possible -- haven't even tried that yet) and use my Soundcore bluetooth earbuds for all my other activities. Disappointing experience!
These deliver high fidelity sound but they lack volume and fullness.  They have the classic sound of a great high-end speaker.  However, they require a cable to pair.

Pretty good bluetooth headphones. The battery life is definitely good, at the very least the headphones will get uncomfortable before they get to low battery, I was able to wear them for about 6 hours straight before they got too uncomfortable. Before that point they are super comfortable though, I found the medium silicone ear pieces fit best for me and while theres no active sound cancelation the fit does block out a decent amount of sound. The sound isnt as great as a lot of people implied in my opinion, but These are also my first pair of bluetooth earbuds and Im not sure what the standard is. these are VERY bulky and as some people mentioned most of the weight is pretty far from the ear, which is part of what makes them uncomfortable over long periods of time but also makes them super awkward to wear due to how far they stick out. I will probably be returning these and looking into a different set that is less bulky and more comfortable.

9/1/18 - Sadly, I've had to edit my review from 5 stars to 3. The headset on its own is, of course, beautiful and has held up well with 40 hours a week of constant use, but alas I lost the audio on the left side. I can jiggle the wire and voice and sounds will flit through, or I can try to toss my head about, swishing the sound from the right to left ear, but it does make it hard to work that way. I think perhaps this was made for a leisure and not a work environment. Too bad It should be built for both.

I know these were manufactured for music but I bought these because I transcribe for a living and needed a great set of headphones where voice quality has to reign supreme. The type of transcription I do is for recordings taken in some difficult encounters and environments with some pretty darned difficult people, and I have to catch every word and every utterance. I have a great little cache of headphones and earphones at my desk. Each gives different voice quality and oftentimes I have to switch them out depending on the circumstances but none were really good. My last headset that was very good lasted about a year, but it was the 2nd one in two years, so it looked as if it were going to be an annual purchase and the reviews on it were getting shaky. I was reluctant to purchase these because they were a little more than twice the price but my less expensive options just weren't cutting it. The first thing when this arrived, is these headphones arrived in a beautiful wooden box. I mean who does that? I thought these people are serious about quality. The next thing I loved is the braided cord. No more broken and worn cords. And the part that plugs into the ear cuffs are real plugs, no more frayed and broken wires at the junction. The headphones are beautiful and I've received many compliments. They seem to work well for sound deafening (not necessarily cancelling but I work in a loud office with many background conversations going on simultaneously). I have a fat head but they fit nice, and the length of the head band is adjustable for a customizable fit. Cord is a tad short for me, but is not a deal breaker. I like the length better than the 10' one on my old set which was always getting tangled and run over by my chair. I have no opinion on how good these are for music as I'm looking for voice clarity, but for my purpose I am more than pleased. Five stars.

I transcribe for a living.  The type of audios I transcribe have to be transcribed verbatim; every uh, um, uh-huh, gasp, sigh, cuss word, slang, malapropism, must be clearly heard and transcribed and this headset goes a long ways towards making that possible.  I've compared and contrasted different headsets and earbuds with the same audio on the same day with all the same equipment, save the headset, and this *clearly* comes in ahead of all others.  I find the over the head headset a better feature for me as it seems sturdier, better environmental noise control.  I have UPDATED this from a five star to a three star rating.  The headset does indeed produce voice clarity that is superior to others that I have paid twice as much for.  HOWEVER, the quality of the this piece of equipment seems to be lacking.  I was purchasing it every six months because the ear cups would break or the wiring would start to fray and on my last purchase add the voice "swished" from one side of the headset to the other, depending on how I held my head, LOL.  I wish the company would take more pride in the manufacture of their product as this truly could be a superior product.

TL;DR

The Kindle Fire HD 8 is a serviceable tablet if you don’t intend to use it for much outside of consuming media, primarily from Amazon’s in-house apps. If you’re interested, I recommend that you wait until they’re on sale before making the purchase.

Full Review:

I bought my Kindle Fire HD 8 primarily for listening to music. I use Amazon Music (Unlimited subscriber) and it has a headphone jack. Not wanting to deal with the ads from the lockscreen, I paid to have them removed. Over the past few weeks, I’ve been playing around with the device to see what it’s capable of when it comes to media consumption. Here’s what I’ve come up with! I did manage to sideload Google Play and several apps. I’ll reflect on those experiences, though any issues I had from this will not count against the device, as Google Play and the apps from it are not officially supported.

Interface and Build Quality
You are pretty much stuck with their stock interface. You can’t remove ANY of the Amazon apps from the homescreen. However, you can hide them away in a folder. This cleaned things up, nicely. Toward the top of the screen, you have a static bar that shows your last 2 apps, as well as some recommended apps. They do manage to sneak a sponsored app in there from time to time. Seeing that I paid to get rid of ads, this annoyed me (though it really doesn’t impact my use.) I actually like typing on this more than I do my Samsung Galaxy Tab S6 Lite or my Samsung S22 phone, which surprised me. One would think they’d make sure their own apps are working on their own devices at least as well as the apps work on their competitors devices.

The tablet itself feels kinda cheap, but not as cheap as I expected. The screen’s glass isn’t as smooth as my Samsung devices, but it’s quite functional. You can tell there’s not much power under the hood, as apps take a few seconds to load, and there’s sometimes interface lag when interacting with them. The onboard speakers suck, but I don’t use them. Headphones are the way to go… and since it has a headphone jack, I’m all set. The display is plenty for what I use it for.

Support
I’ve reached out to Amazon a few times to ask questions, or to get help. They’ve been incredibly responsive. The reps have always been courteous and informative. High marks here!

Audio and Video Quality
Music sounds great through my Audio Technica ATH-M50x headphones, especially HD and Ultra HD from Amazon Music. Strangely, the app does not have an EQ option (I can adjust the EQ on my Windows PC and on my other Android devices.) It supports my Fosi Audio DS1 with no problems. This improves the sound a bit (mostly making things a bit louder.) It did not power up my Fosi Audio K5 Pro, however. Unfortunately, the Kindle Fire HD 8 did not support my Bluetooth Audio Technica ATH-SR50BT’s, which was a disappointment. On the flipside, I was able to sideload 4Stream and the Andover Songbird app to get it to stream HD audio to my Denon D-M41, which was a pleasant surprise.

I took some time to watch some streaming video via Prime Video, Netflix and YouTube (sideloaded via Google Play.) Even though it’s not a true “HD” display, the screen is small enough to make it not matter so much. Lord of the Rings - Fellowship of the Rings probably benefited from this, as the movie didn’t age well in our HD world. The audio on it was also quite engaging through my headphones. Ash vs the Evil Dead on Netflix also streamed flawlessly, and looked great on the screen. YouTube videos play just fine as well, even though the app was sideloaded.

As an eReader
The Kindle Fire HD 8 works great as an eReader, as one would expect. Since I don’t plan to read much from it, I didn’t explore it much. Books loaded just fine, and you can interact with them as you’d expect (the Kindle is pretty robust for this, for those who’re interested.)

Non-media Consumption
I tried getting Discord to work on the Fire HD 8. While I was able to install it, the experience was pretty terrible. Browsing the internet with the Silk browser leaves some to be desired, and the mail/calendar apps are not something I’m interested in using. Again, I’m using this primarily for music, so I’m fine with this. However, if I needed to use it for anything productive, I’d be quite frustrated.

Google Play
Instructions on how to get Google Play installed are readily available online, and it’s easily doable within an hour’s time. I was able to install an EQ for my music, which works okay (I did have the app crash once.) The Gmail app loaded fairly well, as did Google Chrome. However, I can’t sync Chrome, as my email account was already used to activate the Kindle. There haven’t been any issues with YouTube. Dragon Quest 1 and 2 installed flawlessly and seem to work fine. However, Baldur’s Gate 1 & 2, along with other Beamdog games did not install at all (these aren’t officially supported, but folks claim it works. Not for me!) Again, none of these experiences with Google Play will count for or against my overall rating for this device. I’m simply stating them in case anyone else is interested in tinkering.

Ultimately, the Kindle Fire HD 8 is okay for the money (when on sale.) It works for my purposes, but I can tell it’d leave a lot to be desired if I wanted to use it for anything more. The fact that they still advertise apps on the home screen, even after you pay to remove ads is annoying (enough to knock my rating down a star.) I do suspect that the Kindle Fire devices are probably loss-leaders, and any ads they can cram in help generate income.

I don' t have a way to test the claims of an 1800-foot line-of-sight range for this driveway sensor, but it does work on a heavily wooded lot at 200-plus feet, right through the trees. It will be months before I'll know if the sensor's rechargeable battery actually works for nearly a year on a single charge, but for now, it's working.

The receiver accepts up to eight separate sensors. Each sensor has an individual sensitivity setting (you have to remove the back of the sensor to adjust it), and a group of switches to set the channel for each. Once paired to the receiver, a simple process, each sensor can be assigned its own alert tone.

And there are a lot of alert tones. Some of them I thought were quite funny.

The receiver can be powered via the included power supply, which also recharges the sensor, or it can run on three AA batteries (not included). With batteries installed, the detector system will still work during power outages.

Some things I think could be improved:

- In just the first couple of nights the receiver sounded three false alerts on three separate channels that have no sensor paired to them. I checked the manual to see if the unused channels could be switched off, but there was no option for that. So I checked to see if there was a silent alert tone to assign to unused channels, but their isn't. So alerts on unused channels can't be silenced or stopped.

- There's a volume control for the alert tone, but no brightness control for the display, and it's pretty bright.

- There's no memory feature for reviewing previous alerts and when they occurred.

- There's no slot on the back of the receiver for wall mounting.

- The sensor mounting plate holes are spaced almost 3-1/2 inches apart, which puts them right on the edges of a standard US 2 X 4, making it difficult to mount on one. I got around this by rotating the mounting plate to diagonal, cutting off the side corners, and using the top and bottom holes to mount the sensor.

- The back of the sensor must be removed to make some adjustments. (The included screwdriver works fine for that.) I noticed there was no weather proofing gasket when I removed it. That's not a problem for me since I mounted the sensor in a three-sided, roofed box I built some years ago for a driveway sensor. Without a gasket, though, I'm not too confident some water wouldn't get in there eventually if the sensor were mounted directly in the weather.

- When batteries are installed, the receiver apparently runs on the batteries even if the power supply is plugged in. The low battery alert started going off---in the middle of the night---after two weeks of running with the receiver plugged into the adapter. This probably means the batteries aren't really working as a backup power source but the primary one when batteries are installed. So it's an either/or situation---install batteries and run the receiver off of them, or remove the batteries to run on the external power supply.

Other than that, setup is easy. The included sensor is already paired with the receiver, and a quick start guide is printed directly on the back of the box. A more thorough manual, which includes instructions for adding receivers and setting alert tones, is included in the box. Mounting screws and a screwdriver are included too.

As I write this, the heading says this is a 2-in-1 laptop. That usually means the screen will fold into a tablet mode. It doesn't.
