Original review through Amazon Vine:

Okay, like some other reviewers, I had a frustrating experience getting this anti-glare screen protector installed properly on my Kindle Fire. When you buy this three-pack, figure they are giving you two hands-on lessons in how to install it! (Considering I paid over twice as much for just one Zagg screen protector for my Kindle 2, the price for this Fosmon product is still very reasonable.) I had read all the reviews and warnings before I began, and I still ruined my first two.

First, who lives in a "dust-free environment"? You have to be very careful. You should first shake any dust off the protector itself; after I'd failed to install the first two, I used one of the wipes that came with them to wipe down both sides of my last protector to clear it of all packing dust that it arrived with. Then clean your Fire screen, including the cracks around the sides of the screen. Clean it again. And again.

My first effort went very well until I went to remove the #2 (face) plastic. I didn't realize I had to very slowly pull up on the tab to get the top piece started coming away from the actual shield protector before pulling—so I pulled the whole thing off! One down, two to go. On my second effort, I didn't quite get the protector perfectly positioned so I had a very slight overlap on the right-hand side, resulting in a large unattached area. Unusable. The third time, I folded the #1 plastic down halfway, just so I could hold the protector flat above my Fire and not touch the actual protector (to avoid fingerprints), edged the upper right corner in perfectly straight, anchored it across the top, and then let the protector kind of glide itself onto the screen as I pulled off the remaining #1 plastic. I had some larger bubbled areas, but I did not try to use the little cardboard piece to squeegee them out; I used my thumbs to press outward toward the nearest edge. This gave me a near-perfect installation. I carefully removed the #2 plastic, slipped my Fire back into its [[ASIN:B005QBK5V2 rooCASE Dual-View Multi Angle (Black) 100% Genuine Leather Leather Folio Case Cover for Amazon Kindle Fire 7-Inch Android Tablet]], tucked one of the little squares of screen-cleaning cloth behind the Fire for later cleaning use if needed, and it was all good to go.

After regularly fighting the glare from my Kindle Fire, it took me a little while for my eyes to adjust to the difference with the anti-glare shield protector in place, but I LIKE it! Reading is now easier on my eyes, and my [[ASIN:B005EM6IAA GreatShield 2-in-1 Ballpoint Pen and Capacitive Touchscreen Stylus for Amazon Kindle Fire Tablet]] seems to be working with more precision than it was before. Despite the hassles, I do recommend this product and I'm glad I've got it.

We have found that a [[ASIN:B001I0B262 5 Empty Standard White Vinyl Replacement Disney VHS Boxes #VHBV30DW (Cases, Tapes, Clamshell, Clam Shell)]] works just right to hold 3.5" drives, although the interior space is taller than the drive.

But this extra area allows you to include a foam shock absorber above and below the drive. I recommend white polyethylene foam, not the gray polyurethane. Our AV department bought a BDP-300 so we could release our HD video content on Blu-ray. We bought the expensive Blu-ray burner for the computer, we bought the expensive authoring software, we bought a bunch of expensive BD-R and BD-RW recordable disks and we bought the expensive Sony BDP-300 player, with an eye toward buying a bunch more for our conference rooms if the system worked. It didn't.

We found that the BDP-300 will not play back BD-R or BD-RW discs. Though it might have been possible to be upgraded via a firmware update (like its REALLY expensive big brother can be firmware upgraded) it most likely never will. Thanks a lot, Sony. Way to make an integrated system. No wonder Blu-ray has been so slow to catch on. Thus we as a very large company cannot commit to Blu-ray because we can't play the recorded Blu-ray disks back on even a $400 player. Sigh.

Secondly, if you connect to a digital display that only has DVI-in via an HDMI/DVI adapter or an HDMI/DVI cable adapter, the player doesn't work. I suspect the problem is connected to copy protection schemes built into the multiple HDMI standards.

So, if you have an older HD display that only has DVI-in, forget this "reasonably priced" Blu-ray player. You'll most likely need to use the analog YRB (component) outputs, which is an inferior signal to the digital HDMI output. I did a component/HDMI comparison for my wife and she definitely picked the HDMI as the superior output picture.

There is a workaround that allows the HDMI/DVI to work, but it's a pain: First, connect both the HDMI and component cables to their respective inputs on the display. Now, before powering the player on, manually disconnect the HDMI cable from the back of the player while leaving the component cables connected to the display. Then power up the player and switch the display to the analog "component" input. You can now see the menus and the Blu-ray disk will be able to be played. After you get the movie running, manually plug the HDMI/DVI cable into the back of the player and switch the display to the digital DVI input. The Blu-ray disk now works and allows the menus and other overlaid controls to function normally. As different HDMI copy protection schemes get adopted this trick might fail.

If you have HDMI-in on your display, the player might work, but no guarantees. Bear in mind that the HDMI standard is constantly changing. I think they're up to at least HDMI 1.3 so far, and counting. And a totally new plug protocol is on its way for computer monitors, too, called DisplayPort, which might make it to TV sets, but who knows?

After this little problem was overcome, I finally got to see the picture. It was very nice, especially after I got to see it via my HDMI-DVI workaround. Definitely better than the analog component feed.

The overlaid menus allow you to access the menu anytime, without leaving the movie. Pretty cool. The menus are also more animated and better integrated.

Audio quality is fabulous. Both Dolby and DTS sound great because with all the storage capacity on the disk, the signals don't have to be compressed as much as they are for a standard DVD.

If you want the very, very best audio, though, you can select "uncompressed" and route the RCA audio outputs directly into your amp's dedicated preamp inputs. This takes the Dolby and DTS compression systems out of the picture altogether. So you are hearing multiple uncompressed audio tracks sent directly to your amp.

The worst part of the Blu-ray player is the time it takes to "boot" up. It's really a dedicated computer running an operating system. Java, at least, and maybe more. Thus it takes a full two minutes to fire up. You press the power button and nothing happens. After about ten seconds, you get a display that says "power on." After about 90 seconds, the machine is finally ready to play your disk. Give it a lot of time to fire up, especially the very first time you plug it in. After the initial plug-in/power-on sequence, the manual says it will be subsequently faster. But not by much. And the system can "crash," requiring you to turn it off and reboot. It happened several times to me as I moved too quickly between menu selections.

Overall, this player can put out a great picture, eventually, and after learning a bunch of quirks. I don't think it's ready for prime time, though. For the price it should be much better: faster boot up and with the ability to play back recorded Blu-ray disks.

Buy the BDP-300 knowing you will be replacing it for some reason in a year or two.

I rented Universal's Hellboy II on Blu-ray tonight.

It crashed the player. Think "Blue Screen of Death" but without the blue screen and a longer boot sequence. I repeated the process six times.

I was about to flame this inop player when here on Amazon it was suggested to update to Firmware 4.20.

I went to Sony's site and found even newer 4.30 firmware. You download the exe and click on it to uncompress it. This creates an ISO disk image. You burn this to a new CD as an image (very important--an IMAGE, not a data disk.) Turn on the player and stick the CD in. It took 13 minutes for the update to install. When it's done it says "DL OK" on the player.

Player works like it's supposed to. It will play BD-R, too. In fact, it can even play a weird hybrid I can make with Sony Vegas editing software where I can burn a Blu-ray disk image to a standard DVD and play it as a
Blu-ray.

TL;DR: It’s an awesome keyboard for the most part, and my score will go up pending receipt of a non defective unit.

I entered the arena of mechanical keyboards in 2014 with what was at the time the cheapest genuine Cherry MX blue keyboard I could find on Amazon. It has served me well these past few years, but the ABS keycaps have shined up dramatically, and the edges of the keys aren’t rounded or beveled in any way, making prolonged typing somewhat uncomfortable. Since I bought the keyboard specifically as an entry-level item to upgrade down the road, I decided to go searching for a better alternative. Cherry and its sundry clones seem to dominate the mechanical keyboard market. However, having tested most of their switches with and without dampeners, I decided to look elsewhere. After hearing the sound of the glorious keyboards of old from vintage tech shows like The Computer Chronicles, I knew I had to experience that sweet symphony for myself, and this keyboard certainly offers an authentic sound.

It’s a very loud keyboard, so *please* don’t get this if you live in a dorm with a roommate. It’s also difficult to listen to music while typing continuously, but I love the thunderous THUNK THUNK that emanates from the keys as I type.

The layout is a typical 104 key layout, with one perplexing deviation: the alt and start keys on the right side of the space bar are swapped. I have no idea why they chose to do this, and I expect it will infuriate Europeans who need all those extra accent marks accessible via the right alt key. I too was skeptical especially since I regularly switch between a PC and a Mac, which uses the start key as the much more frequently used command key. I found out, however, that the new key locations more closely resemble those of Apple’s own keyboards, with the command, then option, then control key to the right of the spacebar. The only hiccup is the nonsymmetrical left modifier keys and the useless-on-Mac menu key.

The keys themselves feel wonderful. The edges are slightly rounded, unlike my Cherry MX blue board. The tops are also textured for extra grip, and they’re made of PBT plastic that won’t get slippery. The nubs on the F, J and numpad 5 keys aren’t as prominent as on some boards but still obvious enough to be noticed quickly while touch typing. There’s a tactile bump toward the bottom of the stroke before the key bottoms out, which adds some haptic confirmation to go along with the euphonic sound of the keys. These buckling spring switches are a little tougher to actuate than Cherry MX blues, which may be a concern for gamers, but this board isn’t designed with gaming in mind, and I don’t play much anymore, so it’s not an issue for me. The upside is that I can rest my hands on the home row without accidentally pressing any keys.

Unfortunately, the spring under the scroll lock key—which I frequently use to switch between machines on a KVM—was loose, and caused a distracting rubbing sensation when pressed. This is my reason for returning it. Speaking of defects, many people have complained about poor quality molding on the chassis and off center key labels. The case isn’t exactly rock solid. While heavy enough, it creaks loudly when picked up and handled, and the edges of the case surrounding the keys felt uneven. I believe Unicomp inherited all of the old equipment IBM used to manufacture the Model M, so that potentially makes those machines over three decades old. Having said that, I’m not concerned with a creaky chassis as long as it’s strong enough to withstand typical keyboard abuse. Case blemishes aren’t a concern for me as long as the typing experience isn’t hampered. Assuming my loose spring isn’t a common issue, I’ll happily give the product a higher rating.

The Onkyo HT-S5100 Home Entertainment System sounded quite good when listening to the radio, and I really loved the self-calibration feature to set the speaker phase/power-level based upon our optimum seating position.

When the receiver is played at low to mid volume ranges, the system was impressive, but there was distoration at higher levels when the speakers were driven beyond their capabilities.

As far as a Stereo Receiver goes, I'd give it high marks, but as far as a Home Entertainment system goes... in my opinion, I'd purchase something else.

I found after many frustrating hours of trying to get the receiver to work with my other HDMI components, that all of my attempts were in vain.

I'd essentially purchased the system on the recommedation of Consumer Reports (They crowed about the HT-S5100 having the best sound of any system they'd ever tested, and it was one of the only ones offering 7.1 versus 5.1 stereo surround).

I eventually re-read the Onkyo Owners Manual and found a small blurb regarding the audio of the system not working with HDMI...

I freely admit I'd blown-off the fact that analog/digital connectors were shown on the Quick Hook-Up illustrations (thinking these were alternative connections for those unlucky soul's who didn't have HDMI), when I finally resorted to contacting Onkyo for assistance/confirmation.

They confirmed my worst-fear, their HDMI's were (Pass-Though). When asked why they even bothered to put HDMI connectors on the system, the reply was (some consumers desired them).

Personally, I feel if a system has HDMI connectors present, that is implies they're fully compliant, otherwise their presence is misleading.

What this meant was all of my new toy's (50" Plasma, Blu-ray player, and Xbox 360) could only pass on video (not the higher quality audio signals through the HDMI connectors), and that I'd have to accept a lower quality audio output due to the use of standard audio connectors.

Perhaps I'd missed this in CR's review (or it wasn't stated), as I had to purchase additional digital cabling so that I could even hear the audio content of the devices hooked into the Onkyo (added expense/wiring woe's).

If I had to do it all over again, I'd purchase the HT-S5100 as a Stereo Receiver, but I wouldn't recommend it as the hub for a Home Entertainment System to interconnect your HDMI devices.

Another pearl-of-wisdom, don't rely strictly upon the written advice of a third-party, go out and listen/view the equipment yourself, as that's what I'm wishing I'd have done!

UPDATE June 2018. I spent sometime reading various forums and such and it made no sense why Netflix wouldn't work. How it works now I'm not sure but here is what I did. If you have your TV directly connected to the soundbar - under settings for sound it will default to PCM if connected via optical cable (what it's supposed to do). I decided to hit 'reset sound settings' (I have a Samsung Smartv) and it reset it to dolby digital. Netflix started working and my VCR continued to work as well. Netflix had told me they don't support all soundbars, well this one works.

HP gave a message saying that this printer does not support Chromebook. I could not connect wirelessly to my work laptop, only with USB cables. But my personal computer linked wirelessly. The installation is simple, but took an awful lot of time to download HP programs to get the printer going. This printer also supports mobile printing with iPhone, but I did not try that feature. Another feature that I didn’t have in my previous printer is the use of SD card to print quality pictures. The machine has a SD card port and you can insert the card and print effortlessly. The touch screen interface is easy to operate the printer, but first you need to get familiar with it

Other cons are that it does not have built-in fax capability, and does not have Ethernet network interfaces, which may be an additional feature some users may be looking. Such a feature is an ideal choice for printer sharing with your family or the home office or for business. It is a little heavy and an average size printer. I did not sign up for the "HP Instant Ink" program. You have the choice not to sign up if you don’t want it. But if you are planning on this option, make sure that if you sign up and then cancel your subscription anytime, the printer will not get disabled. I have rated this product three stars for overall satisfaction.

Great Addition to Home Security System

First I should say there is no 100% perfect home security system. That is why I have a home security “solution” that incorporates several different, but tied together systems. I have a full Lorex Camera System, Smart Things Hub and a wired alarm system. But even with all that there was something missing. If I wasn’t home, all of the other items were only good after the fact. Meaning I could see who was at my door, or in my house after I got back home. Sure I could set alerts on those other devices, but when your phone chirps 10 alerts per hour, it just becomes white noise. These other systems had so many false positives I ultimately turned them off.

Pros: But the Ring Bell filled several voids in these other systems. One, the false positives are almost nonexistent due to the ability to mask the alert area of the camera. My existing security system may alert me, but then I had to log into the camera system to see what was going on. The time it takes to do that could make a real difference. The ability to answer and interact with someone who rings your bell from your couch or from at work is invaluable! The person ringing the bell has no idea where you are answering from. But the best part is being able to ignore solicitors and screen people before you answer. It’s as easy as answering a phone call and the live image is instantaneous. The fact that it integrates with my SmartThings hub is just icing on the cake.

I was able to install the Ring Bell Pro in about 15 minutes following the simple instructions. It is extremely well thought out. The video quality of the Ring Pro is excellent! It does not have a very wide angle and there is a slight fisheye distortion, but it should be more than sufficient for most applications. The mobile app is also very intuitive. As I mentioned, when you get an alert, you can immediately see who is at the door and you can choose to answer and speak, or just watch.

Cons: I was confused by the wall plate not having the mounting holes line up with the existing wall plate holes. This required drilling holes above and below the existing holes to mount the plate. I could see no reason for this.

The unit can easily be ripped off the wall with one hand. Because the main unit mounts onto a plastic wall cover, it would take about 2 seconds to remove and disable the unit. But at least you will get an alert and when you went to log in you would know something was wrong. However, the Ring Pro has a unique purchase protection that sates “If your Ring™ Video Doorbell is stolen at any time after your purchase, Bot Home Automation, Inc. will replace your Ring™ Video Doorbell at no charge to you”. That’s pretty impressive!

If you want to keep your Ring History, you have to sign up for their paid service. Otherwise you only see live views. Prices vary by plan, but they do offer one free month for new customers.

Overall: There is no perfect security system. Each one has its plusses and minuses. But the Ring Pro should be part of every home security solution. Also, if I had to choose only one component for a complete home security solution, this would be high up on my list.

First impression - not as impressed as some

Disclaimer: Everyone's ear is different, and tips make a big difference. Because of my ears, I have to use big tips and a shallow fit. Those who can get a deeper fit my hear something completely different. Also, I'm being really picky to help others decide if this is the right phones for them.

I wanted to try these on my computer because that is where all my music is stored that I've used for decades to audition audio gear. So this will be based on Pandora on my phone at 192kb. This is fine because this is how I will be listening to them.

I could not get a comfortable fit with the included tips. The largest tips were not large enough for my ears. So I dug through my collection and found a good fit. Pairing went fine.

They feel a little heavy to me but maybe that is the price of Bluetooth and the magnets? This is my first pair of Bluetooth in-ears. Build quality seem good for the price (I got them on sale) and I'd say the build quality is about average for their normal selling price. While they look like they have good strain relief it's actually very stiff plastic creating a 'hard point' where the wires come out. I like the little magnet for when I want to take them out but not take them off. It's one of the reasons I got these. If you run, I'd worry a little bit about the weight they add.

The sound. I like tight bass, well controlled, no extra bloom/extension But these are bass shy to my ears. For a workout, I like a fun sound and these ain't that. They are a bit bright and brassy at times I noticed the most on 70s classic rock. They lack a richness in the mids that I noticed most with male vocals. Turning them up did not improve they sound, as they got louder they became painful bright/brassy and bass did not improve. They went loud enough to distort the drivers so volume should not be an issue for anyone.

They do a pretty good job of revealing detail and room acoustics are rendered decently and there is some space around the instruments but not much of a soundstage.

While not sterile they lack some musicality that I'd prefer. Did I mention that male voice sound thin. They lack a fullness and resonance for the male voice. I notice this lack of 'something' on drums as well which are buried in the mix. It seems like the SQ is geared to making them sound impressive and accurate and while they succeed in that to some extent it's at the expense of other parts of the sound. I can see getting some fatigue after a while if you listen for more than an hour or so. Sibilance is not an issue. You hear the sibilance on some songs because it's there but it's not going to wear you out.

I can see why some people would like these especially if you are coming from lower quality mushy sounding earphones. If you are used to better earphones and looking for some less expensive earphones for working out you may like these if you like a 'clear' sound but the word that keeps coming to mind as I listen to them more and more is 'thin'. Not thin/thin but a lack of richness and resonance. If you want some bass especially some extension/bloom (again wearing/tips can make a difference) and a bit of 'drive' I'd consider a different set.

Update: Changing tips really improved these phones. The tri flange tips really hit the sweet spot in my ear. I can 'tune' the bass now by how far I shove them in my ears.

Still not for critical listening but a very easy to listen to headphone. Cymbals sound better now. Bass is more balanced with good extension/bloom for < $100 IEM's. They are forgiving of poor source material and/or using with portable electronics. They strike a good middle ground between musical and detailed, though it's somewhat a case of not doing either one particularly well but that's getting nit picky.

The phones are bit bulky and heavy and the cord bounces while running. I also find I tend to futz with them a lot while wearing them. Adjusting the fit, playing with the cables, etc. But all and all they fit well and stay put for most activities. The thicker/flat cord bothers me at times. It always feels like it's going to come off my ears but in reality it doesn't. I think with more wearing they will drape nicer over the ear.

But to my ear they still lack 'something'. If I had to do it over I'd probably try the NuForce 700's or Thinksound ts02/MS01.

Upping my rating to 4 stars for being perfectly good, if some what uninspiring phones.

Original review:
Too thumpy and not in a good way. It's all, ok mostly boom with no 'good' thud. (I'm guesing there are even boomier headphones I out there.

I got them an hour a go and I already know they are going back.

And I like bass and I like warm and forgiving over 'accurate' and 'lively'.

I like the $22 Vsonic GR99 better than these. Though to be fair these are 'technically' and are better in the treble than both of them but it's not enough to offset the excessive bass for me and again I like bass. If you want to hear not just the bass drum but also the beater side of the bass drum these are not the phones for you. If you like the sound of all the drums, including the rack toms, these are not for you.

If you want to hear bass instruments that sound like they do in real life, these are not for you.

They are so V-shaped they sound like they have hole in the frequency response. If you know what that means and feel like you hear that kind of things these are not the phones for you, if like me you are being swayed by the number of good reviews.

If you think 'beats' sound good you might like these. If you 'bump' in the car and or like hip hop/rap than you might like these. If you are coming from crap phones you might like these because they probably have better highs and more bass extension (rumble I see people call it and rumble it is, and not in a good bass extension way). If your frame of reference for drum sounds is EDM you may very well like these.

I'll be returning these and sticking with the GR99 until I can find something better. I don't think these are worth the $60 they cost based on owning Vsonic VC02 and Vsonic VSD1's (which I really liked but just couldn't get a good fit).

While the highs have fairly nice extension and no sibilance or tizzinesss don't expect to hear the metal of the cymbals, mostly you get the sound of the tip of the drum stick on the cymbals. But that is pretty common until you get to better phones/speakers. While not expensive the Vsonic VC02 was very good at 'cymbal' sounds.

These are v-shapped to the point of sounding like they have hole in the frequency response. If you know what that means and think you can hear such a thing, these phone are definitely not for you, in case like me you are being swayed by the number of good reviews.

Do they sound 'terrible' no, unless you have heard better. Do not get these if you are looking for good phones with a little more bass than what you have now I like I was trying to do over the Vsonic VC02. I like the VC02 but wanted something with more bass to use while working out. I also like my Vsonic VSD1's but I put them through the wash and never could get a very good fit, so I'm not replacing them.

I was worried about these and the bass sound but wanted to try them since I almost always wear phones with the cord over my ears. and in that aspect they are pretty comfortable and were easy to fit and get a good seal with the stock size tips. They feel a little big to me but I'm coming from Vsonic VC02 which are very small.

All music was 320k MP3 or FLAC using the DAC headphone amp in the Topping VX1 amp using foobar 2000.

If accurate reproduction of bass sounds, including drum sounds is important to you look else where.

I like BASS. The GR99 are bass heavy as are the Skull Titans. The Vsonic VSD1 are not shy of bass compared to other phones, but the bass sounds more natural on those even though they are bass heavy in comparison to accurate/neutral phones.

I'm being generous giving them 3 stars but 2 stars felt too low since so many people like them and mine is just one opinion. One persons and one person's boomy is another person's good bass extension.

LIke so many others, loved the sound but lost one of the drivers. Plenty of people have described the sound accurately. They are very comfortable to wear and one of the few earphones I can wear to go to sleep (sleeping on my back). They are very light and very easy to get a good seal. I have one ear canal that is a little funky but with the ability to get these in deep I can get it feeling 'right' in that hard to fit ear. But you don't have to shove them in all the way to your skull to get sound.

Some might say they are bass shy, everybody has their own idea of what is the right amount of bass. I can sort of agree in that I have phones with (a little more) bass and especially when working out they are more fun to listen to. But these VC02 play the bass that is there, no more, no less.

The VSD1 are a warmer sound, you might say more musical. Think tube amp vs solid state. Don't take that to mean the VC02 are too analytical, they aren't. Where they really shine is reproducing the drums in music. It's a more accurate reproduction of the drums, especially the kick drum and floor toms. They are more defined and just sound more like drums in real life.

Ultimately I would choose the VC02 over the VSD1 because I'd rather EQ in a little bass, rather than try to clean up a little too much bass. Not that the VSD1 have too much. Since I'm older and use to work for live bands I've lost some of my abiity to hear treble so the VC02 work better for me. But models are very good at music reproduction for the amount they cost.

Note: I started with the GR99 phones the cheaper brother to the above vsonics. After listening to the above two pairs I thought I'd hate the GR99. But I don't. What they do, they do well with out any horrible sound issues. For $20 for the GR99 you can't go wrong I still use them places where I wouldn't want to risk losing the more expensive phones. Hiking is a good example.

===============================================

Sound: 4 stars (they are only $50)
Value: 5 stars
Overall I have to give them 3 stas because of how easy it is to lose one of the drivers. If you get them do something to hold the cables on better.

I've always hated this style of CMP. But then, I actually got to try two different brands that I actually liked - one was a cleaner and slightly smaller version with perhaps a different style of plastic, while the other was actually metal.

What I learned to appreciate about both of those - and this one - is the holes that allow you to also pass through to the back of the rack. Although I still don't like to see that in enterprise solutions, I now realize it is mostly unavoidable as a home user with some consumer equipment.

But those first two were pretty easy to use and I didn't get frustrated with the covers or the lids (whereas, I had always disliked this style because they are always abused in an enterprise setting and they end up broken and/or the covers lost.

Anyway, so I don't hate this style so much anymore, but I don't like these as much as some. They are very large and squared, so that might provide some extra volume, but it also tends to shadow and hide the equipment so it's harder to get in to move cables around. But the covers are difficult to remove and can be quite frustrating - I even have concern that I'll band my hands on something or smash a cable by the time I can get them off. Then the fingers are very stiff and seem more likely to break than some other types - also more likely to crush cables.

Anyway, they're really not bad, it's just that I learned what I like better in recent months.

I hate to give this a 3 since that is often perceived as negative, but since I can't get it working perfectly (and it's always hard to know if it's just my setup or the AP itself), I can't give it a great review. I must say that I have two older Netgear APs that work perfectly and are a pleasure to use.

Here are some specifics, so hopefully this is helpful:

1) Uses PoE++. Will work with PoE+, but run at reduced throughput. This is understandable, but just beware (because I know I don't have PoE++ yet, and using the AC adapter really does limit where you can or want to install this). I wish it could just use both ports as PoE ports to get the power it needs that way.

2) Unit is HUGE! Picture looks just like the other ones I have, but it's quite big in real life. Again, just be aware, because this may affect where you install it. On the other hand, it's

3) Has a 2.5 Gb port (which I can't use yet) or you can port bind two 1 Gb ports. Port binding does not use LACP from what I can tell, so you have to set it up as static. Seems like they should offer more details on the web GUI, because it just seems like you can't even tell if it's working except through your switch web GUI. Also...

4) That 2.5Gb port screws up all the LEDs, because one of them ends up amber instead of green or blue if you're using 1Gb, so it looks like you have issues when you don't. I don't know why, but that throws me off, especially if this is visible to anyone who isn't the admin.

5) All that I can deal with easily, but my problem is, it just keeps saying the Internet is disconnected on the web sign in page. Even when that is the case, most of my devices seem to work just fine, but one computer always has issues randomly. I had reset everything to factory default and still had intermittent issues. So even though I realize that everyone has a different setup with different equipment on their network, I don't think I should be having these issues, as mostly, APs should be plug-n-play. I'm hoping for a magic cure via FW update or something like that.

If it ever starts working perfectly and consistently, I'll let you know. I certainly hope it will soon, because the newness premium is wearing off quickly.

BLUF: I've long ago installed a 2-(Clearstream) antenna setup in the 8'+ mark of my attic. I currently get about 30 channels with those (including simulcast), but I could only get the local PBS (4 simulcast channels) with this in the same configuration. Plenty of details below, if you're interested:

The construction and design of this is rather good (except that I don't know that it actually works that well, or at least not to my expectations). It's an engineering marvel in itself that all this stuff could fit into the small box it came in. They give you plenty of extras including a long and short Cat6 cable (although I prefer thicker - even if it is just cladding, you can expect thicker cables are less likely CCA - cables with compression connectors and without sharp bends for the best installation possible). And you get a good rod for mounting, all for a fairly inexpensive price tag.

The two Clearstream antennae setup I have costs probably more than $200 by the time I bought the amp separately. One is UHF and one is VHF. Those claim 70+ mile range when used outside, while this one claims 150 mile range, but has less gain. I actually thought it might work better anyway, just because my other setup has not worked as well lately, and I assume it is because they've been paring down the frequency range for television and I thought maybe antenna design has changed, and maybe it became cheaper to get a better signal. Plus, I saw one of these before under a different brand name, so I thought this new, smaller design may be a thing.

Anyway, I don't understand the 150-mile claims. The others exaggerate, but not too awful much. I know I don't have it outside, but I should get a comparable signal for a comparable setup.

Recommend tvfooldotcom to research. Highly recommend cutting the cord. This is better than nothing, but recommend getting the best equipment you can find and have room for. Price apparently matters, at least to some degree.

Oh...this one does move if you use the remote, which is an interesting concept, but may only work well if you have a TV that can "add channels" rather than one where you have to scan from scratch every time (My two Sony TVs allow you to add channels, and I always get better reception with them than my two Samsung TVs that do not allow you to add channels). If you can't add channels and you want to move the antenna from one direction to the other, you'll likely have to rescan with each move.

I did try hooking this straight up to one TV, not going through a grounding block or splitter, just in case that's what it would take to work (because the gain is not very high), but no dice. It does have two outputs, so you can avoid a splitter if you only have two TVs.

The remote for moving the antenna is IR, so if your amp is not near your TV, you'll either have to run to the basement to adjust or have some kind of IR repeater setup.

I don't like the size or look of the amp power supply or the power injector box.

This has slightly wider - but very similar - frequency ranges than my legacy antennae, so I don't think things have changed so much with digital OTA TV.

I've always been happy with the setup I have after putting in some serious research. It cost more than this, but not enough to think twice about considering I'll never pay for TV again. However, I'm still not sure why I've had a degraded signal recently. Regardless, this newer antenna style did not fix the problem.

There are both positives and negatives about this product, my perspective being that I am using it to replace an old-sko0l red LED alarm buzzer with staticy radio.

+ Looks sleeker (one would hope, as the old had a plastic wood finish), smaller footprint, and slightly raised clock makes it easier to see.

+ I love the USB port, so I can get rid of two power cords and replace it with one.

+ Shows the weather as according to Accuweather, which is at least a rough estimate of what it's like outside.

+ Better sound if you want to set it to stream music.

+ Shows the date.

+ 2 programmable buttons allow you to control "smart" devices. This could be really handy if you have a light for the room plugged into a receptacle across the room. You could also cut your overhead light cord and put in a socket for control from your bed if you're into that sort of thing. I just have a lamp beside the bed, so I really don't care, but this is something I can actually see being useful.

+ Can use it as a Bluetooth speaker. Would be better if you could integrate it with other home WiFi speakers, even though I'm more into big, hardwired speakers for serious listening from a whole-house audio system

Things that are both positive and negative, so I guess I have to call them neutral:

= microphone has a button to turn it off. A switch would be more believable, and then it wouldn't have a red light showing on the top all the time. I have no doubts the CIA can still turn it on, but I like to think the manufacturer won't listen in. I'm sure they could have put a back door in, too, but I would hope they would be sued severely if that is ever discovered. The red light is good when talking on the phone to show the phone is muted but otherwise the light shouldn't be on all the time...

= Buttons on the top are always lit up, which I consider to be a negative. Should be able to control them separately. Front display has 6 dim levels and off, and the lowest level is good for sleeping even with the thing pointed at you (at least in my opinion), but then it's really not bright enough during the day (at least if it's a bright day). I know it's petty, but I'm really not into doing anything more than I already do to get ready for bed, and that includes pressing a button 5 or 6 times to get it back to the way I wanted it. Should work on a light sensor or just be able to program it for day and evening. I mention this stuff because I'm sure it can be added via firmware (not the sensor part, obviously). Overall, not as bright as the old red LED thing, but somehow less see-able.

= You can do random light shows with the colored LEDs at the bottom. I suppose setting it to come on before your alarm is useful, but just playing with them is not.

Negatives:

- I just hate the Internet sometimes, and this reminds me why. (I'm a fairly young Systems Engineer, FYI, so it's not that I'm some geezer that can't use technology). I just hate that I need an app to control this thing. It's an alarm clock, so shouldn't I be able to do the basics without my phone? Is this just so they can get on my phone and steal my data/identity/whatever? I got news for you guys - I set this kind of crap up with a burner phone that is linked to fake Email, fake everything, location and everything else turned off. Let me at least set the bloody time without hooking up to the Internet! What happens when Comcast freezes and my WiFi temporarily doesn't have Internet connection?

To use Spotify with this (which I don't use and never will since I just have all the music I could ever want on a local server), you have to buy the Premium version. I'm sure that was absolutely necessary. Is anything not contrived multi-layered big business anymore?

Just to DL the app, Google and my burner phone both try to trick me into thinking I have to put credit card details in to get it. Sometimes I'm just ready to forego the digital age and find an old ticking clock that loses 5 minutes every day to run my life by. I am so sick and tired of adds, apps that want to control and steal your life, and companies that can't think further than next quarter...

- No battery backup. Should be built in. Even my '70s POS could be backed up via 9v battery. It saves some settings, but turns back to archaic Fahrenheit on me when power is lost...

- ...worse...when power comes back on, it screams at you. Power in my area is good, but on occasion goes out for a few seconds multiple times in a night. That may be the end of this thing (OK, I just lowered my star rating to 3, because the truth is, that probably will be the end of this thing's reign in my bedroom).

- No radio. No internal memory for music. You're at the mercy of streaming accounts and everything working properly on your network.

- Going along with the first negative point, you can't even set an alarm with this thing if you don't sign in with an Amazon account and do the Alexa thing. More ways to get grips on you. More ways to complicate a simple alarm clock.

Do I really hate simple and easy so much? I almost gave this four stars due to the fact that it looks pretty and adds some functionality, but what's wrong with a highly visible dump clock beside the bed? That's all I'm using this for, when it all comes down to it. Well, my feelings may change for the better when they inevitably fix some of the simple things on this that they can do by firmware. I will let you know if my feelings change significantly.

Although there are a lot of positive points to be said about this product, a major flaw with it is that - even on low volumes and on songs without much bass - you can hear a bit of distortion, like crackly static, that sounds like a speaker that you're either working too hard or is at the end of its life. This becomes worse as the battery gets low. I consider this issue to be "understandable and sort of acceptable" considering the whole system has to run on battery power and most people aren't expecting high power out of such a setup. They might just have a high-pass crossover set too high to conserve power, and too much is cut off, resulting in messy sound.

When you charge your phone with the speaker's battery (which in itself is sort of a nice, if cannibalistic, feature, one that other devices claim even though it is inherent to the device; with this, the USB-A port was added specifically for this purpose), it lowers the volume to level 8 (there is nothing to tell you what level you're at) to keep from draining the battery quickly. Even at this medium level and below, this problem can be recognized.

The bike mounts are 4" apart, center to center, so make sure you have room on your bike handlebars if that is your purpose for ordering. Included bike mounts are good. It also comes with a neoprene case, a USB cable, and an audio cable, both red. With all these extras trying to give the appearance of premium, it doesn't actually come with a charger, not that this will be an issue for most people (you probably already have more than you know what to do with).

There should be keyhole slots built into the bike mounts so it could also be hung on the wall and removed easily, making it more versatile.

The unit pairs easily and immediately with my Blackberry every time, and it can control the tracks through the BT connection as well. It looks well made and has a good feel to it. It looks like it could almost be waterproof, although I noticed no mention or claim of that feature (so I'm sure it's not).

The sound overall isn't bad for a low voltage battery operated speaker, as long as you're not sitting down and listening too closely. I guess for the purposes of making noise as you ride around the neighborhood, it'll do just fine.
The Volume on this is not loud at all. IT is nice and convenient to keep on your belt but I wish it had more volume.

When you turn them on they speak in Chinese and i do not believe there is a way to change that. If so I can not understand the language to change it. But that being said it was easy to just listen and set the right channel to be able use them. They have great range and the sound quality is great.

These earbuds actually felt quite comfortable. After the initial pairing process, I noticed that the sound was cutting in and out. However, I thought perhaps it was just an initial problem that would go away. I wore these today for about 20 minutes, and found that the cutting in/out happened regularly. It would stop and work fine for a while, and then it would cut in/out again for a little while and then work again for a while. Although the earbuds were comfortable, the cutting in/out were not comfortable for me, so I ended up returning these.

The sound quality is pretty poor - on my Samsung Note, I have to go to max volume to be able to hear anything clearly (when experimenting with both buds, it seems to be slightly better).  The touch controls are very finicky and not very intuitive.  It does block noise well, but that doesnt translate to better audio quality for listening to music (primary use was for walking/jogging).  They fit fine and didnt have any issues when doing yard work or jogging.  The unit seems to keep the charge as advertised.  But the biggest issue is of course is the sound volume and quality - even at this pricepoint - this is not a good value.  For a backup or travel purposes where you wont beat yourself up if you misplace or lose , there are better options available.

No one positions a sub-30$ player in same performance category as an iPod! Having said that for this pricepoint, the mp3 player provides a very good audio output with sub-par storage size and software options. Even at this price, one could locate models that provide other features such as FM radio for example - RCA's 6204 model [[ASIN:B004ZEZGHO RCA M6204 4 GB Video MP3 Player with 2-Inch Color Display]].  The cable-less USB connector can be challenging for some laptop users depending on where your USB ports are - I couldn't find one that will enable me to see the player's screen handily.  For this price, this is an OK investment for a additional mp3 player for short trips or for jogging etc. - the newer model is a better investment than this one.

These earbuds are not especially impressive. I would have given them 3.5 stars if I could have. The noise cancelation is pretty decent. The earbuds last the five hours they say they do. The earbuds don't get very loud, which would perhaps be good for a child or teenager to protect their hearing. For an adult, though, it can be a bit frustrating in situations where you really want to rock out. The charging case is adequate. In all, it covers all its claims, but there just isn't anything impressive about the sound quality and shorter battery life.

I bought this because my new camera has a 58mm lens and I didn't have a 58mm polarizing filter yet, and I feel that a polarizing filter is essential. I haven't used this to take many pictures yet other than to test it out when it arrived. The few shots I took turned out okay except for some minor vignetting on shots at 18mm. This is expected because the metal ring is a bit on the thick side. It does the job of a polarizing filter; cuts glare, darkens the sky, removes reflections, so from that perspective it is adequate. However, the aluminum ring feels rough-cut and it threads onto my lens with a slight scraping sound. If you tighten it a bit too hard it is almost impossible to remove. If you tighten it a wee bit less, then it will begin to loosen when you attempt to turn the filter to adjust the polarity because the resistance between the threaded ring and the polarizing circle is fairly stiff. It feels like the filter itself is made of plastic, so you can expect some haze and color from it and I would avoid cleaning it vigorously because it will probably scratch easily. All in all, I rated it 3 because it's just so-so; about what you'd expect for the money, really. It will have to do until I can justify getting a quality replacement.

I really like these headphones. Sound quality is quite good, and no more issue with AirPods falling out of my ears while exercising/gardening or ear pain when lying down with buds in. Yay! Also, these are great at keeping my ears warm during morning walks in cool weather.

The bluetooth is quite efficient, even at a distance. It kept overriding a phone call when I was outside and many yards away from the headband which was left inside sitting on a counter. I finally had to turn off my bluetooth to carry on the conversation without interruption.

Unfortunately, there are two downsides:

1) The stretchy fabric is difficult to move out of the way to access the charging port.

2) When paired with glasses, the headband puts too much pressure on the "temple tips' causing sizable discomfort behind the ears.

Yet to be determined: Laundering. There are clear instructions with pics on removing the electronics before laundering. The wires are quite small however, and I'm a bit concerned I might break something in the process. Not wanting to experiment unneccessarily, I'm opting to wait until the headband really needs cleaning before I attempt this. If all goes well, I'll come back and up the rating. But for now, I don't feel comfortable giving this more than 3 stars.

Bottom line: I DO like this headband, and will use it a lot. But I would not recommend it for those who wear glasses.

It seems to have everything you need, all kinds of options for connection which is nice. The bar looks good, you can tell by handling it that it's not the best quality but I was looking forward to hearing it, it has to be better than the tinny sound of my small tv. The instructions are terrible and only show the connections no other information. I hooked this up and nothing. I took the wires and plug out and tried again -nothing. I hate wasting my time. Maybe it's me but it's not working.

Almost made it three months before totally pooping out on me yesterday. I work out a lot and sweat quite a bit so I go through earbuds constantly. However, this particular brand supposedly had a good reputation for active people so my hopes were high. But these too have failed me. Oh well. Having the app being able to control the sound was a very cool and different feature. The hear through feature was annoying & when I was at the gym I always had to put music in full blast so I couldn't hear people talking around me. Won't ever try this brand ever again but maybe these would work for a less active person.

This is an interesting device as a scientific experiment, but not a very good quality speaker. It is interesting as a novelty, but if you care about the quality of sound in your music, I would not recommend it.

I have the same problem that another reviewer has.  It does not work with my Samsung Galaxy S8+ phone.  Guess it only works on Samsung Note products.  I will give it a neutral review since I can't use it to test it.  The picture does come across beautifully, but no sound comes across.  Make sure you have an MHL capable device.

The boombox radio works well for both AM and FM, cassette player works fine. Can be powered with batteries. Pretty loud and clear for the size of the unit.

Cons: The unit is super light and cheap feeling, creeks and cracks if you grab it too hard buttons also feel very flimsy. The volume knob has a huge dead spot in the beginning and then all of a sudden you get super sensitive control.

I can only recommend this if your looking for a small and stationary unit, I would not recommend this as a portable unit I feel if this got hit hard or dropped it would break.

This is one of those products that praise needs to be qualified with “for the price.” So, for the price, these are not bad at all. The sound quality is decent, as is the comfort – both are better than you would expect for the $20 price point. Where the price point really rears its head is build quality. These feel and look like $20 (or less) headphones.

The sound quality emphasizes bass response but still retains a decent amount of clarity to the mid and upper ranges. Again, for the price, the sound quality is better than expected. Sound isolation was decent as well.

Ear comfort is quite good, with ear cushions that are soft and pliable. Comfort is not as good on the headband since it has essentially no padding. Even so, I can able to wear these for a good hour and not find them tiresome or irritating.

These are hard wired headphones and come with a M/M 3.5 mm cord. I wanted to use a longer (and better quality) cord but had a little trouble doing so, since the input jack on the earcup is recessed. The hole was not large enough to allow my cord (which has a larger surround than the included jack) to fit. A little work with a Dremel and the problem was solved. Since the size of the recessed hole is fine for the included cord I won’t detract from the rating for that. Just wanted to mention it in case others wanted to use it with a longer or different style cord.

What does factor into the rating is the build quality. This feels and looks really cheap. The plastic is of so-so quality; the hinges are creaky and lack smooth articulation; the ear cup adjustments are similarly creaky. This is a head set that will not stand up to much punishment without falling apart.

These look and feel like $20 (or less) headphones; they sound like $40 ones. I’d rate sound quality and comfort as 4 stars; built quality as 2 stars. Overall rating of 3 stars. Worth getting if you want a better sounding set of headphones without breaking $20 but don’t mind the less than ideal build quality.
[Sample provided for review]

This is one of the quietest laptop coolers I’ve come across. It truly is whisper quiet even when all the fans are going on high speed. Excellent when it comes to sound level.

It is also excellent with regard to size. It offers an ample size work surface (roughly 15 inches wide by 10 inches deep) and has a flip up ledge to hold the laptop in place. The top of the pad is a metal mesh that is pretty sturdy. That’s an important feature not only for the look and feel, but also that the perforated metal will greatly speed heat dispersion.

You can control the number of fans and the speed of the fans. There are three settings for fan selection (inner two only; outer four only; or all six) and four settings for fan speed. Lots of choices for customizing the output.

The fans are powered by the laptop’s USB port. You can also power the fans by using a powerbank or anything else that has a USB power output.

The bad news is the build quality. The frame and prop stand are very lightweight plastic. This will not stand up to any measure of rough handling. When I was first using it I accidentally bumped it when moving my laptop. It wasn’t a horribly bad bump, but it caused one of the fans to pop out of its holder. I was able to seat it back in after taking the frame apart, but this is not the stand to get if you’re even somewhat rough on your gear.

The other annoyance was the bright red indicator that shows the fan setting and speed. Even when the fans are off, it has a bright red line through it. Very annoying – had to resort to some tape to cover it up since the red was so bright. It would have been much better if it had a more subtle indicator (perhaps some type of small pinpoint LED) or the ability to turn the display off.

The fans also have lights, but they are a soft blue light that surrounds them and looks rather nice.

While this has some pluses, the negatives bring my rating to average (3 stars). It’s worth a look, but it’s not an outstanding product.
[Sample provided for review]

There's a lot to like about this monitor, but also some clear drawbacks. Let's start with the good news.

In typical HP fashion it comes very well packaged to survive pretty much any measure of rough handling in transit. There's a "quick start" guide that is taped to the front of the monitor that walks you through the setup (which is very straightforward). There's also an excellent user guide in PDF on the included disk.

The overall design is very attractive. It's very slim, lightweight and easy to position. I'm using it with the included table stand since my wall-mount options can't handle a monitor this large (it does come with a metal plate with VESA-compatible holes should you want to use it with a mount).

I used this on both a PC and as a video monitor hooked up through my AV receiver. For both situations I used the HDMI interface.

The sound quality is very good compared with the typical built-in speaker. It lacks bass "punch" but is quite acceptable.

Now for the so-so news: picture quality. It's good, but not "wow" good. Picture quality was somewhat drab looking, lacking crispness and contrast despite spending a lot of time tweaking the video quality with the many options available. It becomes worse when viewed off center (although it does have a decent viewing angle).

It comes with a remote which could be very handy for switching inputs, tweaking the picture, adjusting the sound, etc. I say it "could be" since the remote it comes with is horrible. It's small, which is good, but all the buttons are flush mount and have black on black lettering. It is very, very hard to see which button is which even in bright light. Forget about finding the right button in dim light. Truly horrible design work.

While there are pluses, and it is hitting an attractive price point, I can't see this being worthy of anything more than a little above average (3.5 star) rating. It's a decent, but not exceptional monitor (with a total design failure of a remote). Worth considering if you are looking for a large monitor without breaking the bank, and have moderate expectations as to video quality.

This is a workable, but not outstanding way to record phone calls. It only works with a corded phone. You plug the handset cord into the recorder dock, then plug the dock into the phone. It runs on either 2 AAA batteries or via a 5v adapter that plugs into the dock. The adapter is NOT included.

While it’s simple and easy to install, it’s not so simple to actually use. The screen is small and hard to read, and the buttons are tiny. Navigating (or even seeing) the on screen menus is tough.

You can pick from different recording options including recording speed (long play, regular and high quality), auto record or manual record. Some of the options are easy to select, such as record speed. Others, such as the timer function (e.g., setting it to record at a specific time) are cumbersome to set up.

The voice quality when recording on the dock in HQ mode is decent. Nothing spectacular, but workable. The device will store 2 hours on HQ mode, 5.5 hours in SP mode and 14 hours in LP mode. You can organize files into folders, delete files and protect files from the device itself without having to connect to a PC.

You can also use this as a regular digital recorder by detaching it from the dock. It has an internal mic that has limited pickup capabilities. It’s very unimpressive when used as a regular digital recorder – there are far better choices out there.

Playback can be via the device itself, with pause, FF and reverse functionality. You can also transfer the file to a PC using the USB connector on the dock. It includes software that must be used to transfer files. That’s the weakest part of the package by far – the software looks and works like it was programmed 20 years ago. It works, but it’s not at all intuitive or capable compared with even the most basic audio management program currently available.

I got this on an auction site for about $17 and, for that price, it’s OK. I only use it to record calls in manual mode, and play back the recording using the device so I don’t have to deal with the PC interface. For me that makes it worth the cost. However, if you have more demanding needs or want to transfer and work with files on a PC, give this a pass. There are too many limitations and problems to make it a worthwhile tool.

Summary: The Matchstick address what is for me the biggest shortfall of the Fire: sound quality. The docking system provides MUCH better sound than the built-in speakers, and bundles that with some useful features. However, these pluses are countered by a remote with limited functionality and a balky on/off switch.

Main review: I was getting really frustrated trying to find a docking system for my Fire. I'd see all these great systems but they were only for the iPod, iPhone or iPad. I have been using an Altec Lansing iM227 Orbit portable speaker, but that didn't provide the functionality I wanted So, I was really looking forward to trying out the Matchstick when I was offered a system by the manufacturer to review.

This is a docking station for the Fire that provides dual speakers. The dock rotates so you can use the Fire in portrait or landscape mode. It charges the Fire when it is docked.

There's a lot to like about this. The overall design is nice. Nothing fancy, with lines that blend well with the clean design of the Fire. Unfortunately, the speakers are covered in a rather cheap feeling fabric. I like that it's a simple black-on-black color scheme, but better quality cloth would have been nice.

The power cord has a manageable "wall wart" on the end that is not too bad to deal with. The power cord could have been a bit longer - it's about 4.5 feet, which can be a problem if you want to use this on a shelf.

The dock charges the Fire while it is in place, but you can also run the Matchstick off of a battery. Battery power is a nice touch since it allows for portability. The catch is that you have to buy the battery separately -- it is a proprietary design. While I don't begrudge anyone from making a profit, it would have been nice if you could use standard size rechargeable batteries such as Eneloops. A battery pack was not included in my review model, so I can't speak to the battery capabilities.

The Fire slides into the dock and connects with the Matchstick for power and audio. There is a button on the Matchstick that allows you to turn the Fire on and off. It's a simple plastic peg that presses against the Fire's power button. I like the simplicity of the approach, but the execution could have been better. The peg is a wee bit too short (or perhaps just misaligned) so that you have to press REALLY hard to get it to turn the Fire on or off. Most times I found it easier to pop the Fire out the doc and press the power button myself. VERY annoying!

I was really looking forward to the remote since I often use the Fire at my desk, and it would be great to be able to control the Fire without touching it since it's out of easy reach. But, I found that the remote was too basic to be of much help.

On the plus side the remote is small -- about 1/4 thick and about 1.5 by 3.5 inches. The buttons allow for bass up/down, treble up/down, volume, mute and power. You can also use it to reset the bass/treble to "normal" and change input source (more on that later).

What is sorely missing is a track skip and a pause. So, the remote turns out to have very little use since I have to touch the screen to pause, change tracks, etc. Since the remote does not take the place of those key needs, you end up wondering why it's there at all. After a short while I stopped using it and just touched the screen or used the volume controls on the docking station.

The speakers perform very well at "soft-normal" levels (such as watching a movie at your desk at work), and are quite respectable at "loud-normal" volume (e.g., loud enough to make it difficult to converse with someone next to you, but not so loud that you can't hear the phone ring). It's better suited to reproducing dialog than music.

Excellent bass considering that it uses two 3-inch full-range speakers, but it gets boomy quickly at loud volumes. The spec's say 16 watts but this guy does not like to get pushed much when it comes to volume. It will get real ugly real quick.

But that's OK. The speakers are not designed to be audiophile quality or provide for room-filling sound for a large party. They are meant to produce better sound than what you get out of the Fire, and it does that admirably. Will your 16 year old son call them "wimpy"? Probably.

Still, they are a VAST improvement over the internal speakers and are much better than any of the single-speaker options I've tried (such as the Altec Lansing, the iHome and others). They won't compare at all to the quality of sound from some of the better multimedia speakers in the $70+ range (such as the GigaWorks T20 or T40), but that's the price you pay to gain the convenience of a dock.

There is an aux port on the back of the Matchstick that you can use to plug in a MP3 player (or anything else that will work with a 3.5 inch plug). Very nice feature since I have some music on various devices that I have not moved to the Fire. They also include a M/M 3.5 inch cable. Works well, although the port is hard to access. You'll find it easier to leave the M/M cable attached.

In summary, there are some clear strengths to this. It would be a 5-star product if it were priced in the $60 range, but at the $100'ish point some of the misses (especially the power button) are not acceptable. 3.5 stars, rounded down to 3 since the power button is such an annoying flaw.

Overall, these are a generally OK pair of headphones. While the sound quality won't please an audiophile, it is more than acceptable for general use. I found them to be better suited for movie watching rather than music listening since the bass and upper range are rather muted. Decent quality midrange.

It scores pretty high with regard to comfort. Lightweight, easy to adjust, and nicely cushioned.

I was not impressed with the noise cancellation feature. Yes, it does cut down on some background noise when the cancellation feature is engaged (simple switch on the earpiece turns it on and off; it runs on a AAA battery). But, the sound isolation is actually less than I get with a quality pair of properly-fitted ear buds. I could easily hear ambient sounds with the headphones on.

The track skipping feature does not work with the Fire. The manufacturer does not claim it would, so no stars are detracted for that. I mention it only in case Fire owners are thinking about using that feature. Other than that, it works perfectly with the Fire - made it much more enjoyable to watch videos than using the internal speakers.

I'll give this 3 stars. It offers OK sound quality and decent comfort, but it's billed as having noise cancellation, and that feature is not well implemented.

There's several things that I really like about this MP3 player, with the sound quality being top of the list. Great sound, even with the included ear buds (which are, as you would expect at this price point, pretty low-end). I swapped them out with a better quality paid of buds, and the sound is just fantastic.

I also like the overall size of the player. While there is always a trade-off between size and ease of use (e.g., finding/seeing the controls) the small size makes it much easier to use when working out. Construction quality also seems pretty good - feels more solid than I expected it would be.

However, all these good points are marred by a poor user interface. Getting music onto the player is not difficult, but arranging it when it is there is much more difficult than it should be. The controls are also very "touchy" - sometimes they worked; sometimes not. Hitting them accidentally was a common occurrence as well. The expansion capability is also hit and miss - sometimes it read the card, other times I had to do a re-set. I know the cards are OK since I use them in other MP3 players without a problem. Very glitchy.

If the usability issues were solved this would be a great MP3 player. As it now stands it's a great sounding unit when it works, but the cursing you go through to get it to work (and continue to work) drowns out the sound.

This is basically a souped-up surge protector. It's compact - measures about 3.5 wide, 8.5 long (10" including the mounting tabs) and about 1.5" deep. It comes with a variety of mounting options including velcro and an aluminum plate so you can stash it behind a wall-mounted flat screen and keep the cord jungle to a minimum. For most wall mounts it should work well, but it may be too thick for some of the ultra slim LCD TVs that are now available.

I elected to use it on the floor rather than try to wrestle a 90+ pound plasma off the wall. The included cords are beefy and well-made, but very short. It worked out OK for me since the outlet is right there, but given the price, I would think a longer cord should be included. It seems that the cords are mainly designed for those who want to stash the unit behind the TV.

There are coax attachments on the side to protect against surges/spikes transmitted via coax.

According to the manufacturer this not only offers surge protection but also filters out electrical noise so as to improve the picture and sound. That point is debatable. I didn't notice any difference in the picture with or without this. However, others in the house said they did see a slight improvement. Is that real or imaginary? Can't say for sure since the only way to truly test it is to have two of the same TVs running the same inputs, with one protected with the Panamax and the other not protected. I don't have the ability to run that test, so the only statement I can make regarding picture improvement is "maybe."

The build quality at first glance seems decent, but the unit I received had something rattling on the inside, like a small loose screw or perhaps a remnant of plastic. Not what I was expecting given the price of this unit. I would be hard pressed to recommend this over a standard, good quality surge protector that, while a bit more bulky, offers more outlets and a longer cord at a much lower price point.

While I like the compact size, the rattling makes me concerned about the long-term reliability of the unit. That, plus the short cord and only 2 outlets makes me rate this at only 2.5 stars (rounded up to 3).

These are decent headphones for anyone who doesn't need amazing sound quality and just wants a decent pair of headphones lying around. Stylistically, they look really nice. Comfort wise, I love the padding that they have on the ear part, I just wish the ear part was a little larger. I have smallish ears and these sit right on top of them. When wearing them for long periods of time, they tend to make my ears start hurting. I would prefer over ear headphones as opposed to on ear headphones. The band adjusts nicely to accommodate a variety of size heads. Sound quality isn't the best, but for just plugging in to watch an episode of a tv show on netflix or something like that, they are fine. I wouldn't recommend them for someone who is really into music and wants to use them for that purpose.

I was unable to use this product. I wanted to use these speakers on either side of my tv to enhance my movie watching experience, but when I opened the box and took everything out, I discovered that there are no wires included to attach them to your receiver. It would have been nice if that information was included somewhere in the description. I can't comment on the sound quality, for obvious reasons, but the speakers themselves are very nice looking and seem to made of great quality. They are extremely large and heavy though, so make sure you check out the size and weight information before purchasing.

I love this headset but it's also very annoying because of a few certain aspects. First off, the sound quality is great! When speaking on the phone I call hear very well and I've been told that my voice it clear as well. My issue are that the earbuds tend to loosen up and fall out every few minutes. The other issue is that the controls are on the ear bud itself, so while on phone calls, I've hung on so many people while trying to reinsert the earbuds or adjust so that they don't fall out. It's gotta to be so annoying and I hate that because the battery life and sound quality are great but I'm so tired of mistakenly hanging up and having to call back and apologize for my earbuds hanging up because I lightly glazed my finger on top of them.

I couldn't get the microphone to work (light was green) so I had to watch about 4 "how to get your microphone to work on windows 10" tutorials on Youtube until one of them actually worked.  I was finally able to test the microphone and could see the sound bar going up and down as I spoke louder and softer into it.  However, no matter  how many tutorials I watched, I could never hear myself through my headset to actually hear the sound quality of the microphone.  So, I don't know if I sound wonderful, super tinny or somewhere in between.  I'll keep working with it but at this point I have to give it a rest for a while.  The little pamphlet included with the microphone is absolutely useless and doesn't offer any troubleshooting.

I definitely prefer to use Bluetooth earbuds any day over wired, but sometimes it can't be helped.  Such as times when my Bluetooth earbuds weren't charged.  The sound of these is o.k. but not what you'd be getting from a high end pair.  I teach classical guitar so my acid test for any earbud is playing that and seeing how it sounds.  I'm doing it now and the trebles come through o.k. but the bass is pretty weak.  These will be good to keep a pair in my car or purse for those times when my Bluetooths won't work for whatever reasons.  The volume doesn't work so it has to be adjusted on the device they're plugged into.  They come with extra earbud covers and they feel fine in my female ears the way they are.  I don't know what these cost as of this review but I wouldn't want to pay more than $15.00 for them.
